title: Python
blurb: The foundation everything else is built on — syntax through advanced features.

lessons.title: Aptech Beginner 1 — Python environment, execution & foundations
lessons.explanation: Before syntax becomes useful, you need a reliable workflow: know which Python version is running, how a .py file is executed, how the command line and editor fit together, how environment variables affect programs, and how help() and dir() let you inspect unfamiliar objects.
objectives: Understand and apply Python environment & foundations in Python.
Explain how Python versions changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Python versions with installation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
examples:
import sys, keyword
name = "Ahmed"
print(sys.version_info.major)
print(type(name))
print(keyword.iskeyword("class"))

student_name = "Ahmed"
MAX_RETRIES = 3
print(student_name, MAX_RETRIES)

text = "python"
print([name for name in dir(text) if name.startswith("is")][:6])

import os
mode = os.environ.get("APP_MODE", "development")
print(mode)
print(str.upper.__doc__.splitlines()[0])
commonMistakes: Treating variable names as fixed-type boxes.
lessons.explain: Before syntax becomes useful, you need a reliable workflow: know which Python version is running, how a .py file is executed, how the command line and editor fit together, how environment variables affect programs, and how help() and dir() let you inspect unfamiliar objects.

lessons.title: Variables & types
lessons.explain: A variable is a name bound to a value. Python is dynamically typed — you don't declare the type, it's inferred.
lessons.example:
age = 21
name = "Ahmed"
print(f"{name} is {age}")
objectives: Bind values to names and recognize Python's core built-in types
Use valid, descriptive Python names and explain dynamic name binding
Explain how dynamic typing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect dynamic typing with f-strings and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Assuming a variable's type is fixed once assigned -- Python lets the same name later be rebound to a completely different type.
lessons.explanation: A variable is a name bound to a value. Python is dynamically typed — you don't declare the type, it's inferred.

lessons.title: Basic syntax, strings, formatting & conversion
objectives: Format, slice, join, and convert strings
Read basic Python syntax and safely convert user input
Explain how f-string changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect f-string with f" and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Python uses indentation to define blocks and # for comments. Strings are immutable sequences.
examples:
# A comment explains intent
course = "Python"
hours = 20
print(course, hours)

text = "Python Programming"
print(text.upper())
print(text[:6])
print(text[-11:])

name = "Ahmed"
score = 92
print("{} scored {}".format(name, score))

raw = "21"
age = int(raw)
print(age + 1)
print(float(age))

name = "Ahmed"  # imagine this came from input()
print("Welcome,", name)

name = 'Ada'
print(f"{name} is great")     # Ada is great
s = 'hello'
print(s[1:4])                  # 'ell'
print(', '.join(['a','b','c'])) # 'a, b, c'
print(int("5") + 3)            # 8
commonMistakes: Forgetting a slice's end index is exclusive (s[1:4] gives 3 characters, not 4), or trying to add a string and number directly without converting first.
lessons.careerRelevance: f-strings, slicing, and explicit conversion are used constantly in real formatting and parsing code.

lessons.title: Conditionals, boolean logic & operators
lessons.explain: Conditionals choose which code runs. if/elif/else combines comparisons with boolean logic.
objectives: Write clear if/elif/else branches
Combine comparisons with boolean logic
Recognize when bitwise operators are appropriate
commonMistakes: Writing a while loop whose condition never becomes false, causing an infinite loop.

lessons.title: Loops in depth: for, while, break, continue & enumerate
objectives: Choose between for and while loops
Control loops safely with break and continue
Use enumerate() instead of a manual index when appropriate
lessons.explanation: Loops repeat work. A for loop is best for iterating through a sequence or range; a while loop is useful when repetition depends on a changing condition.
examples:
attempts = 3
while attempts > 0:
    print("attempts left:", attempts)
    attempts -= 1
print("done")

total = 0
for value in [2, 4, 6]:
    total += value
print(total)
commonMistakes: Using a while loop whose condition never becomes false (forgetting to update the loop variable), causing an infinite loop.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly choosing and controlling loops, and using enumerate(), signals real day-to-day Python fluency.
lessons.explain: Loops repeat work. A for loop is best for iterating through a sequence or range; a while loop is useful when repetition depends on a changing condition.

lessons.title: Lists, tuples, sets & sorting
objectives: Choose between lists, tuples, and sets
Build and transform collections
Sort without confusing in-place and returned results
lessons.explanation: Python's core collections serve different jobs. Lists are ordered and mutable, tuples are ordered and immutable, and sets store unique values with fast membership checks.
examples:
names = ['Zara', 'Ali', 'Mona']
print(sorted(names))
print(names)  # original list is unchanged

tags = {'python', 'git', 'python'}
print(tags)
coords = (25.2, 55.3)
print(coords[0])

nums = [1,2,3]
print(len(nums))       # 3
nums.append(4)         # nums is now [1,2,3,4]
doubled = [x*2 for x in range(3)]  # [0,2,4]
commonMistakes: Confusing a list comprehension's iteration order — [x*2 for x in range(3)] iterates 0,1,2, giving [0,2,4], not starting from 1.
lessons.careerRelevance: List comprehensions are idiomatic Python — real codebases and interviews both expect comfort reading and writing them.
lessons.explain: Python's core collections serve different jobs. Lists are ordered and mutable, tuples are ordered and immutable, and sets store unique values with fast membership checks.

lessons.title: Mutability, identity & copying
objectives: Explain mutation and aliasing
Distinguish equality from identity
Choose shallow or deep copying intentionally
lessons.explanation: Lists and dictionaries are mutable, while strings and tuples are immutable. == compares values; is compares object identity.
examples:
import copy
original = {'items': [['A'], ['B']]}
shallow = copy.copy(original)
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)
original['items'][0].append('changed')
print(shallow['items'][0])  # shares nested list
print(deep['items'][0])     # independent

a = [1,2,3]
b = a          # b refers to the SAME list object
b.append(4)
print(a)        # [1,2,3,4] -- a changed too

t = (1,2,3)     # tuple: immutable

print(type(5/2))   # <class 'float'> -- / always gives a float
print(type(5//2))  # <class 'int'> -- // (floor division) gives an int when both inputs are ints
commonMistakes: Assuming `b = a` creates an independent copy of a mutable object — it doesn't; both names point to the same list.
lessons.careerRelevance: This distinction directly explains a whole category of confusing bugs involving shared, unexpectedly-mutated data.
lessons.explain: Lists and dictionaries are mutable, while strings and tuples are immutable. == compares values; is compares object identity.

lessons.title: Dictionaries: creation & membership
objectives: Create and update dictionaries
Check or retrieve optional keys safely
Use a dictionary for lookup/counting tasks
lessons.explanation: A dictionary maps unique keys to values. Use key in d when you only need to test existence and d.get(key, default) when a missing key should produce a fallback.
examples:
d = dict()          # {}
d['name'] = 'Ada'
print('name' in d)   # True
print('age' in d)    # False -- no error raised
commonMistakes: Accessing a missing key directly (d['age']) instead of checking with `in` or using .get() first — this raises a KeyError.
lessons.careerRelevance: Safe key-checking is a small habit that prevents a very common runtime crash in real programs.
lessons.explain: A dictionary maps unique keys to values. Use key in d when you only need to test existence and d.get(key, default) when a missing key should produce a fallback.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.explain: Functions package one responsibility behind a name. Parameters receive inputs and return sends a reusable value back to the caller.
objectives: Define reusable functions
Use parameters and return values
Explain the difference between returning and printing
commonMistakes: Expecting a variable assigned inside a function to be visible outside it, without an explicit return.
lessons.explanation: Functions package one responsibility behind a name. Parameters receive inputs and return sends a reusable value back to the caller.
examples:
def area(width, height):
    """Return rectangle area."""
    return width * height

print(area(4, 3))
print(area.__doc__)

lessons.title: Function arguments in depth
objectives: Design flexible function signatures
Use *args and **kwargs appropriately
Avoid mutable default argument bugs
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: recursion.
lessons.explanation: Function signatures describe how callers provide data. Default arguments make parameters optional, keyword arguments improve readability, *args gathers extra positional arguments, **kwargs gathers extra named arguments, and docstrings document the contract.
examples:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}"

print(greet("Ahmed"))
print(greet(name="Ahmed", greeting="Welcome"))

def report(scores, *tags, **meta):
    print(sum(scores) / len(scores))
    print(tags)
    print(meta)

report([80,90,100], "DSA", level="beginner")
commonMistakes: Using a mutable default argument like def f(x=[]) — the same list object is reused across calls that don't pass x.
lessons.careerRelevance: Flexible function signatures (*args/**kwargs) are common in real library code you'll write and read. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: Function signatures describe how callers provide data. Default arguments make parameters optional, keyword arguments improve readability, *args gathers extra positional arguments, **kwargs gathers extra named arguments, and docstrings document the contract.

lessons.title: Variable scope & None
objectives: Predict which binding a name refers to
Use None to represent an absent result
Explain how local scope changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect local scope with enclosing scope and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Scope determines where a name can be resolved. Function-local names normally stay inside the function; enclosing and global scopes are searched when a name is not local.
examples:
def f():
    x = 5
    return x
print(f())     # 5
# print(x)     # NameError -- x doesn't exist out here
result = None  # explicitly 'no value yet'
commonMistakes: Expecting a variable assigned inside a function to be accessible outside it without being returned — it isn't, by default.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding scope prevents a very common category of 'variable not defined' confusion.
lessons.explain: Scope determines where a name can be resolved. Function-local names normally stay inside the function; enclosing and global scopes are searched when a name is not local.
lessons.example:

    x = 5
    return x
print(f())     # 5
# print(x)     # NameError -- x doesn't exist out here
result = None  # explicitly 'no value yet'

lessons.title: First-class functions, lambda & closures
objectives: Pass functions as values
Use lambda for small expressions
Explain how a closure remembers enclosing state
lessons.explanation: Python functions are first-class objects: they can be stored, passed to other functions, and returned. A lambda is a compact anonymous function for a small expression.
lessons.explain: Python functions are first-class objects: they can be stored, passed to other functions, and returned. A lambda is a compact anonymous function for a small expression.
examples:
records = [('A', 3), ('B', 1), ('C', 2)]
print(sorted(records, key=lambda item: item[1]))
commonMistakes: Using lambda for multi-step logic makes code harder to read; use a named function when the behavior needs explanation or multiple statements.

lessons.title: Aptech Beginner 6 — Modules & the standard library
lessons.explanation: Modules organize reusable Python code. You can import your own files or standard-library modules, inspect available names with dir(), and choose clear import styles so dependencies stay readable.
objectives: Organize code into modules and use common standard-library modules confidently.
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: virtual environments (venv), dependency isolation.
Explain how modules changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect modules with import and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
examples:
import math
print(math.sqrt(81))
print(math.pi)

import sys
print(sys.version_info.major)
print(len(sys.argv))

from math import ceil, floor
print(ceil(3.2), floor(3.8))

import time
start = time.perf_counter()
sum(range(10000))
print(time.perf_counter() - start)

import math
public_names = [name for name in dir(math) if not name.startswith('_')]
print(public_names[:8])
commonMistakes: Naming your own file math.py or time.py can shadow the standard-library module you intended to import.
lessons.explain: Modules organize reusable Python code. You can import your own files or standard-library modules, inspect available names with dir(), and choose clear import styles so dependencies stay readable.

lessons.title: Exceptions, raise & custom errors
objectives: Catch expected exceptions narrowly
Use else/finally correctly
Raise and define a simple custom exception
lessons.explanation: Exceptions represent runtime failures that normal control flow cannot complete. Catch only errors you can handle meaningfully, use else for work that depends on the try block succeeding, finally for cleanup that must run, and raise when your own function must reject invalid input.
examples:
resource = 'open'
try:
    print('using resource')
finally:
    resource = 'closed'
print(resource)
commonMistakes: Catching every possible exception with a bare `except:` instead of the specific one expected — this can hide real, unrelated bugs.
lessons.careerRelevance: Graceful error handling separates a robust program from one that crashes on the first bad input.
lessons.explain: Exceptions represent runtime failures that normal control flow cannot complete. Catch only errors you can handle meaningfully, use else for work that depends on the try block succeeding, finally for cleanup that must run, and raise when your own function must reject invalid input.

lessons.title: Files, directories & safe serialization
objectives: Read and write files safely
Work with paths and directories using pathlib
Explain why pickle must not load untrusted data
lessons.explanation: Use with open(..) so files close reliably even if an error occurs. Choose read/write/append modes deliberately, use pathlib for paths and directory operations, and handle expected I/O failures.
examples:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('notes.txt')
p.write_text('First note\nSecond note', encoding='utf-8')
with p.open(encoding='utf-8') as f:
    contents = f.read()
print(contents)
p.unlink()

from io import StringIO
stream = StringIO()
stream.write('hello')
stream.seek(0)
print(stream.read())

from pathlib import Path
p = Path('example.txt')
p.write_text('alpha\nbeta', encoding='utf-8')
print(p.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
p.unlink()

from pathlib import Path
p = Path('.')
print(p.exists(), p.is_dir())

import pickle
data = {'scores': [10, 20]}
blob = pickle.dumps(data)
print(pickle.loads(blob))
commonMistakes: Opening a file without `with` (or a matching close()) — the file can remain open longer than intended.
lessons.careerRelevance: Safe file handling is a baseline expectation in any real, non-toy Python script.
lessons.explain: Use with open(..) so files close reliably even if an error occurs. Choose read/write/append modes deliberately, use pathlib for paths and directory operations, and handle expected I/O failures.
lessons.example:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('notes.txt')
p.write_text('First note\nSecond note', encoding='utf-8')
with p.open(encoding='utf-8') as f:
    contents = f.read()
print(contents)
p.unlink()

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 1 — Classes, objects & special methods
lessons.explain: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance built from it. __init__ runs at creation; self refers to the specific object.
objectives: Define a class and create instances from it
Explain how class changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect class with __init__ and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Forgetting `self` as the first parameter of an instance method, or confusing the class (blueprint) with an object (instance).

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 2 — Encapsulation & valid state
objectives: Bundle data and behavior together, and control access to internal state
Explain how encapsulation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect encapsulation with internal state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Encapsulation means bundling data (attributes) and the methods that operate on it inside one class, while controlling what's exposed to the outside. A leading underscore (_balance) is Python's convention signaling 'internal, don't touch directly,' even though it's not strictly enforced.
commonMistakes: Exposing internal attributes directly and letting external code modify them freely, bypassing any validation the class's own methods would apply.
lessons.careerRelevance: Encapsulation is one of the four pillars of OOP and directly prevents a whole category of 'object got into an invalid state' bugs.
lessons.explain: Encapsulation means bundling data (attributes) and the methods that operate on it inside one class, while controlling what's exposed to the outside. A leading underscore (_balance) is Python's convention signaling 'internal, don't touch directly,' even though it's not strictly enforced.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 3 — Abstraction
objectives: Expose only what's necessary, hiding implementation detail
Explain how abstraction changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect abstraction with abstract class and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Abstraction means exposing a simple interface while hiding the complex implementation behind it. When you call .sort() on a list, you don't need to know which sorting algorithm runs underneath -- that detail is abstracted away.
commonMistakes: Exposing every internal implementation detail through the public interface, forcing users of a class to understand its internals just to use it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Abstraction is what lets large codebases stay usable -- you can use a well-designed class without reading its internals.
lessons.explain: Abstraction means exposing a simple interface while hiding the complex implementation behind it. When you call .sort() on a list, you don't need to know which sorting algorithm runs underneath -- that detail is abstracted away.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 4 — Inheritance & super()
lessons.explain: A subclass reuses a parent's code and overrides what differs. super() calls the parent's version.
objectives: Reuse and extend a parent class's behavior in a subclass
Explain how inheritance changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect inheritance with super() and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Overriding a method entirely when you meant to extend it -- forgetting to call super() loses the parent's behavior.
lessons.explanation: A subclass reuses a parent's code and overrides what differs. super() calls the parent's version.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 5 — Polymorphism & duck typing
lessons.explain: Same method name, different behavior. Code calling .area() works for any shape without type checks.
lessons.example: total = sum(s.area() for s in shapes)
objectives: Write code that works with any object implementing the expected interface
Explain how polymorphism changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect polymorphism with duck typing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Adding explicit type-checks (isinstance chains) instead of relying on polymorphism to handle each type correctly.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 6 — Composition vs inheritance
objectives: Choose between 'is-a' inheritance and 'has-a' composition
Explain how composition changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect composition with is-a and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog IS-A Animal). Composition models a 'has-a' relationship (a Car HAS-A Engine) by holding an instance of another class as an attribute, rather than inheriting from it.
commonMistakes: Reaching for inheritance by default for every kind of code reuse, even when the relationship is really 'has-a' rather than 'is-a.'
lessons.careerRelevance: "Favor composition over inheritance" is one of the most repeated, real pieces of OOP design advice in professional codebases.
lessons.explain: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog IS-A Animal). Composition models a 'has-a' relationship (a Car HAS-A Engine) by holding an instance of another class as an attribute, rather than inheriting from it.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 7 — Interfaces & abstract base classes
objectives: Use abstract classes to enforce a shared contract across subclasses
Explain how abstract class changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect abstract class with contract and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An abstract class defines a contract -- methods every subclass MUST implement -- without providing (or only partially providing) the implementation itself. This lets you write code that works with ANY subclass polymorphically, as long as it fulfills the contract, without needing to know which specific subclass it is at runtime.
commonMistakes: Trying to instantiate an abstract class directly -- it's meant to be subclassed, not used on its own, and most languages enforce this.
lessons.careerRelevance: Programming against an interface/abstract contract, not a concrete class, is a foundational skill for writing flexible, testable code.
lessons.explain: An abstract class defines a contract -- methods every subclass MUST implement -- without providing (or only partially providing) the implementation itself. lessons.title: Aptech OOP 8 — SOLID principles
objectives: Recognize each of the five SOLID principles
Explain how SOLID changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SOLID with single responsibility and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: SOLID is five design principles: Single Responsibility (a class should have one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification -- add new behavior without editing existing code), Liskov Substitution (a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent class is expected, without breaking things).
examples:
# Single Responsibility violated: a class that both saves to a database
# AND formats a report AND sends an email -- three reasons to change

# Dependency Inversion: a function that depends on an abstract 'Notifier'
# interface, not a concrete 'EmailSender' class directly -- swap implementations freely
commonMistakes: Treating SOLID as rigid rules to follow everywhere regardless of context, rather than principles that guide judgment about trade-offs.
lessons.careerRelevance: SOLID vocabulary is widely used in real code reviews and design discussions -- recognizing the terms is expected of an experienced engineer.
lessons.explain: SOLID is five design principles: Single Responsibility (a class should have one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification -- add new behavior without editing existing code), Liskov Substitution (a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent class is expected, without breaking things).

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 9 — Design patterns & design judgment
objectives: Recognize a few common design patterns and what problem each solves
Explain how design pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect design pattern with singleton and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: A design pattern is a reusable, named solution to a recurring design problem. Singleton ensures a class has only one instance globally.
commonMistakes: Forcing a design pattern into code where it doesn't actually fit, just because it's a known pattern -- patterns solve specific problems, they're not universally 'better.'
lessons.careerRelevance: Recognizing common design patterns by name is a frequent, practical interview and code-review topic.

lessons.title: Aptech Beginner 10 — Regular expressions
lessons.explanation: Regular expressions describe text patterns. Learn literal and special characters, character classes, quantifiers, grouping, anchors, match objects, substitution, splitting, compilation and flags.
objectives: Build and explain practical regular expressions using Python re.
Explain how re changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect re with character classes and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
examples:
import re
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z]+', 'Python')))

import re
m = re.search(r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})', 'Date: 2026-08-13')
print(m.groups())

import re
print(re.sub(r'\s+', '-', 'data structures and algorithms'))

import re
print(re.split(r'[,;]\s*', 'python, dsa; sql'))

import re
pattern = re.compile(r'^python$', re.IGNORECASE)
print(bool(pattern.match('PYTHON')))
commonMistakes: A greedy quantifier can consume more text than you intended; tighten the pattern or use a non-greedy quantifier when appropriate.
lessons.explain: Regular expressions describe text patterns. Learn literal and special characters, character classes, quantifiers, grouping, anchors, match objects, substitution, splitting, compilation and flags.

lessons.title: Iterators & generators
objectives: Understand the iterator protocol and write memory-efficient generators with yield
Explain how iter() changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect iter() with next() and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: An iterator produces one value at a time instead of building every result up front. Python for-loops use the iterator protocol internally: iter(obj) gets an iterator and next(iterator) requests the next item until StopIteration.
commonMistakes: Converting a generator to list immediately removes its memory advantage.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

lessons.title: Python concurrency: threads, asyncio, locks & race conditions
objectives: Explain Python concurrency choices and protect shared state with a lock
Explain how threading changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect threading with asyncio and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Concurrency lets tasks make progress during the same time period. Threads are useful for many blocking I/O workloads, asyncio coordinates many I/O tasks cooperatively, and processes are often preferred for CPU-heavy parallel work.
lessons.example:
from threading import Lock

balance = 100
lock = Lock()

def withdraw(amount):
    global balance
    with lock:
        if balance >= amount:
            balance -= amount
            return True
        return False

print(withdraw(30), balance)
commonMistakes: Assuming the GIL makes shared-state logic automatically safe.

lessons.title: Decimal & money-safe arithmetic
objectives: Represent monetary values without binary floating-point surprises
Explain how Decimal changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Decimal with integer cents and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Financial code should avoid using binary floating point for money because values such as 0.1 cannot be represented exactly. Two common approaches are Decimal constructed from strings, or storing the smallest currency unit as an integer (for example cents).
lessons.example:
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

price = Decimal("19.99")
tax = Decimal("0.05")
total = (price * (Decimal("1") + tax)).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
print(total)

amount_cents = 1999
print(amount_cents + 501)
commonMistakes: Creating Decimal from a float, such as Decimal(0.1), imports the float approximation.

description: The foundation everything else is built on — syntax through advanced features.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is using a mutable default argument (like `def f(x=[])`) considered a common Python bug?
interviewPreparation.a: Default argument values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, not fresh on every call. A mutable default (like a list) is shared across every call that doesn't explicitly pass their own -- mutations from one call silently leak into the next. The fix is to default to None and create a new mutable object inside the function body when it's None.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between a list and a generator, and when would you choose one over the other?
interviewPreparation.a: A list holds all its items in memory at once; a generator produces items lazily, one at a time, computing each only when requested. For large or unbounded sequences, a generator avoids loading everything into memory -- at the cost of only being iterable once, unlike a list you can loop over repeatedly.

interviewPreparation.q: What is the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock), and why does it matter for concurrency in Python?
interviewPreparation.a: The GIL ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time in the standard CPython interpreter, which means CPU-bound multi-threaded code doesn't get real parallelism from threads alone. For CPU-bound work, multiprocessing (separate processes, each with its own GIL) is the common workaround; for I/O-bound work, threading still helps since the GIL is released during I/O waits.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you structure a Python project so it's genuinely maintainable and testable?
interviewPreparation.a: Separate concerns into modules with clear responsibilities, keep business logic separate from I/O/side effects so it's testable in isolation, use a proper package layout with a pyproject.toml, write tests that cover real behavior (not just imports succeeding), and avoid tightly coupling code to a specific execution context so it can be reused and tested independently.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between `is` and `==` in Python, and why does this trip people up?
interviewPreparation.a: `==` checks value equality (are these two things equal in content); `is` checks identity (are these the literal same object in memory). Small integers and short strings are sometimes cached by CPython and happen to pass an `is` check that wouldn't hold for larger values, which misleads people into thinking `is` checks values -- it doesn't, and using `is` for value comparison is a real, if subtle, bug.

lessons.title: Big-O notation
lessons.explain: Big-O describes how runtime or extra memory grows as input size n grows. Analyze the structure of the algorithm rather than memorizing labels: identify loops/recursion, account for nested work, and state meaningful best/average/worst cases when they differ.
lessons.example:
nums = [4, 1, 7, 3]
# O(n): one pass
steps = 0
for x in nums:
    steps += 1
print(steps)

# O(n^2): nested passes
pairs = 0
for i in nums:
    for j in nums:
        pairs += 1
print(pairs)
objectives: Describe how an algorithm's runtime or memory grows with input size
Understand and apply Algorithm analysis & Big-O in Python.
Explain how time complexity changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect time complexity with space complexity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Confusing the WORST-case complexity with typical or best-case performance -- Big-O usually describes the worst case.
examples:
nums = [4, 1, 7, 3]
# O(n): one pass
steps = 0
for x in nums:
    steps += 1
print(steps)

# O(n^2): nested passes
pairs = 0
for i in nums:
    for j in nums:
        pairs += 1
print(pairs)

nums = [10,20,30]
print(nums[0])

nums = [3,1,9,2]
best = nums[0]
for x in nums[1:]:
    if x > best: best = x
print(best)

n = 64
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n //= 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)

nums = [1,2,1,3,2]
seen = set(nums)
print(len(seen))
lessons.explanation: Big-O describes how runtime or extra memory grows as input size n grows. Analyze the structure of the algorithm rather than memorizing labels: identify loops/recursion, account for nested work, and state meaningful best/average/worst cases when they differ.

objectives: Understand and apply From C pointers to Python references in Python.

lessons.explanation: Linear search checks each element one at a time -- O(n), works on any list. Binary search repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the middle element -- O(log n), but REQUIRES the data to already be sorted.
examples:
def binary_search(sorted_arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(sorted_arr) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if sorted_arr[mid] == target: return mid
        elif sorted_arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

def binary_search(nums,target):
    low,high=0,len(nums)-1
    while low<=high:
        mid=(low+high)//2
        if nums[mid]==target: return mid
        if nums[mid]<target: low=mid+1
        else: high=mid-1
    return -1
print(binary_search([1,3,5,7,9],7))

def first_at_least(nums,target):
    low,high=0,len(nums)
    while low<high:
        mid=(low+high)//2
        if nums[mid]>=target: high=mid
        else: low=mid+1
    return low
print(first_at_least([1,3,5,7],4))

from bisect import bisect_left
nums=[1,3,5,7]
print(bisect_left(nums,5), bisect_left(nums,4))

low,high=0,len(nums)-1
while low<=high:
    mid=(low+high)//2
    print(low,mid,high,nums[mid])
    if nums[mid]==target: break
    if nums[mid]<target: low=mid+1
    else: high=mid-1

lessons.title: Sorting II — Merge sort & quicksort
lessons.explanation: Merge sort divides the input, recursively sorts each half, then merges sorted halves. Quicksort chooses a pivot and partitions values around it.
objectives: Understand and apply Merge sort & quicksort in Python.

examples:
def merge_sort(nums):
    if len(nums)<=1: return nums[:]
    mid=len(nums)//2; left=merge_sort(nums[:mid]); right=merge_sort(nums[mid:])
    out=[]; i=j=0
    while i<len(left) and j<len(right):
        if left[i]<=right[j]: out.append(left[i]); i+=1
        else: out.append(right[j]); j+=1
    return out+left[i:]+right[j:]
print(merge_sort([5,1,4,2]))

def quick_sort(nums):
    if len(nums)<=1: return nums[:]
    pivot=nums[len(nums)//2]
    left=[x for x in nums if x<pivot]
    middle=[x for x in nums if x==pivot]
    right=[x for x in nums if x>pivot]
    return quick_sort(left)+middle+quick_sort(right)
print(quick_sort([5,1,4,2,4]))

a=[1,4,7]; b=[2,3,8]; i=j=0; out=[]
while i<len(a) and j<len(b):
    if a[i]<=b[j]: out.append(a[i]); i+=1
    else: out.append(b[j]); j+=1
out += a[i:]+b[j:]
print(out)

nums=[7,2,5,3,5]; pivot=5
print([x for x in nums if x<pivot])
print([x for x in nums if x==pivot])
print([x for x in nums if x>pivot])

nums=[9,1,7,3,8,2]
print(sorted(nums))
commonMistakes: Saying quicksort is always O(n log n).

lessons.explain: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to smaller versions of itself. A correct recursive solution needs a base case and progress toward that base case.
lessons.example:
def subsets(nums):
    out = []
    path = []
    def dfs(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            out.append(path.copy())
            return
        dfs(i + 1)
        path.append(nums[i])
        dfs(i + 1)
        path.pop()
    dfs(0)
    return out

print(subsets([1, 2]))
commonMistakes: Forgetting to undo mutable state after exploring a branch, or writing recursion that does not move toward a base case.

description: The core of coding interviews — patterns that solve whole problem classes.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you approach a DSA problem you've never seen before in an interview?
interviewPreparation.a: Restate the problem in your own words to confirm understanding, work through a small concrete example by hand, identify a brute-force approach first even if inefficient, then look for patterns (sorted data suggests two pointers or binary search; 'have I seen this before' suggests a hash set) to optimize from there -- rather than guessing at a clever solution immediately.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose a hash map over a balanced tree for lookups?
interviewPreparation.a: A hash map gives O(1) average-case lookup/insert/delete, versus a tree's O(log n) -- so for pure lookup speed with no ordering requirement, a hash map usually wins. Choose a tree instead when you need ordered traversal, range queries, or predictable worst-case performance, since a hash map's worst case can degrade under pathological input.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you explain time complexity to someone non-technical?
interviewPreparation.a: It describes how the AMOUNT OF WORK grows as the input gets bigger, not the exact speed on one machine. An analogy: searching a phone book by flipping through every page (linear) versus jumping to the right section alphabetically (much faster growth) -- as the phone book gets 10x bigger, one approach's work barely changes while the other's grows a lot.

interviewPreparation.q: What's your process for debugging a solution that fails on some test cases but not others?
interviewPreparation.a: Look specifically at what's different about the failing cases -- empty input, a single element, duplicates, or boundary values are common culprits. Trace through the failing case by hand with the actual algorithm logic, rather than guessing, since the specific pattern of which cases fail usually points directly at the bug.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does knowing multiple approaches to the same problem matter, beyond just solving it once?
interviewPreparation.a: Different approaches have different trade-offs (time vs space, average vs worst case, simplicity vs performance), and real systems have different constraints. Being able to discuss why you'd choose one over another demonstrates genuine understanding of the trade-offs, not just memorization of one solution.

careerApplications: The core of coding interview rounds (OAs and live coding).

capstone.title: Benchmark and compare 3 approaches to the same problem
capstone.description: Pick a classic problem (e.g. finding duplicates, computing the k most frequent elements, or detecting a cycle in a graph). Implement it three different ways with genuinely different time/space trade-offs (e.g. a brute-force O(n^2) approach, a hash-based O(n) approach, and a sorting-based O(n log n) approach). Measure and compare their actual runtime on inputs of increasing size, and write up which approach you'd actually choose in a real system and why.
deliverables: Three distinct, correctly-working implementations of the same problem with different complexity classes
A benchmark script measuring actual runtime across at least 3 input sizes (e.g. 100, 10,000, 1,000,000 elements)
A short written comparison explaining WHY the runtimes diverge as input size grows, tied to each approach's real complexity
A clear recommendation: which approach you'd actually use in production, and under what conditions you'd choose differently (e.g. very small n, memory-constrained environment)
capstone.portfolioTips: This project demonstrates something a simple 'I solved LeetCode problem X' claim doesn't: that you understand WHY complexity matters in practice, not just how to state Big-O notation -- explicitly call this out in your README.

industryUsage.usage: Google's interview process is famously DSA-heavy, since efficient algorithms directly affect infrastructure operating at massive scale, where an O(n²) vs O(n log n) difference has real cost.
Uses graph algorithms (shortest-path variants) as a core part of real-time route matching and ETA calculation across its ride-hailing platform.
Relies heavily on graph data structures and traversal algorithms to power its connections network and 'people you may know' recommendations.

commonMistakes: A common mistake in Dynamic programming: states, transitions & optimization is copying syntax without tracing ownership, boundaries, state changes, or complexity.
lessons.careerRelevance: Useful for C++ engineering, systems work, competitive programming, and technical interviews; you should be able to explain both correctness and performance.

lessons.title: Understanding the problem first
objectives: Restate a problem and ask clarifying questions before solving it
Explain how restat changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect restat with clarifying questions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Restating a problem in your own words surfaces misunderstandings early, before any code is written to fix the wrong problem. Ambiguous problems often have several valid interpretations -- asking clarifying questions before diving in avoids solving the wrong one.
examples:
# before writing any code:
# 1. restate the problem in your own words
# 2. ask: what's the input range? what should happen on empty input?
# 3. define done: 'this function returns X for input Y, handling Z edge case'
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to code before confirming you understand what's actually being asked -- this can waste significant effort solving the wrong problem.
lessons.careerRelevance: Interviewers and real projects both reward this step -- it's often what's actually being evaluated.

lessons.title: Working examples & brute force first
objectives: Use small examples and a brute-force solution before optimizing
Explain how small example changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect small example with brute force and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Working through a small example by hand helps you discover the actual pattern needed, and gives you a test case to check against.
examples:
# example: 'find the longest streak of a repeated number'
# work a tiny example by hand first: [3,3,3,5,5] -> streak of 3, length 3
# THEN write the brute-force version: check every position, count how far the streak goes
commonMistakes: Trying to write the optimal, clever solution immediately -- without a working brute-force baseline, it's hard to tell if the 'clever' version is even correct.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is one of the most reliable, transferable problem-solving habits across any domain.

lessons.title: Breaking problems down
objectives: Split a problem into smaller subproblems, and reduce it to a known pattern
Explain how subproblems changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect subproblems with divide and conquer and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Breaking a problem into smaller subproblems makes each piece easier to reason about, implement, and test independently. Divide and conquer is a specific version of this: split into smaller, similar subproblems, solve each, then combine the results.
examples:
# instead of solving 'sort and deduplicate and count' all at once:
# subproblem 1: sort the list
# subproblem 2: remove duplicates from the sorted list
# subproblem 3: count what's left
# each piece is small enough to get right and test on its own
commonMistakes: Trying to solve a large, multi-part problem in one single pass instead of splitting it into independently checkable pieces.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the core strategy behind managing any large, complex real project, not just small exercises.

lessons.title: Constraints & complexity
objectives: Identify constraints and reason about time complexity
Explain how constraints changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect constraints with time complexity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Identifying constraints (input size, time limit, edge cases) before choosing an approach matters because they determine which approaches are even feasible -- an O(n^2) approach might be fine for small inputs but impractical for millions of records.
examples:
# a solution that's O(n^2) might run instantly on 100 items
# but take minutes or crash on 10 million items --
# always ask: what's the REAL expected input size?
commonMistakes: Ignoring stated or implied constraints (input size, time limits) when choosing an approach, only to discover the solution doesn't scale.
lessons.careerRelevance: Complexity reasoning is one of the most consistently tested skills in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Edge cases & verification
objectives: Test against edge cases and verify your solution by hand
Explain how edge cases changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect edge cases with verify and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An edge case is an input at the boundary of what's expected -- empty, zero, negative, maximum size, duplicates -- easy to overlook but a common source of real bugs. Testing your solution against these edge cases, not just the 'normal' example, catches algorithms that work for typical input but silently fail at boundaries.
examples:
# always explicitly test:
# - empty input: []
# - a single element: [5]
# - duplicates: [3,3,3]
# - the largest size you're told to expect
commonMistakes: Testing only the 'normal' example from the problem statement and skipping empty/boundary cases entirely.
lessons.careerRelevance: Edge-case awareness is one of the most commonly checked-for habits in code review and interviews alike.

lessons.title: Communication & problem-solving habits
objectives: Think aloud, use diagrams, and track what you've tried
Explain how thinking aloud changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect thinking aloud with explaining your reasoning and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Explaining your reasoning out loud (in an interview or otherwise) makes your thought process visible, which is often what's actually being evaluated, and can surface your own reasoning gaps. Drawing a diagram or table can reveal a problem's structure faster than abstract reasoning alone.
examples:
# habits that compound:
# - narrate your thinking, even the uncertain parts
# - sketch the data structure or flow on paper before coding
# - jot down 'tried X, didn't work because Y' so you don't repeat it
commonMistakes: Going completely silent while thinking, especially under observation (like an interview) -- this leaves the listener with no way to help or evaluate your approach.
lessons.careerRelevance: These communication habits are frequently what actually differentiates similarly-skilled candidates.

lessons.title: After solving: reflection & careful translation
objectives: Reflect after solving, and translate your idea into code carefully
Explain how translating changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect translating with reflection and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A common mistake is rushing the translation of a working idea into code, introducing small implementation bugs (off-by-one, wrong variable) that don't reflect any flaw in the actual idea. After solving, briefly reflecting on what made it hard, and whether a simpler or more general approach existed, compounds your skill over time.
examples:
# after solving:
# - did I translate the idea into code carefully, or rush it?
# - what made this hard? would I recognize this pattern faster next time?
# - could I explain this solution clearly to someone else right now?
commonMistakes: Treating a problem as 'done' the instant it passes, without any reflection on whether the approach was accidental or genuinely understood.
lessons.careerRelevance: This reflection habit is what turns solving many problems into actually getting better over time, rather than just repeating effort.

lessons.title: Heuristics & simplifying first
objectives: Use heuristics and simplified versions to make progress on hard problems
Explain how heuristic changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect heuristic with simplest and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A heuristic is a practical rule-of-thumb approach that often works well, even without a guarantee of the best possible result. Starting with the SIMPLEST possible version of a problem, even if the real problem is more complex, often reveals the core structure needed, which you then extend for the full complexity.
examples:
# simplify first: if the real problem is 'find the best route through 50 cities,'
# first solve it for 3 cities by hand -- the core idea often becomes clear at small scale
commonMistakes: Attempting the full, complex version of a problem directly instead of starting from a deliberately simplified version to find the core idea first.
lessons.careerRelevance: Heuristic thinking and simplification are practical tools used constantly in real-world problem solving, not just academic exercises.

What part of the process was skipped, and when should it have happened -- before or after writing the code?

description: Breaking hard problems into tractable pieces — compounds with everything.

interviewPreparation.q: Why do interviewers care about your process, not just whether you get the right answer?
interviewPreparation.a: A correct answer reached by luck or memorization doesn't predict how you'll handle a genuinely novel problem on the job, but a visible, repeatable process (clarify, brute-force first, analyze complexity, check edge cases) does -- it's evidence of a transferable skill, not a one-off result.

interviewPreparation.q: Why write a brute-force solution first, even when you suspect a better approach exists?
interviewPreparation.a: It gives you a working baseline you can verify correctness against, clarifies the problem in concrete terms, and often reveals the actual bottleneck that suggests the optimization -- jumping straight to a clever approach without this baseline risks solving the wrong problem efficiently, or getting stuck with nothing working at all.

interviewPreparation.q: How do stated constraints (like 'n up to 10 million') actually help you choose an approach?
interviewPreparation.a: They let you estimate what complexity is actually required before writing any code -- roughly, 10^8 operations is a reasonable ceiling for typical time limits, so n up to 10 million rules out O(n²) and points toward O(n log n) or better, which narrows down which approaches are even worth attempting.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the risk of only testing your solution on the 'normal' example given in the problem?
interviewPreparation.a: The given example is usually chosen to illustrate the normal case, not to stress-test your solution -- edge cases (empty input, a single element, all duplicates, boundary values) are exactly where solutions that look correct actually fail, and they're often not covered by the example at all.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you handle getting stuck on a problem during an interview?
interviewPreparation.a: Say what you're stuck on out loud rather than going silent, try simplifying to a smaller or more restricted version of the problem first, and revisit your assumptions -- being stuck and communicating about it clearly is a normal, expected part of the process, not a sign you should have already known the answer.

careerApplications: The actual skill coding interviews are trying to measure.

capstone.title: Work a genuinely unfamiliar problem end-to-end, under real interview conditions
capstone.description: Given a problem you haven't seen before (or a Company Path course capstone reframed as an unfamiliar prompt), work through the FULL process deliberately and visibly: restate it in your own words, ask the clarifying questions you'd actually need, write a brute-force solution first, identify the constraints that determine what complexity is actually required, find the edge cases before being surprised by them, and write up your reasoning as if explaining it to an interviewer. This capstone is about the process being visible and repeatable, not just arriving at a correct answer.
deliverables: A written restatement of the problem in your own words, including inputs, outputs, and at least one clarifying question you'd ask
A brute-force solution written first, before any optimization -- with a note on its actual complexity
A stated read of the problem's constraints and what complexity they actually require, justifying whether the brute-force solution is already good enough or needs improving
At least 3 edge cases identified and verified against, found BEFORE being surprised by a failure, not after
A written explanation of your final approach as if talking an interviewer through it, including why you didn't pick a different reasonable-sounding approach
capstone.portfolioTips: This is less a portfolio artifact and more a rehearsal -- the value is in practicing the visible, narrated process itself under real conditions, since that's exactly what a live technical interview is actually evaluating, not just whether the final code is correct.

industryUsage.usage: Technical interviews explicitly evaluate the problem-solving PROCESS -- clarifying questions, brute-force-first reasoning, complexity analysis -- not just whether a candidate eventually reaches a correct answer.
Interview guidance commonly emphasizes reading and using stated constraints to gauge required complexity before writing code, since this is a frequent, visible signal of engineering maturity.
Structured problem-solving communication (restating the problem, thinking aloud, checking edge cases) is explicitly part of what interviewers are trained to evaluate, separate from raw coding speed.

lessons.title: Classes & objects
lessons.explain: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance built from it. __init__ runs at creation; self refers to the specific object.
objectives: Define a class and create instances from it
Explain how class changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect class with __init__ and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Forgetting `self` as the first parameter of an instance method, or confusing the class (blueprint) with an object (instance).

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.explain: A subclass reuses a parent's code and overrides what differs. super() calls the parent's version.

commonMistakes: Overriding a method entirely when you meant to extend it -- forgetting to call super() loses the parent's behavior.

lessons.explain: Same method name, different behavior. Code calling .area() works for any shape without type checks.

lessons.title: Encapsulation
objectives: Bundle data and behavior together, and control access to internal state

lessons.explanation: Encapsulation means bundling data (attributes) and the methods that operate on it inside one class, while controlling what's exposed to the outside. interviewPreparation.q: What does it mean for a subclass to violate the Liskov Substitution Principle, with a concrete example?
interviewPreparation.a: It means code written to work correctly with the parent class breaks when given an instance of the subclass instead -- the classic example is Square inheriting from Rectangle: code that sets width and height independently and checks the resulting area works fine for any Rectangle, but breaks for Square, since setting one dimension unexpectedly changes the other.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose composition over inheritance?
interviewPreparation.a: When the relationship is genuinely 'has-a' rather than 'is-a' -- a Car has an Engine, but a Car isn't a kind of Engine. Composition also avoids the fragility of deep inheritance hierarchies, where a change to a base class can unpredictably affect many subclasses; favoring composition generally makes systems easier to change safely.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is forgetting super().__init__() in a subclass a real bug, not just a style issue?
interviewPreparation.a: Overriding __init__ completely replaces the parent's version unless you explicitly call super().__init__() -- so any state or setup the parent class was responsible for simply never happens, leading to missing attributes and confusing failures later when parent methods assume that setup occurred.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide if a class violates the Single Responsibility Principle?
interviewPreparation.a: Ask what would force this class to change -- if there are multiple unrelated reasons (a change to how data is saved, a change to report formatting, a change to email logic, all in the same class), it's doing too much. Each of those responsibilities changing independently is a sign they should be separate classes.

interviewPreparation.q: What's a practical benefit of designing to an interface or abstract base class, beyond satisfying a design principle?
interviewPreparation.a: It lets you swap implementations without changing the code that depends on them -- genuinely useful for testing (substituting a fake/mock implementation) and for extensibility (adding a new implementation later without touching existing code that already depends on the interface).

careerApplications: Interview topic on its own and the design basis of most production codebases.

capstone.title: Refactor a working-but-messy system into clean, SOLID-aligned design
capstone.description: Take a small system that technically works but has real design problems (a class doing too many unrelated things, inheritance used where composition would fit better, hardcoded dependencies that make testing hard) and refactor it applying SOLID principles deliberately -- not just because a checklist says to, but because you can explain what specific problem each change fixes. This capstone is about design judgment under a realistic 'this already works, don't break it' constraint, not designing a clean system from a blank page.
deliverables: A 'before' version with at least 2 genuine design problems (e.g. a class violating single responsibility, inheritance misused where composition fits better)
A refactored 'after' version, with a written explanation of exactly what problem each specific change fixes -- not just 'applied SOLID'
At least one interface or abstract base class enabling real polymorphic use (not just present for its own sake)
A test suite that still passes after refactoring, proving the refactor didn't silently change behavior
A short note on one thing you deliberately did NOT change, and why over-engineering it would have been worse than leaving it alone
capstone.portfolioTips: The 'before' and 'after' together, with a clear explanation of what each change actually fixes, is far more convincing than a clean greenfield design -- it's direct evidence you can improve real code under real constraints, which is most of what actual engineering work looks like.

industryUsage.usage: Java and Python style guides historically emphasize composition over inheritance and interface-driven design, reflecting exactly the kind of design judgment (not just syntax knowledge) this course builds.

SOLID principles and dependency inversion specifically underpin much of the design guidance in the .NET ecosystem, where testable, loosely-coupled class design is treated as a first-class engineering concern.
Maintaining large, long-lived codebases at scale makes design judgment (not reinventing every class from scratch, refactoring safely) a genuinely practical daily skill, not just an academic topic.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between merge and rebase, and when would you choose each?
interviewPreparation.a: Merge preserves exactly what happened, including a merge commit joining two branches -- honest history, but can get tangled with many contributors. Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing clean linear history, but rewrites commit hashes -- fine for your own not-yet-shared work, unsafe for branches others have already pulled.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is it dangerous to rebase and force-push a branch that others have already pulled?
interviewPreparation.a: Rebasing rewrites commit history -- the commits get new hashes. If someone else already pulled the old commits and built work on top of them, force-pushing the rebased branch effectively erases the history their work depends on, leaving them with confusing conflicts and duplicate-looking commits when they try to reconcile.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you clean up a messy sequence of commits (like several 'wip' commits) before opening a pull request?
interviewPreparation.a: Interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`) against your own not-yet-shared commits, squashing the messy intermediate commits into one or a few clean, well-described commits -- since these commits haven't been pushed/shared yet, rewriting them is completely safe.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you resolve a merge conflict in a shared file?
interviewPreparation.a: Open the conflicted file, look at the conflict markers showing both versions, decide (often with the other author) what the correct combined result should be, remove the markers, stage the resolved file, and complete the merge with a commit -- ideally with a message explaining the resolution, not just 'fix conflict.'

interviewPreparation.q: What makes a pull request description actually useful to a reviewer?
interviewPreparation.a: What changed and why, not just what -- the reasoning a reviewer would otherwise have to reconstruct by reading every diff line by line. A good description lets a reviewer approach the code with the right context before they've read a single line of it.

capstone.title: Manage a realistic collaborative Git workflow, cleanly and safely
capstone.description: Simulate a real team workflow on a repository: feature branches, a clean commit history achieved through interactive rebase (not just merge commits everywhere), a genuinely resolved merge conflict, and a pull request with a clear description. This capstone is about Git discipline under realistic collaborative conditions, not just knowing individual commands in isolation.
deliverables: A repository with a clean, readable commit history -- meaningful commit messages, no 'wip' or 'fix typo' commits left in via interactive rebase before merging
At least one feature branch rebased onto the latest main before merging, keeping history linear

A pull request with a clear description of what changed and why, as if a real reviewer needed to understand it without asking you
A written note on one situation where you would use merge instead of rebase, and why
capstone.portfolioTips: A repo with genuinely clean history and a well-written PR description is a small, quick thing for a reviewer to check -- and one of the fastest ways to signal you'd be easy to collaborate with on a real team, versus someone who's only used Git solo.

lessons.explanation: Linux files and directories form a hierarchical filesystem. `pwd` shows your current directory, `ls` lists its contents, and commands such as `cd`, `mkdir`, `cp`, `mv`, and `rm` let you navigate and manage files. cd ..

rm -r old_folder

lessons.explanation: A shell script is just a text file of commands you'd otherwise type one by one, run as a program -- the first line, `#!/bin/bash` (the shebang), tells the system which interpreter should run it. examples:
#!/bin/bash

FOLDER=$1
if [ -d "$FOLDER" ]; then
  tar -czf "${FOLDER}_$(date +%Y-%m-%d).tar.gz" "$FOLDER"
  echo "Backed up $FOLDER"
else
  echo "Error: $FOLDER not found" >&2
  exit 1
fi

lessons.explanation: SSH (Secure Shell) lets you log into and run commands on a remote machine over an encrypted connection -- `ssh user@host` opens a remote shell session, and SSH keys (a public/private key pair) let you authenticate without typing a password every time, which is both more convenient and more secure than password auth.
examples:
ssh ahmed@my-server.example.com          # open a remote shell session
scp local-file.txt ahmed@my-server:/home/ahmed/   # copy a file TO the server
scp ahmed@my-server:/var/log/app.log .            # copy a file FROM the server

curl https://api.example.com/health      # quick check: is this endpoint responding?
curl -X POST -d '{"key":"value"}' https://api.example.com/data
commonMistakes: Relying on password authentication for SSH instead of setting up key-based auth -- beyond being less convenient, password auth over SSH is a much more common target for automated brute-force.

description: The environment real engineering happens in.

interviewPreparation.q: A command works when you type it directly but fails when run from a script or cron job. What would you check?
interviewPreparation.a: Whether PATH is set up the same way in that context -- scripts and cron jobs often run with a much more limited PATH than your interactive shell, so a command that resolves fine when you type it can fail with 'command not found' in a script unless it's referenced with its full path or PATH is set explicitly.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is key-based SSH authentication preferred over password authentication?
interviewPreparation.a: It's both more convenient (no password prompt every connection) and more secure -- password authentication over SSH is a much more common target for automated brute-force attempts, while key-based auth requires possessing the actual private key, which is far harder to guess or brute-force.

interviewPreparation.q: What does a script's exit code communicate, and why does it matter beyond just 'did it crash'?
interviewPreparation.a: Exit code 0 means success, nonzero means failure -- and other scripts, CI pipelines, and tools rely on this to decide what to do next (like whether to proceed to the next step or stop). A script that always exits 0 even when something went wrong will silently let failures pass through undetected by anything checking its exit code.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you diagnose a 'command not found' error right after installing something with a package manager?
interviewPreparation.a: First confirm the package manager actually believes it's installed (its own query/list command), then check whether the installed binary's location is actually in PATH -- a genuinely failed install and a PATH problem look identical from the error message alone but need different fixes.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between curl and a full script for checking whether a service is healthy?
interviewPreparation.a: curl is fast for a one-off manual check -- hit an endpoint, see the response, done. A script is worth it when you need this repeated automatically, combined with other logic (alerting, logging, retries), or run on a schedule -- curl alone doesn't decide what to do with the result, a script does.

capstone.title: Automate a real task with a script, deployed and run on a remote server
capstone.description: Write a genuinely useful bash script (not a toy example) that automates something real -- log analysis, a backup routine, a health check -- then actually deploy and run it on a remote server you connect to over SSH, using a package manager to install anything it needs there. This capstone is about practical Linux fluency under real conditions: a script that only works on your machine, in your exact environment, isn't actually done.
deliverables: A bash script with real logic (variables, at least one conditional, at least one loop) solving an actual problem, not a 'hello world' demo
The script made executable and run successfully, with its exit code checked and used correctly (nonzero on failure)
SSH access set up to a remote server (key-based, not password), with the script copied over via scp and run there
Any dependency the script needs installed on the remote server via a package manager -- not assumed to already be present
A short written note on one thing that behaved differently on the remote server than locally, and how you diagnosed it
capstone.portfolioTips: The note about something that broke on the remote server and how you fixed it is the most convincing part -- it's concrete evidence you've actually operated on a real server, not just written a script that happens to run in one specific environment.

industryUsage.usage: Bash/shell scripting for everyday automation and SSH-based remote server work are baseline, constantly-used skills across nearly every backend and infrastructure role, not specialized knowledge.

Operating real Linux servers (via SSH, package management, and shell scripting for automation) underlies most of AWS's own infrastructure and is assumed fluency for engineers working close to production systems.
Given its scale, automating repetitive operational tasks with shell scripts (log analysis, health checks, backups) is routine, practical daily work, not an advanced or optional skill.

lessons.explain: SELECT picks columns; FROM names the table; WHERE filters rows; ORDER BY sorts. This is the backbone of every query.

Explain how WHERE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

LIMIT 5;

objectives: Explain primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL, and UNIQUE
Explain how primary key changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect primary key with foreign key and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: A primary key is a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table -- no two rows can share one. A foreign key links a row to a row in another table, enforcing that the reference actually exists.
commonMistakes: Adding a foreign key column without actually enforcing (or checking) that the referenced row exists -- this silently allows orphaned references.

lessons.title: Working with NULL
objectives: Compare against NULL correctly
Explain how NULL changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect NULL with IS NULL and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: NULL means 'no value,' and it doesn't equal anything -- not even another NULL. Comparing with = or != against NULL never matches, even for rows that ARE NULL; you must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL instead.
examples:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;      -- correct: finds active users
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL;        -- WRONG: matches nothing, ever
commonMistakes: Writing `column = NULL` or `column != NULL` -- these silently match zero rows, which is a very easy mistake to miss.

objectives: Distinguish INNER and LEFT JOIN, and avoid accidental cartesian products
Explain how INNER JOIN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect INNER JOIN with LEFT JOIN and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, with NULLs filling in for any unmatched right-table columns.
commonMistakes: Writing FROM a, b with no WHERE/ON condition linking them -- this produces a cartesian product, not the intended matched pairs.

lessons.title: GROUP BY & HAVING in depth
objectives: Aggregate data with GROUP BY and filter groups with HAVING
Explain how GROUP BY changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect GROUP BY with HAVING and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing the same value in a column into groups, letting you compute one aggregate (COUNT, SUM, AVG) per group. HAVING filters those GROUPS after aggregation -- it's evaluated later than WHERE, which is why HAVING can reference an aggregate like COUNT(*) but WHERE can't.
examples:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS num_items, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
commonMistakes: Using HAVING for a condition that doesn't need aggregation (it belongs in WHERE, which runs earlier and is usually more efficient).
lessons.careerRelevance: GROUP BY + HAVING is the core toolkit for any real reporting or analytics query.

objectives: Add, change, and remove rows safely
Explain how INSERT changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect INSERT with UPDATE and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: INSERT adds new rows. UPDATE changes existing rows (always pair it with a WHERE clause, or every row gets updated).
commonMistakes: Running UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause -- this affects every single row in the table, usually not what was intended.
lessons.careerRelevance: These are the most consequential SQL statements to get right, since mistakes here directly change real data.

lessons.title: Indexes & performance basics
objectives: Explain what an index does and its trade-offs
Explain how index changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect index with CREATE INDEX and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An index is a data structure that speeds up lookups on a column, similar to a book's index -- the database can jump directly to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. The trade-off: indexes use extra storage and slightly slow down writes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), since the index has to be updated too.
examples:
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
-- now WHERE email = '...' can use the index instead of scanning every row
commonMistakes: Adding an index to every column 'just in case' -- each index adds real write overhead, so they should target columns actually used often in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY.

objectives: Use LIKE for pattern matching and write a basic subquery
Explain how LIKE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: LIKE '%text%' matches any value containing 'text' anywhere -- % is a wildcard for any sequence of characters. A subquery is a query nested inside another, often used in a WHERE clause to filter against a dynamically computed set of values.
commonMistakes: Assuming LIKE 'smith%' and LIKE '%smith%' behave the same -- the % placement changes whether it matches the start, end, or anywhere in the text.
