lessons.title: Window Functions & CTEs
objectives: Use CTEs to structure complex queries and window functions to compute running totals and rankings without collapsing rows
Explain how CTE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CTE with common table expression and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A CTE (Common Table Expression, written with WITH) names a subquery so you can reference it like a temporary table, making a complex multi-step query readable instead of deeply nested.
examples:
WITH monthly_totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id, month
)
SELECT customer_id, month, total,
  SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month) AS running_total
FROM monthly_totals;
-- running_total accumulates per customer, resetting for each new customer,
-- while every row (one per customer per month) stays visible -- unlike GROUP BY,
-- which would have collapsed this into one row per customer
commonMistakes: Reaching for GROUP BY when what's actually needed is a running total or per-row ranking -- GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group, which loses the per-row detail a window function (SUM().
lessons.careerRelevance: Window functions and CTEs are the dividing line between basic SQL and the SQL fluency real data-facing interviews and dashboards actually require -- a very common interview and take-home assessment topic.

description: Query and shape data — SELECT through window functions.

interviewPreparation.q: Why might joining two tables and then summing a column give a wildly inflated result?
interviewPreparation.a: If the join has a one-to-many relationship (like orders to order_items), each row on the 'one' side gets duplicated once per matching row on the 'many' side -- summing a column from the 'one' side after that join adds the same value in multiple times. Aggregate the many-side table first (often with a CTE), or aggregate before joining, to avoid this.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between GROUP BY and a window function, and when would you need a window function specifically?
interviewPreparation.a: GROUP BY collapses rows into one output row per group, losing per-row detail. A window function (SUM()/RANK()/ROW_NUMBER() OVER ...) computes an aggregate or ranking across related rows WITHOUT collapsing them -- needed whenever you want the aggregate value AND the individual row detail together, like a running total shown alongside every original row.

interviewPreparation.q: Why use a CTE instead of a deeply nested subquery?
interviewPreparation.a: Readability and maintainability, mainly -- a CTE names each step of a multi-stage calculation so the query reads top-to-bottom like a sequence of steps, instead of nesting subqueries inside subqueries that are hard to trace. They're not usually faster, just clearer to write, read, and debug.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you check whether a slow query is actually using an index?
interviewPreparation.a: Run EXPLAIN (or the database's equivalent query-plan tool) and check whether it shows an index scan or a full table/sequential scan on the relevant table -- a full scan on a large table for a query that should be selective usually means the index either doesn't exist or doesn't match what the query actually filters or joins on.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does `WHERE column = NULL` never match any rows, even when the column genuinely contains NULLs?
interviewPreparation.a: NULL represents an unknown value, and SQL's three-valued logic means comparing anything to NULL with `=` returns unknown, not true -- even NULL = NULL is unknown, not true. Use `IS NULL` (or `IS NOT NULL`) specifically, which is designed to test for NULL correctly.

lessons.explanation: A database is software that stores data durably and lets many programs read/write it safely at once, with guarantees a plain file can't give you: concurrent access without corruption, crash recovery, and fast lookups even at huge scale.

# Without a DBMS: two processes writing to the same file

lessons.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table (often an auto-incrementing id). A foreign key is a column in one table that references a primary key in another, and the database ENFORCES that the referenced row must exist — this is called referential integrity.
commonMistakes: Deleting a parent row (a customer) while orders still reference it — most databases block this by default unless you explicitly cascade or nullify.

lessons.title: Indexes & how lookups get fast

lessons.title: NoSQL vs SQL: when to use which
objectives: Contrast document/key-value/relational models

Connect document store with key-value store and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: SQL databases enforce a fixed schema and strong relational integrity — great when your data has clear structure and relationships (orders, customers, inventory). NoSQL stores relax this: document stores (MongoDB) hold flexible JSON-like records; key-value stores (Redis, DynamoDB) trade query flexibility for extreme speed at massive scale.

# SQL: 'give me all orders over $50 for customers in Dubai, joined with product names'
# -> relational, needs joins and constraints -> SQL

# Key-value: 'get this user's session by session_id, sub-millisecond'
# -> no relationships, pure lookup speed -> Redis/DynamoDB
commonMistakes: Choosing NoSQL purely because it's trendy, then rebuilding joins and constraints in application code — usually a sign SQL was the right choice.

lessons.title: Transactions & ACID Properties
objectives: Explain why transactions exist and use commit/rollback to keep multi-step operations consistent
Explain how transaction changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect transaction with ACID and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: A transaction groups multiple database operations into one all-or-nothing unit -- either every operation in it succeeds and is committed, or if anything fails partway through, the whole thing rolls back as if none of it happened.
commonMistakes: Performing a multi-step operation (like a funds transfer) as separate, un-transacted writes -- if anything fails between the steps, the database is left in a genuinely inconsistent state.

lessons.title: Transaction isolation levels & anomalies
objectives: Explain dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, and what isolation levels trade off
Explain how Read Committed changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Read Committed with Repeatable Read and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Isolation controls how concurrent transactions can observe one another. Weak isolation improves concurrency but can expose anomalies; stronger isolation reduces anomalies at the cost of more coordination or retries.
lessons.example: Two transfers read the same balance of 100. If both independently decide that withdrawing 80 is allowed, a weakly coordinated implementation can overspend. A transaction must protect the invariant with appropriate locking, serializable behavior, or a conditional atomic update.
commonMistakes: Assuming ACID means every transaction automatically behaves as if it ran alone.

lessons.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking
objectives: Choose between optimistic version checks and pessimistic row locks for concurrent updates
Explain how SELECT FOR UPDATE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SELECT FOR UPDATE with optimistic locking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Pessimistic locking reserves rows before changing them, which is useful when conflicts are likely but can block other work. Optimistic locking lets work proceed and rejects an update if a version changed, which is useful when conflicts are rare.
lessons.example: Pessimistic pattern: BEGIN; SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (...) FOR UPDATE; validate both rows; UPDATE accounts ...; COMMIT. Optimistic pattern: UPDATE accounts SET balance=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?; verify exactly one row changed.
commonMistakes: Locking the same pair of rows in different orders in different code paths.

Explain how Redis changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Redis with cache-aside and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explain: Redis is often used as an in-memory cache because reads are fast and data structures are convenient. In cache-aside, the application reads the cache first, falls back to the database on a miss, then populates the cache.
lessons.example:
Read: cache GET key -> on miss read DB -> SET key with TTL.
Write: commit DB transaction first -> invalidate cache key.
If invalidation fails, retry it and keep TTL finite so stale data cannot live forever.
commonMistakes: Updating the cache first and then treating the database write as guaranteed.

lessons.title: B+ trees & LSM trees: how storage indexes work
objectives: Compare B+ tree and LSM-tree trade-offs for reads, writes, and storage layout

lessons.explain: B+ trees keep sorted keys in page-friendly tree nodes and are widely used for database indexes because they support point lookups and ordered range scans. LSM trees buffer writes and later merge sorted files through compaction, trading faster sequential writes for more complicated reads and background work.
lessons.example: B+ tree intuition: follow a small number of page pointers to a sorted leaf, then scan neighboring leaves for a range. LSM intuition: write to memory/log first, flush sorted runs, and compact runs in the background.
commonMistakes: Calling one structure universally faster.

interviewPreparation.q: Why do you need a database transaction for something like a funds transfer, instead of just two separate UPDATE statements?
interviewPreparation.a: Without a transaction, a crash or error between the two writes leaves the database in a genuinely inconsistent state -- money debited from one account with no corresponding credit -- and there's no way to know from the outside which steps actually completed. A transaction's atomicity guarantees both writes happen or neither does.

interviewPreparation.q: What does the 'I' in ACID (isolation) actually protect against?
interviewPreparation.a: Race conditions between concurrent transactions -- without isolation, two transactions reading and writing the same row can interleave in ways where each looks correct on its own, but the combined result is wrong (e.g. two withdrawals both reading the same starting balance before either commits, overdrawing an account that should have been prevented).

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide which columns to index on a large table?
interviewPreparation.a: Look at the actual query patterns hitting that table -- which columns appear in WHERE clauses, JOINs, or ORDER BY on the queries that are actually slow -- rather than indexing preemptively. An index on a rarely-queried column adds write overhead for no real benefit, while a genuinely hot query without the right index causes full table scans.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose NoSQL over a relational database for a given use case?
interviewPreparation.a: When the access pattern is simple key-based lookups with no need for joins or complex reporting, and schema flexibility matters more than strict consistency guarantees -- a session store or a shopping cart by session ID is a common example. For anything needing multi-table relationships, transactions across multiple records, or ad-hoc reporting, relational usually wins.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you diagnose a slow-running query in production?
interviewPreparation.a: Check whether it's actually using an index (via the database's query plan/EXPLAIN output) or falling back to a full table scan, and confirm the index that exists actually matches the columns the query filters or joins on -- a common real-world surprise is an index existing on the 'wrong' column relative to what's actually slow.

capstone.title: Design, index, and transact against a real data layer
capstone.description: Take the backend service and API you've already built (or a new one) and give it a real, production-minded data layer: a normalized schema with correct keys and constraints, indexes chosen from actual query patterns rather than guesswork, and at least one multi-step operation correctly wrapped in a transaction so it can't leave data in a half-finished state. This capstone is about the data layer specifically -- the discipline that makes a backend trustworthy under real, concurrent load, not just correct in a single-user demo.
deliverables: A normalized schema (justify your normal form choices) with correct primary/foreign keys and constraints
At least one index added specifically because of a real, stated query pattern -- not a guess -- with a before/after note on what it improved
At least one multi-step operation (e.g. a transfer, an order-plus-inventory-decrement) correctly wrapped in a transaction, with a written explanation of what would go wrong without it
A short note on one deliberate SQL vs NoSQL (or table design) trade-off you made and why
capstone.portfolioTips: The transaction requirement is the detail that separates 'I can write SQL' from 'I understand data integrity under real, concurrent, occasionally-failing conditions' -- make sure your written explanation of the failure mode you're preventing is concrete, not just a definition of ACID.

industryUsage.usage: Relies heavily on database transactions for payment processing, where a partially-completed money movement is not an acceptable failure mode under any circumstance.
Uses careful indexing and query-pattern-driven schema design at massive scale, where an unindexed query on a huge table can measurably affect real infrastructure cost and latency.
As a fintech, transaction correctness (ACID guarantees around account balances and transfers) is a first-order engineering requirement, not an optional nicety.

lessons.explanation: Once an API has real clients, changing it is no longer just an internal decision -- a breaking change (renaming or removing a field, changing a field's type, changing what a status code means) can crash every client that depends on the old shape, often with no warning.

# becomes
# /v1/users/42  ->  {"username": "asha"}   # same version, field renamed
# any client reading response['user_name'] now crashes or gets undefined -- no warning, no migration window

# CORRECT: introduce the change in a new version instead
# /v1/users/42  ->  {"user_name": "asha"}     # unchanged, old clients keep working
# /v2/users/42  ->  {"username": "asha"}      # new clients opt in when ready
# /v1/ is deprecated with a stated end-of-life date, giving clients time to migrate

interviewPreparation.q: How would you version an API to avoid breaking existing clients?
interviewPreparation.a: Either a URL-based version (/v1/, /v2/) or a version header, with old versions kept running until clients have time to migrate. The key discipline is never changing an existing version's contract in a breaking way -- new fields can usually be added safely, but renaming, removing, or changing the type of an existing field can't happen without a new version.

interviewPreparation.q: Why shouldn't an API return HTTP 200 for a failed request?
interviewPreparation.a: Clients, caches, monitoring, and retry logic all rely on the status code to know whether a request succeeded, not just the response body. Returning 200 for a failed login (for example) means anything downstream that checks status codes -- not just your one hand-written client -- silently treats a failure as a success.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you decide on a pagination strategy for an endpoint returning a large list?
interviewPreparation.a: Offset-based pagination (page/limit) is simple but can skip or repeat items if the underlying data changes between requests; cursor-based pagination is more complex to implement but stays correct under concurrent writes. For a feed that changes frequently, cursor-based is usually worth the extra complexity; for a mostly-static list, offset-based is often fine.

interviewPreparation.q: What would you consider when designing rate limiting for a public API?
interviewPreparation.a: What the limit actually protects against (abuse vs. genuine capacity), what a client sees when they hit it (a clear 429 with a Retry-After header, not a vague error), and whether different endpoints or client tiers need different limits -- a search endpoint and a webhook endpoint have very different real costs.

interviewPreparation.q: What makes API documentation actually useful to someone integrating against it, versus documentation that exists but isn't used?
interviewPreparation.a: Concrete request/response examples for every endpoint, not just a schema; clear documentation of error cases, not just the happy path; and staying accurate as the API changes, since documentation that lies is often worse than no documentation, because it costs someone real debugging time to discover it's wrong.

interviewPreparation.q: Walk me through what happens between a client sending a request and your server sending a response.
interviewPreparation.a: DNS resolves the domain, a TCP (or QUIC) connection is established, the server's web layer routes the request to the right handler, the handler validates input, does whatever business logic/DB work is needed, and constructs a response with the right status code and body, which travels back over the same connection.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide between session-based and token-based authentication for a new API?
interviewPreparation.a: Sessions are simpler and easy to revoke server-side, but require server-side state, which complicates horizontal scaling. Tokens (like JWTs) are stateless and scale more easily across multiple servers, but revocation before expiry is harder. For a single web app, sessions are often simpler; for a mobile app plus web app plus third-party integrations, tokens usually win.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you prevent SQL injection in practice, not just in theory?
interviewPreparation.a: Use parameterized queries or an ORM that parameterizes for you by default -- never build SQL by concatenating user input into a string. Input validation is a second layer of defense, but parameterization is the actual fix, since validation alone is easy to miss an edge case on.

interviewPreparation.q: A service that was fine at low traffic is now timing out under load. How do you start diagnosing it?
interviewPreparation.a: Check whether it's the app layer or the database first -- slow query logs and connection pool exhaustion are common root causes that look like 'the app is slow' from the outside. Only after ruling out the database would I look at app-level concurrency or a genuinely undersized server.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the N+1 query problem, and how do you fix it?
interviewPreparation.a: It's when fetching a list of N items triggers one query for the list plus N additional queries, one per item, instead of a single batched query -- often invisible until traffic or data volume grows. Fixed with a join, a single IN-clause query, or an ORM's eager-loading feature instead of querying inside a loop.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you approach testing a backend service beyond manually hitting endpoints with a tool like Postman?
interviewPreparation.a: Automated tests for the core business logic and endpoints, including edge cases (invalid input, unauthorized access, empty results) -- not just the happy path. Manual testing is fine for exploration, but it doesn't scale and doesn't catch regressions when you change something later.

lessons.title: A systematic method: reproduce, hypothesize, test
objectives: Apply a repeatable method instead of guessing

lessons.explanation: First, reproduce the bug reliably -- without a reliable reproduction, you can't confirm whether any change actually fixed it. Then form a specific hypothesis about the cause, and test it directly (often by printing a value you 'assumed' was correct).
examples:
# 1. Reproduce: run the exact steps that trigger the bug, confirm it happens every time
# 2. Hypothesize: 'I think X is None when it shouldn't be'
# 3. Test: print(X) right before the failing line to check
# 4. Bisection: if unsure WHERE it broke, check a point halfway through the logic, narrow from there
commonMistakes: Trying a fix before reliably reproducing the bug -- you can't tell if the fix actually worked or the bug just didn't happen to trigger that time.
lessons.careerRelevance: This method scales from tiny scripts to huge, unfamiliar codebases -- it's genuinely how experienced engineers debug.

lessons.explanation: An off-by-one error is a loop or index boundary that's one step too far or too short (range(n) vs range(n+1)). An 'undefined' or 'not defined' error means the code references a name that was never assigned in the reachable scope.
examples:
for i in range(len(items) + 1):   # off-by-one: this goes one index too far

interviewPreparation.q: Walk me through how you'd approach debugging an issue you've never seen before, live, in an interview.
interviewPreparation.a: Read the error/symptom carefully first rather than jumping to a fix, form a specific hypothesis about the cause, test that hypothesis directly (not just stare at the code), and narrow down systematically -- reproduce, hypothesize, test, repeat. Narrating this process out loud is itself part of what's being evaluated, not just arriving at the right answer.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you approach a bug that only happens intermittently, not every time?
interviewPreparation.a: Look for what's different between the runs that fail and the ones that succeed -- shared state between test runs, timing/race conditions, or an environment difference are common causes. Trying to reproduce it in isolation, and changing one variable at a time, is more productive than re-running the same thing hoping to catch it by luck.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the value of a minimal reproducible example when debugging?
interviewPreparation.a: Shrinking a large failing case down to the smallest version that still fails removes noise and irrelevant variables, making the actual cause much easier to spot -- and if you need to ask someone else for help, a minimal repro respects their time and gets you a faster, more useful answer than a 500-line dump.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is verifying a fix actually works more than just 'the error went away'?
interviewPreparation.a: The error going away could mean the actual bug is fixed, or it could mean the failure condition just isn't being hit anymore for an unrelated reason -- confirming the fix means re-running the exact scenario that originally failed and checking the expected output specifically, not just that nothing currently looks broken.

interviewPreparation.q: What would a good postmortem for a production bug include, beyond 'here's the fix'?
interviewPreparation.a: The actual root cause (not just the symptom), why it wasn't caught earlier (a missing test, an untested edge case, insufficient logging), and a concrete follow-up action that would catch this class of bug faster next time -- the goal is preventing a repeat, not just resolving this one instance.

careerApplications: Evaluated implicitly in every technical interview and every day on the job.

Document the investigation as you'd write it up for a teammate, not just the final fix.

Use of either a real debugger (breakpoints/stepping) or a bisection approach to narrow down the cause, not just print-statement guessing
A verified fix -- proof the specific failure no longer reproduces, not just 'it seems fixed'

lessons.title: Unit testing
lessons.explain: A unit test checks one small piece of behavior in isolation. Arrange inputs, act (call the function), assert the expected output.
objectives: Write a unit test that isolates and verifies one piece of behavior
Explain how assert changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect assert with arrange-act-assert and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Writing a test with no real assertion -- the code runs but nothing is actually verified as correct.

lessons.title: Integration tests
objectives: Distinguish integration tests from unit tests
Explain how integration test changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect integration test with component boundaries and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An integration test checks that multiple components work correctly TOGETHER -- a database, an API, and business logic interacting -- unlike a unit test, which isolates one function or class alone. Integration tests catch bugs that only appear at the boundaries between components, but they're typically slower and more complex to set up than unit tests.
examples:
# unit test: does calculate_total() return the right number, in isolation?
# integration test: does the checkout FLOW correctly save an order to the
# real database AND correctly call the payment API AND return a receipt?
commonMistakes: Only writing unit tests and assuming components will work correctly together -- integration bugs specifically happen AT the boundaries unit tests can't see.
lessons.careerRelevance: A healthy test suite needs both unit and integration tests -- they catch different categories of bugs.

lessons.title: Mocking
objectives: Use mocks to isolate a unit test from its real dependencies
Explain how mock changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect mock with mocking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A mock is a fake stand-in for a real dependency (a database, an external API) used in a unit test, so the test doesn't actually hit the network or a real database -- making it fast, reliable, and independent of the real service being available.
examples:
from unittest.mock import Mock
payment_api = Mock()
payment_api.charge.return_value = {'status': 'success'}

result = process_order(payment_api)
payment_api.charge.assert_called_once()
commonMistakes: Over-mocking so heavily that the test no longer verifies anything meaningful about the real code's behavior.
lessons.careerRelevance: Mocking is essential for fast, reliable unit tests that don't depend on real external services being up.

lessons.title: Test coverage
objectives: Interpret test coverage and its limits
Explain how coverage changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect coverage with test coverage and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Test coverage measures what percentage of your code actually runs during your test suite. High coverage is a useful signal, but it's not the same as correctness -- a line can be 'covered' by a test that runs it without actually checking the output is right.
examples:
# a test that calls a function but asserts nothing meaningful:
def test_process():
    process(data)   # covered! but nothing was actually verified

# a real test:
def test_process():
    result = process(data)
    assert result == expected
commonMistakes: Chasing a high coverage percentage as the goal itself, rather than writing tests that actually verify correct behavior.
lessons.careerRelevance: Coverage is a useful metric to track, but experienced engineers know not to over-trust it alone.

lessons.title: Regression testing
objectives: Explain why regression tests matter as code changes over time
Explain how regression changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect regression with regression test and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A regression is when a previously-working feature breaks due to a later change. A regression test suite -- run before every change ships -- catches this by re-verifying old behavior still holds, not just the new feature being added.
examples:
# every time you fix a bug, add a test for that EXACT bug --
# this becomes a permanent regression test, ensuring it never
# silently comes back in a future change
commonMistakes: Fixing a bug without adding a test for it -- the same bug can silently resurface in a later change with nothing to catch it.
lessons.careerRelevance: A strong regression suite is exactly what lets a real, growing codebase change safely over its lifetime.

lessons.title: Test-Driven Development: an overview
objectives: Describe the TDD cycle: red, green, refactor
Explain how TDD changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect TDD with red green refactor and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Test-Driven Development writes a failing test FIRST (red), then writes the minimum code to make it pass (green), then improves the code's structure without changing its behavior (refactor) -- repeating this cycle for each small piece of functionality.
examples:
# 1. RED: write a test for behavior that doesn't exist yet -- it fails
def test_add():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5   # fails -- add() doesn't exist yet

# 2. GREEN: write just enough code to pass
def add(a, b): return a + b

# 3. REFACTOR: clean up if needed, tests still pass
commonMistakes: Writing all the implementation code first and adding tests as an afterthought -- this is the opposite of TDD's intended discipline.
lessons.careerRelevance: TDD is a real, actively-practiced methodology at many companies, even if not used universally.

lessons.title: Debugging failing tests
objectives: Apply a systematic workflow when a test fails
Explain how fail changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect fail with actual vs expected and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: When a test fails, first check whether the TEST or the CODE is wrong -- a failing test isn't automatically proof of a code bug; the test itself might have a mistaken expectation. Read the actual vs expected output the test reports, and reproduce the failure in isolation before trying a fix.
examples:
# test failure workflow:
# 1. read the actual vs expected values in the failure output
# 2. is the code wrong, or is the test's expectation wrong?
# 3. reproduce in isolation (run just that one test)
# 4. fix, then re-run the FULL suite to check nothing else broke
commonMistakes: Assuming a failing test always means the code is broken, without first checking whether the test's own expectation is actually correct.
lessons.careerRelevance: This systematic workflow prevents wasted time chasing the wrong cause when a test suite reports a failure.

lessons.title: The testing pyramid & strategy
objectives: Balance unit, integration, and end-to-end tests
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: browser end-to-end automation (Playwright/Selenium).

Connect testing pyramid with end-to-end test and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: The testing pyramid suggests having MANY fast unit tests, FEWER integration tests, and VERY FEW slow, expensive end-to-end tests (which drive the whole system through its real UI/API).

# many unit tests (fast, cheap, isolated)
# fewer integration tests (slower, test real components together)

commonMistakes: Building an 'inverted pyramid' -- mostly slow end-to-end tests and few unit tests -- which makes the whole suite slow and fragile.

lessons.title: Writing clear tests & assertions
objectives: Write test names and assertions that are genuinely useful when they fail
Explain how test naming changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect test naming with clear assertions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A good test name describes the SPECIFIC behavior being verified (test_returns_error_for_negative_input), not a vague name like test1. A good assertion checks the actual expected outcome specifically, so when it fails, the failure message tells you exactly what went wrong without needing to dig through the test's internals.
commonMistakes: Writing vague test names and assertions that don't clearly state what's actually being verified, making failures hard to diagnose later.
lessons.careerRelevance: Clear, well-named tests double as living documentation of what the code is actually supposed to do.

lessons.title: TDD in practice: Red → Green → Refactor
objectives: Apply TDD to business logic by writing a failing behavior test before implementation
Explain how Red-Green-Refactor changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Red-Green-Refactor with edge cases and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explain: Test-driven development is a short feedback loop: write one small test that fails for the right reason, implement the simplest behavior that makes it pass, then refactor while keeping all tests green. Good TDD tests describe observable behavior rather than private implementation details.
lessons.example: Example sequence for transfer(): 1) test a normal transfer; 2) make it pass; 3) test insufficient funds; 4) make it pass; 5) test same-account or invalid amount; 6) refactor shared validation while every test remains green.
commonMistakes: Writing the entire implementation first and then calling the later test suite TDD.

lessons.title: Testing concurrent & transactional behavior
objectives: Design tests for race conditions, transaction boundaries, retries, and invariants
Explain how concurrency test changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explain: Concurrency tests should check invariants rather than depend on lucky timing. For a money-transfer service, useful invariants include total money remaining constant, no negative balance when forbidden, and a failed transaction leaving both accounts unchanged.
lessons.example: Instead of sleep-based tests, coordinate two workers so both reach a known point before releasing them. After both finish, assert the invariant on final balances and verify that retries do not double-apply the transfer.
commonMistakes: Using arbitrary sleep() calls and assuming a race happened.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between a unit test and an integration test, and when do you need both?
interviewPreparation.a: A unit test isolates one function or component, typically mocking its dependencies; an integration test exercises a real boundary between components (e.g. a function actually talking to a real or test database). You need both -- unit tests catch logic errors cheaply and fast, integration tests catch the failures that only show up when real pieces are wired together.

interviewPreparation.q: Why isn't a high coverage percentage the same as a good test suite?
interviewPreparation.a: Coverage only measures whether a line of code executed during tests, not whether anything meaningful was actually asserted about its behavior -- a test that calls a function with no assertions can show 100% coverage on that function while catching zero real bugs. Coverage is a useful signal for what's UNtested, not proof that what IS tested is well-tested.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide when to use a mock versus calling the real dependency in a test?
interviewPreparation.a: Mock dependencies that are slow, external, non-deterministic, or costly to call repeatedly (a payment API, an email service, real network calls) so unit tests stay fast and reliable; use the real thing (or a real integration test) when you specifically need to verify the actual integration works, not just your code's logic in isolation.

interviewPreparation.q: A test passes locally but fails in CI. How do you approach debugging that?
interviewPreparation.a: Suspect something the test doesn't fully control: shared state between tests, system time, test execution order, or an environment difference (a clean database in CI vs. leftover local state). Try to reproduce it by running just that test repeatedly and in isolation, rather than assuming it's a CI infrastructure problem before ruling out the test itself.

interviewPreparation.q: How does TDD (red-green-refactor) actually change how you design code, beyond just testing it?
interviewPreparation.a: Writing the failing test first forces you to think about the function's actual interface and expected behavior before implementation details, which tends to produce more testable, more decoupled code -- it's as much a design discipline as a testing one, which is why some teams use it even when they don't obsess over coverage numbers afterward.

capstone.title: Design and defend a real test strategy, not just a passing test suite
capstone.description: Take a nontrivial function or small module (from a previous course capstone, or new) and build out a genuinely layered test suite: real unit tests, at least one integration test at a real component boundary, deliberate use of mocks where a dependency shouldn't be hit directly, and a written test-strategy justification using the testing pyramid -- not just chasing a coverage percentage. This capstone is about test suite QUALITY and reasoning, the skill that separates 'tests exist' from 'these tests would actually catch a real regression.'
deliverables: A unit test suite covering real edge cases, not just the happy path (built test-first via TDD for at least one function)
At least one integration test exercising a real component boundary (e.g. a function plus the database or API it calls)

A coverage report plus a written note on one thing coverage percentage alone doesn't tell you (tying back to what 'meaningless coverage' actually means)
A short written test strategy citing the testing pyramid: what you tested at which layer, and why
capstone.portfolioTips: The written test-strategy justification is the differentiator here -- a reviewer skimming a repo full of green tests can't tell if you understand WHY the suite is shaped that way; a short, clear rationale proves you do.

lessons.title: How computer networks work
objectives: Explain what a network is and describe LAN, WAN, and topologies at a practical level
Explain how LAN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect LAN with WAN and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: A computer network is simply two or more devices connected so they can exchange data. A LAN (Local Area Network) connects devices in one physical location, like an office or home; a WAN (Wide Area Network) spans a much larger area, connecting multiple LANs together -- the internet is the largest WAN of all.
examples:
# practical scale, smallest to largest:
# your home Wi-Fi = a LAN
# your company's offices connected across cities = a WAN
# a company's internal-only network = an intranet
# the whole public internet = the largest WAN, built of countless smaller networks
commonMistakes: Assuming 'the internet' and 'a network' are different kinds of things -- the internet IS a network, specifically a massive WAN connecting countless smaller networks together.
lessons.careerRelevance: This vocabulary is assumed baseline in any backend or infrastructure conversation.

objectives: Distinguish the roles of the core physical network devices
Explain how modem changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: A modem converts your internet provider's signal (cable, fiber, DSL) into a format your network can use. A router connects separate networks together and directs traffic between them -- typically your home network to the wider internet.
examples:
# a typical home setup, stacked:
# modem (talks to your ISP) -> router (directs traffic, often also acts as a firewall)
# -> switch (built into most routers, connects wired devices) -> access point (built in too, for Wi-Fi)
commonMistakes: Using 'router' and 'switch' interchangeably -- a router connects DIFFERENT networks together, while a switch connects devices WITHIN the same network.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding what each device actually does is essential for diagnosing real connectivity problems, not just naming the boxes.

objectives: Describe both layered models and explain what encapsulation means
Explain how OSI model changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect OSI model with TCP/IP model and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The OSI model is a 7-layer conceptual framework for thinking about networking: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application -- from raw electrical signals up to the applications you actually use.
examples:
# encapsulation, simplified (sending an HTTP request):
# Application layer: your HTTP request data
# + Transport layer header (TCP: source/destination port)
# + Internet layer header (IP: source/destination IP address)
# + Link layer header (MAC: source/destination hardware address)
# -- each layer adds its own header before handing off to the layer below
commonMistakes: Trying to memorize OSI's 7 layers as if they're all equally used in practice -- real-world networking discussions center on the simpler 4-layer TCP/IP model far more often.
lessons.careerRelevance: Layered thinking is exactly how real network problems get diagnosed -- narrowing down WHICH layer is failing (is it DNS? TCP? the app itself?) is the core troubleshooting skill.

lessons.explanation: A MAC address is a hardware address burned into a network interface, used for delivery WITHIN a local network (the Link layer).
examples:
# MAC address: 3C:22:FB:4A:9B:1E -- identifies THIS specific network card, never changes
# Private IP: 192.168.1.42 -- only meaningful inside your home network
# Public IP: 203.0.113.5 -- how the outside internet actually reaches your network
commonMistakes: Assuming a device's IP address is permanent and unique like its MAC address -- private IPs are commonly reused across millions of different home networks, since they're never directly.
lessons.careerRelevance: Recognizing private vs public IP ranges instantly is a routine, practical skill in any backend or infrastructure debugging session.

lessons.title: Subnetting concepts (without the math)
objectives: Explain WHY networks are subnetted, conceptually, without doing subnet-mask arithmetic
Explain how subnetting changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect subnetting with subnet mask and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Subnetting divides one larger network into smaller, separate sub-networks -- this is a PURPOSE-driven decision, not a math exercise: it isolates traffic (a problem in one subnet doesn't flood the whole network), improves security (different subnets can have different firewall rules), and organizes devices logically (all servers in one subnet.
examples:
# conceptual example, no math needed:
# Subnet A (10.0.1.0/24): internal database servers -- no direct internet access
# Subnet B (10.0.2.0/24): public-facing web servers -- internet-accessible, isolated from the databases
# if Subnet B gets compromised, Subnet A isn't automatically exposed
commonMistakes: Thinking subnetting is purely an academic exercise in address math -- in real infrastructure, it's a deliberate security and organization decision.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding subnetting's PURPOSE (not the arithmetic) is what actually comes up when reviewing real infrastructure and security decisions.

lessons.explanation: A port is a number (0-65535) identifying a specific service or application on a device -- port 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH. A socket is the combination of an IP address AND a port, uniquely identifying one specific connection endpoint.
examples:
# socket = IP address + port, e.g. 192.168.1.10:443
# TCP: web browsing, file transfer, email -- correctness matters more than raw speed
# UDP: live video calls, online gaming, DNS lookups -- speed matters more than perfect delivery
commonMistakes: Assuming TCP is always the 'better' choice because it's reliable -- for real-time media, UDP's lower latency is usually the RIGHT trade-off, since a slightly-lost frame beats a frozen.
lessons.careerRelevance: Choosing TCP vs UDP for a given feature is a real, practical backend architecture decision, not just trivia.

lessons.title: The TCP handshake, packets, frames & segments
objectives: Trace the 3-way TCP handshake and distinguish packets, frames, and segments
Explain how 3-way handshake changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect 3-way handshake with SYN and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before any data flows over TCP, both sides perform a 3-way handshake: the client sends SYN (synchronize, 'let's connect'), the server responds SYN-ACK (acknowledging, and requesting its own synchronization), and the client replies ACK (confirming) -- only then is the connection ESTABLISHED and ready for real data.
examples:
# 3-way handshake:
# Client -> Server: SYN
# Server -> Client: SYN-ACK
# Client -> Server: ACK
# -- connection now ESTABLISHED, data can flow

# same data, different names by layer:
# Transport layer: segment (has a TCP header)
# Internet layer: packet (segment + IP header)
# Link layer: frame (packet + MAC header)
commonMistakes: Using 'packet' as a catch-all term for any unit of network data -- in precise usage, packet specifically refers to the Internet-layer unit, not the Transport-layer segment or Link-layer.
lessons.careerRelevance: Tracing a handshake (or knowing it never completed) is one of the first things checked when diagnosing a real connectivity failure.

lessons.explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (like example.com) into IP addresses computers actually use to route traffic -- often through a CHAIN of lookups (a CNAME pointing to another name, which finally resolves to an A record).
examples:
# DNS resolution can chain through multiple records:
# shop.example.com (CNAME) -> cdn.example.com (A) -> 93.184.216.34
# -- the final A record is what actually has an IP address

# ping uses ICMP echo request/reply to test reachability and measure latency
commonMistakes: Assuming DNS always resolves in one direct hop -- CNAME chains (a name pointing to another name) are common and add extra resolution steps before reaching the final IP.

lessons.explanation: HTTP is the application-layer protocol underlying almost all web traffic: a client sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body), the server processes it and sends back a response (status code, headers, body).
examples:
# HTTP request lifecycle:
# 1. DNS resolves the hostname to an IP
# 2. TCP handshake establishes a connection (TLS handshake too, for HTTPS)
# 3. Client sends the HTTP request
# 4. Server processes it, sends back a response
# 5. Connection closes or stays open for reuse (keep-alive)
commonMistakes: Thinking HTTPS is just 'HTTP but encrypted' with no other guarantee -- TLS also verifies the SERVER'S IDENTITY via its certificate, protecting against impersonation, not just eavesdropping.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every backend service handles this lifecycle -- understanding exactly where DNS, TCP, and TLS each fit is essential for diagnosing slow or failing requests.

lessons.explanation: Routing is the process of choosing the best path for a packet to travel across multiple networks toward its destination -- routers maintain routing tables and make this decision hop by hop, not knowing the whole path in advance.
examples:
# NAT in action:
# Device A (192.168.1.10) and Device B (192.168.1.11) both share public IP 203.0.113.5
# the router tracks: 'the request going out on port 51000 belongs to Device A'
# so when the response comes back, it's correctly routed to Device A, not Device B
commonMistakes: Assuming every device on a home network has its own unique address as far as the internet is concerned -- NAT means the OUTSIDE world only sees the router's single public IP.
lessons.careerRelevance: NAT explains a huge share of real-world 'why can't an external service reach my internal server directly' questions.

lessons.explanation: A firewall filters traffic based on rules (allow/deny by port, IP, protocol). A forward proxy sits in front of CLIENTS, making requests on their behalf (hiding the client from the destination server).

# forward proxy: hides the CLIENT from the destination (e.g. a corporate proxy for outbound browsing)
# reverse proxy: hides the SERVER from the client (e.g. nginx in front of your actual backend)

# CDN: serves a cached copy of your static assets from a server physically near the user

lessons.explanation: Regular HTTP is request-response only -- the server can't push data to the client on its own. WebSockets open a persistent, two-way connection, letting either side send data at any time (used for chat apps, live collaboration, gaming).
examples:
# choosing WebSockets vs SSE:
# chat app (client sends AND receives) -> WebSockets
# live stock ticker (server only pushes, client never sends) -> SSE, simpler

# troubleshooting toolkit:
# ping example.com          -- is the host reachable at all?
# traceroute example.com    -- where does the path actually break?
# dig example.com           -- what does DNS actually resolve to?
# curl -v https://example.com  -- see the full request/response, including headers
commonMistakes: Reaching for WebSockets by default for any real-time feature -- if the client never needs to send data back over the same connection, SSE is simpler and sufficient.

lessons.title: Routing protocols: OSPF & BGP fundamentals
objectives: Explain the purpose of OSPF inside a network and BGP between autonomous systems
Explain how OSPF changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explain: Routers need protocols to learn which next hop should carry traffic toward a destination. OSPF is a link-state interior routing protocol commonly used within an organization: routers share topology information and compute shortest paths.
lessons.example: A data-center or enterprise network may use an interior protocol such as OSPF to learn internal routes, while edge routers use BGP to exchange external prefixes with other networks. Application code normally does not run BGP, but infrastructure and network-automation roles need to reason about it.
commonMistakes: Calling BGP simply a shortest-path protocol.

exercises.title: Trace a DNS resolution chain
exercises.prompt: Given that shop.example.com is a CNAME pointing to cdn.example.com, and cdn.example.com is an A record pointing to 93.184.216.34, what IP address does shop.example.com ultimately resolve to?
exercises.hint: follow the chain: CNAME to CNAME/A until you reach an actual A record

exercises.title: Classify an IP address
exercises.prompt: Is 172.20.5.1 a private or public IP address? Explain using the private IP ranges.
exercises.hint: 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255 is a private range

exercises.title: Diagnose a failed connection
exercises.prompt: A user reports 'the website won't load.' DNS resolves correctly, but the TCP connection to port 443 times out. What's the most likely cause, and what would you check next?
exercises.hint: likely a firewall blocking port 443, or the server/service isn't actually listening on that port -- check firewall rules and confirm the service is running and bound to that port

exercises.title: Diagnose a slow API response

projects.title: Network diagnostic CLI tool
projects.desc: Build a command-line tool that runs ping, traceroute, and DNS lookups against a given hostname and summarizes the results in plain language.

projects.title: Simple reverse proxy
projects.desc: Build a minimal reverse proxy that forwards requests to one of several backend servers, based on a simple routing rule (e.g. path prefix).

projects.title: Backend Network Diagnostic Tool (capstone-aligned)
projects.desc: Given a set of simulated network symptoms (DNS failure, TCP timeout, high latency, wrong HTTP status), build a tool that identifies the likely root cause and suggests next diagnostic steps.

interviewPreparation.q: Walk through what happens, step by step, when you type a URL into a browser and press enter.
interviewPreparation.a: DNS resolves the hostname to an IP address (possibly through a chain of CNAME records), a TCP connection is established via the 3-way handshake (plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS), the browser sends an HTTP request, the server processes it and returns a response, and the browser renders it -- each step is a place a real failure could occur, which is exactly why understanding each layer matters.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you diagnose 'the website is down' as a backend engineer?
interviewPreparation.a: Work through the layers in order: does DNS resolve? Does a TCP connection to the right port succeed? Does the server respond to HTTP at all, and with what status code? Tools like dig, curl -v, and checking whether the service is actually listening on its expected port narrow this down quickly, rather than guessing.

interviewPreparation.q: Why would you put a reverse proxy in front of your backend service instead of exposing it directly?
interviewPreparation.a: A reverse proxy centralizes TLS termination, can cache responses, load-balance across multiple backend instances, and hides your actual backend's address and implementation details from the outside world -- all without the backend service itself needing to handle any of that.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose UDP over TCP for a backend feature?
interviewPreparation.a: When low latency matters more than guaranteed, in-order delivery -- live video/audio, real-time gaming position updates, or DNS lookups themselves, where retrying quickly is preferable to TCP's overhead and retransmission delays.

interviewPreparation.q: Why can't an external service on the internet connect directly to a device on your private home network?
interviewPreparation.a: NAT means the outside world only sees your router's single public IP address -- there's no direct route to an internal private IP like 192.168.1.10 without something (a port forward, VPN, or similar) explicitly making that connection possible.

capstone.title: Backend Network Diagnostic Tool
capstone.description: Build a tool that, given a set of simulated network symptoms (DNS resolution status, TCP connection status, HTTP status code, and latency), identifies the most likely root cause and suggests a concrete next diagnostic step -- the same reasoning process a backend engineer actually goes through when a service reports 'can't connect' or 'it's slow.'
deliverables: A working diagnostic function that takes DNS/TCP/HTTP/latency signals and returns the most likely root cause, not just a generic error
Coverage of at least 4 distinct failure categories: DNS failure, TCP/port failure, HTTP-level failure (e.g. gateway timeout), and high-latency-but-otherwise-successful
A short written explanation of WHY each cause maps to its specific combination of signals, tied to the actual mechanics of DNS/TCP/HTTP covered in this course
At least one test case per failure category, verified against your own diagnostic logic
capstone.portfolioTips: This maps directly onto real on-call debugging work -- being able to say 'I built a tool that reasons through network layers the way I would during an actual incident' is a concrete, relatable signal for backend interviews.

industryUsage.usage: Operates one of the world's largest CDN and DNS infrastructure networks, where DNS resolution speed and reverse-proxy/load-balancing logic directly determine most of the internet's perceived performance.
Its VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) networking model is built entirely on the subnetting, routing, and NAT concepts covered in this course -- real cloud infrastructure work assumes this fluency.
Relies heavily on both WebSockets (for real-time chat) and UDP-based protocols (for voice/video), a direct real-world example of choosing the right transport protocol per feature.

careerApplications: Used by backend, cloud, DevOps/SRE, cybersecurity, and distributed-systems engineers to diagnose connectivity, DNS, routing, latency, and service-to-service communication problems.

title: System Design
blurb: Architecting things that scale — the senior-engineer skill.

lessons.title: Scaling basics
lessons.explain: Scaling begins with concrete requirements: request rate, data size, latency target, availability target, and the operations users actually perform. Load balancing and horizontal scaling add capacity, caching removes repeated work, and queues absorb work that does not need to finish inside the request.
lessons.example:
users -> load balancer -> [server, server, server]
              cache <-> database
objectives: Distinguish vertical from horizontal scaling and explain caching's role
Explain how load balancing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect load balancing with caching and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Scaling vertically (a bigger machine) indefinitely instead of horizontally, hitting a hard ceiling on how big one machine can get.

lessons.title: Load balancing
objectives: Explain what a load balancer does and why
Explain how load balancer changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect load balancer with horizontal scaling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple servers, so no single server gets overwhelmed while others sit idle. This also enables horizontal scaling -- adding more servers to handle more traffic -- and improves availability, since traffic can be redirected away from a server that goes down.
examples:
# without a load balancer: all traffic hits ONE server
# with a load balancer: requests are distributed across server1, server2, server3
# if server2 goes down, the load balancer stops sending it traffic
commonMistakes: Scaling by making a single server bigger (vertical scaling) indefinitely, instead of distributing load across multiple servers -- there's a hard ceiling to how big one machine can get.
lessons.careerRelevance: Load balancing is foundational to nearly every real system that needs to handle serious traffic.

lessons.title: Caching
objectives: Explain what caching is and its trade-offs
Explain how cache changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect cache with cache invalidation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Caching trades freshness and complexity for lower latency and less repeated backend work. You must define the cache key, what is stored, how long it remains valid, and what happens when the source data changes.
commonMistakes: Caching data that changes frequently without a clear invalidation strategy -- users can see stale, incorrect data without realizing it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Caching is one of the highest-leverage performance techniques in real systems, and also one of the trickiest to get right.

objectives: Explain database replication and sharding
Explain how replication changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect replication with sharding and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Databases at scale require deciding where data lives and how copies remain useful. Replication creates additional copies for availability or read capacity, while sharding or partitioning divides data across nodes.
examples:
# replication: primary DB handles writes, replicas handle reads,
# spreading read load and providing failover if primary goes down

# sharding: users A-M on shard 1, users N-Z on shard 2 --
# each shard holds only part of the total data
commonMistakes: Sharding a database before it's actually necessary -- sharding adds real complexity (cross-shard queries become harder), so it's usually a later-stage decision, not a starting default.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding replication and sharding is essential once a system's data outgrows a single database server.

lessons.title: Consistency vs availability: making the design choice
objectives: Translate product requirements into consistency/availability choices
Explain what the system should do during a partition
Explain how consistency requirement changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect consistency requirement with availability requirement and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The CAP theorem itself is taught in Distributed Systems. In System Design, the useful skill is turning consistency and availability requirements into an architecture decision.
examples:
Design comparison:
- Payment ledger: reject/queue uncertain writes rather than accept conflicting balances.
- Social activity feed: serving a slightly stale feed may be preferable to becoming unavailable.
The decision starts from the product invariant, not from memorizing CAP labels.
commonMistakes: Saying “choose consistency or availability” without stating the actual product invariant or what happens during a partition.

lessons.title: Messaging & queues
objectives: Explain asynchronous messaging between services
Explain how message queue changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect message queue with asynchronous and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A message queue decouples producers from consumers so work can be processed asynchronously and bursts can be absorbed. Delivery is not automatically “exactly once”: many practical systems provide at-least-once delivery, meaning a consumer may see the same message again after a timeout or retry.
examples:
# synchronous: place_order() waits for send_email() to fully complete
# asynchronous with a queue: place_order() pushes a 'send email' message
# to a queue and returns immediately; a separate worker processes it whenever ready
commonMistakes: Making every operation synchronous even when the caller doesn't actually need to wait for the result -- this needlessly slows down the user-facing request.
lessons.careerRelevance: Message queues underlie most real, resilient systems that handle background work or high traffic bursts.

objectives: Explain what a CDN does and why it improves performance
Explain how CDN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CDN with edge server and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A CDN caches and serves static content (images, videos, JS/CSS files) from servers geographically distributed close to actual users, rather than all requests traveling back to one origin server. This reduces latency (physical distance directly affects network round-trip time) and reduces load on the origin server itself.
examples:
# without a CDN: a user in Dubai fetches an image from a server in the US --
# long round trip every time
# with a CDN: that image is cached at a nearby edge server,
# served with much lower latency
commonMistakes: Serving large static assets (images, videos) directly from the origin server for a global user base, instead of using a CDN to reduce latency and origin load.
lessons.careerRelevance: CDNs are standard infrastructure for almost any real, globally-used web application.

objectives: Reason about redundancy and single points of failure
Explain how availability changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect availability with single point of failure and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Availability is the fraction of time a service successfully provides its required behavior, but engineering teams need a concrete target rather than the vague goal of “high availability.” An SLO states a measurable reliability target such as successful requests or latency over a time window.
examples:
# a single database server with no replica is a single point of failure --
# if it goes down, the whole system goes down
# adding a replica (and automatic failover) removes that single point of failure
commonMistakes: Building a critical system component with no redundancy at all, creating an unnecessary single point of failure.

lessons.explanation: Before designing a system, roughly estimating scale (how many users, requests per second, how much data) determines which decisions even matter -- a design that's fine for 100 users may fall apart at 10 million. This estimation doesn't need to be precise, just roughly right, to rule out approaches that clearly won't work at the real expected scale.
examples:
# rough estimation example:
# 1 million daily active users, each making ~10 requests/day
# = 10 million requests/day = ~115 requests/second on average
# (with peak traffic likely several times higher than the average)
commonMistakes: Designing a system without any rough sense of expected scale, then discovering an approach fundamentally doesn't work once real traffic arrives.

description: Architecting things that scale — the senior-engineer skill.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you start a system design interview when given a vague prompt like 'design Twitter'?
interviewPreparation.a: Clarify requirements and scope first -- what's the actual scale (users, requests/second), which features matter most (posting, reading a feed, search), and what constraints exist (consistency requirements, latency budget). Jumping straight to a diagram without this context usually leads to designing the wrong thing well.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you decide when to introduce caching into a design?
interviewPreparation.a: When you have read-heavy access patterns with data that doesn't change on every request, and you've identified the specific expensive or repeated operation caching would avoid. Caching everything by default without a stated invalidation strategy trades a real, immediate cost (staleness bugs) for a benefit you haven't confirmed you need.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you explain the CAP theorem trade-off in an interview, concretely?
interviewPreparation.a: Rather than reciting the acronym, ground it in a real scenario: during a network partition, do you refuse some requests to guarantee no stale reads (consistency), or keep answering with potentially stale data (availability)? Tie the choice to the actual system -- a banking balance leans consistency; a social media like-count leans availability.

interviewPreparation.q: What's a sign that a candidate is communicating well during a system design interview, beyond having the right answer?
interviewPreparation.a: Narrating trade-offs out loud as they're made ('I'm choosing X over Y because...'), checking in on assumptions rather than working silently, and being willing to revise the design when new constraints are introduced -- this mirrors how real design decisions actually get made and reviewed on a team.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you approach estimating scale for a system you're designing?
interviewPreparation.a: Start from a rough number of users or requests, and derive requests-per-second, storage growth, and bandwidth needs from there -- it doesn't need to be precise, just roughly right, to rule out approaches that clearly won't work at the real expected scale. Stating an explicit estimate, even approximate, is usually more valuable than skipping it.

careerApplications: Common in later-round SWE interviews, even for some internships.

capstone.title: Design, document, and defend a scalable system architecture
capstone.description: Choose a realistic system (e.g. a URL shortener at scale, a ride-sharing dispatch service, or a social media feed) and produce a full design document: requirements and scale estimation, a component architecture diagram, explicit trade-off decisions (and what you rejected and why), and a written incident postmortem for one failure mode you deliberately design for. This should read like something you'd actually present in a system design interview or an internal design review, not just a diagram.
deliverables: A written requirements and scale-estimation section (expected users, requests/second, data volume)
An architecture diagram showing the major components and how they connect
At least 3 explicit trade-off decisions, each stating what you chose, what you rejected, and why
A single-point-of-failure analysis identifying at least one real risk and how you mitigate it
A short incident postmortem: a plausible failure scenario for your design, how you'd detect it, and how you'd respond
capstone.portfolioTips: A well-written design doc is one of the strongest possible interview artifacts -- bring it to system design interviews and reference it directly rather than starting from a blank whiteboard; it shows you can produce this thinking under real conditions, not just in the moment.

lessons.explanation: Gradient descent adjusts each weight a small step in the direction that reduces the loss. Backpropagation is the algorithm that efficiently computes exactly how much each weight, even in early layers, contributed to the final loss, using the chain rule from calculus — working backward from the output to the input.
examples:
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    prediction = model.forward(x)
    loss = loss_fn(prediction, y)
    loss.backward()      # backprop: computes each weight's gradient
    optimizer.step()     # gradient descent: nudges weights to reduce loss
    optimizer.zero_grad()
commonMistakes: Forgetting to zero out gradients between training steps — gradients silently accumulate across batches, corrupting the update direction.
lessons.careerRelevance: Deep-learning engineers use gradient and chain-rule intuition to diagnose exploding or vanishing gradients, frozen parameters, unstable learning rates, and incorrect computation graphs.

description: Neural networks at depth — from perceptrons to transformers.

interviewPreparation.q: Why did attention-based architectures largely replace recurrent (RNN-style) models for language tasks?
interviewPreparation.a: Recurrent models process a sequence step by step, making long-range dependencies hard to preserve and training inherently sequential (hard to parallelize). Attention lets every position directly weigh relevance to every other position at once, both solving the long-range dependency problem and enabling much more parallelizable, scalable training -- which is why it enabled today's much larger language models.

interviewPreparation.q: A deep network's early layers stop updating during training. What's happening and how would you fix it?
interviewPreparation.a: This is the vanishing gradient problem -- gradients shrink as they're backpropagated through many layers, leaving early layers with almost no signal to learn from. Fixes include using activation functions less prone to this (ReLU over sigmoid), batch normalization, or architectural changes like residual/skip connections.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you tell from training curves alone whether a model is overfitting versus just needing more training?
interviewPreparation.a: If training loss keeps improving while validation loss stalls or gets worse, that's overfitting -- the model is memorizing rather than generalizing. If both training and validation loss are still improving together, more training (or a larger model) may genuinely help rather than hurt.

interviewPreparation.q: What's self-attention, in your own words, without jargon?
interviewPreparation.a: A way for each part of an input (like each word in a sentence) to directly look at every other part and decide how relevant it is, all at once -- rather than only being influenced by whatever came immediately before it, the way a step-by-step model works.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose a CNN over a Transformer-based approach, or vice versa, for a given task?
interviewPreparation.a: CNNs remain strong and efficient for tasks with clear local spatial structure, like image processing, where nearby pixels matter most. Transformers excel when long-range relationships across the whole input matter more than local structure, which is why they dominate language tasks -- but they can also be applied to images (vision transformers) when that long-range reasoning is worth the extra compute.

careerApplications: Needed before LLM/CV/NLP specialization.

capstone.title: Train, diagnose, and improve a neural network under real constraints
capstone.description: Unlike the existing transfer-learning projects (apply a pretrained model), this capstone is about the training process itself: train a network from scratch (or nearly so) on a real dataset, deliberately hit a real training problem (vanishing gradients, overfitting, or a loss that won't converge), diagnose it using the actual training curves as evidence, and fix it -- then explain, at a conceptual level, why the attention-based architecture covered in this course would approach the same kind of task differently than the network you just built.
deliverables: A neural network trained on a real dataset (not a toy 10-row example), with training and validation loss/accuracy tracked across epochs

A genuine training problem deliberately encountered (not simulated) -- overfitting, vanishing gradients, or a loss that plateaus or diverges -- diagnosed using the actual loss curves as evidence, not a guess
A specific, correctly-chosen fix for the diagnosed problem, with before/after curves showing it actually worked

A written comparison: for this same task, how would a Transformer-based approach handle long-range dependencies or parallelization differently than the architecture you built, and would it actually be the better choice here
capstone.portfolioTips: The before/after training curves are concrete, checkable evidence that you diagnosed a real problem correctly -- far more convincing than a single final accuracy number, which tells a reviewer nothing about whether you understood what was happening during training.

industryUsage.usage: Built its entire modern language model lineage on the Transformer architecture specifically because attention's parallelizable training scales to far larger datasets than recurrent architectures ever could.
Much of its AI hardware and software stack is optimized specifically around the parallel, attention-based computation patterns that made today's large-scale model training practical.

Uses deep learning across recommendation systems and content understanding, where correctly diagnosing training issues (vanishing gradients, overfitting) directly affects whether a model actually ships or gets scrapped.

title: Transformers
description: The attention mechanism and architecture underlying modern CV, NLP, and LLMs.
blurb: The attention mechanism and architecture underlying modern CV, NLP, and LLMs.
careerApplications: This is the single most valuable architecture to understand deeply for any AI/ML role today — it underlies virtually every state-of-the-art model in language, vision, and beyond.

lessons.title: Why transformers were created
objectives: Explain the core limitation of recurrent models that transformers solved
Explain how recurrence changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect recurrence with sequential bottleneck and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before transformers, sequence models (RNNs/LSTMs) processed tokens one at a time, in order — token 100 couldn't be computed until token 99 was done. This made training slow (no parallelism across the sequence) and made it hard to connect distant tokens (information had to pass through every step in between, degrading over long distances).
examples:
# RNN: token_100 depends on token_99 depends on token_98 ... -- inherently sequential, slow to train
# Transformer: every token can attend directly to every other token, all at once -- parallelizable
commonMistakes: Assuming transformers are just 'a bigger RNN' — the architectural shift (parallel attention vs sequential recurrence) is the actual innovation, not just scale.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is one of the most common 'explain why transformers matter' interview questions in AI/ML roles.
