lessons.title: Tokens, embeddings & positional encoding
objectives: Explain why transformers need explicit positional information
Explain how token embeddings changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect token embeddings with positional encoding and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Text is tokenized (as in the NLP track) and each token is converted to an embedding vector. But since a transformer looks at all tokens simultaneously rather than in sequence, it has no inherent sense of ORDER — 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look identical without help.
examples:
token_embedding = embed(token)          # what the token IS
position_embedding = position_encode(i)  # where the token IS in the sequence
final_input = token_embedding + position_embedding
commonMistakes: Assuming attention alone preserves word order — it doesn't; positional encoding is a deliberately added mechanism to inject that information back in.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this addition is a common follow-up question after explaining self-attention.

lessons.title: Queries, keys & values
objectives: Explain the query/key/value framework attention is built on
Explain how query changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect query with value and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every token produces three vectors: a Query (what am I looking for), a Key (what do I contain, for others to match against), and a Value (what I actually offer if selected). Attention compares each token's Query against every other token's Key to decide how much focus to put on each, then combines their Values weighted by that focus.
examples:
# conceptually, for one token's query:
# score_i = query . key_i   (how well this key matches what I'm looking for)
# attention_weights = softmax(scores)   (turn scores into a 0-1 distribution)
# output = sum(attention_weights_i * value_i)   (blend of others' values, weighted by relevance)
commonMistakes: Trying to memorize Q/K/V as arbitrary labels instead of the underlying intuition (searching for X, offering to be matched on Y, giving Z if picked) — the intuition is what actually helps you.
lessons.careerRelevance: Transformer engineers use this when debugging attention shapes, reading model implementations, optimizing inference, and understanding why attention behaves the way it does.

lessons.title: Self-attention & multi-head attention
objectives: Explain what self-attention computes and why multiple heads are used
Explain how self-attention changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect self-attention with context-aware representations and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Self-attention lets every token look at every other token in the SAME sequence to build a context-aware representation — 'bank' next to 'river' vs 'bank' next to 'money' end up with different representations because attention lets context flow in.
examples:
# self-attention: EVERY token attends to every other token in its own sequence
# multi-head: run this 8 (or more) times in parallel with different learned weights,
# then concatenate the results -- each head can specialize in a different pattern
commonMistakes: Assuming one attention head captures everything relevant — different heads reliably specialize in different relationship types, which is exactly why using several matters.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is directly used when implementing, profiling, debugging, or serving transformer models and when reasoning about long-context cost.

objectives: Contrast encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder transformers, and explain masking

Connect encoder-only with decoder-only and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: An encoder builds a rich representation of an entire input (good for understanding tasks, e.g. classification).
examples:
# masked self-attention during generation:
# when predicting token 5, the model can attend to tokens 1-4,
# but token 5's attention scores to tokens 6+ are masked to -infinity
# (so softmax gives them ~0 weight -- can't see the future)
commonMistakes: Confusing masking (which prevents seeing future tokens during generation) with padding (which just marks unused positions in a batch) — they solve different problems and use different mask.

lessons.title: Inference, context windows & computational limits
objectives: Explain what a context window is and why attention is computationally expensive
Explain how context window changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect context window with quadratic attention cost and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a transformer can consider at once — anything beyond it is simply invisible to the model.
examples:
# attention cost scales as O(n^2) in sequence length n
# double the context window -> roughly 4x the attention compute
# this is why '1 million token context' is a genuinely hard engineering achievement, not just a bigger number
commonMistakes: Assuming you can just keep feeding a model more and more context 'for free' — cost and latency scale non-linearly, and very long contexts can also dilute the model's effective attention over.
lessons.careerRelevance: Context-window trade-offs are a practical, daily concern in RAG and AI-agent system design, covered directly in those tracks next.

lessons.title: Self-attention: a worked example
objectives: Compute a tiny self-attention pass by hand
Explain how worked example changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect worked example with softmax and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Working through a small, concrete attention calculation makes the mechanism tangible. Given query, key, and value vectors for a few tokens, computing the dot-product scores, applying softmax to get attention weights, then taking a weighted sum of values shows exactly how a token's representation gets updated using context from every other token.
examples:
# tiny worked example (2 tokens, 2-dim vectors):
# query for 'bank' = [1, 0], keys = [[1,0], [0,1]] for 'bank' and 'river'
# scores = dot products = [1, 0]
# softmax([1,0]) approx [0.73, 0.27] -- 'bank' attends mostly to itself here
# output = 0.73*value_bank + 0.27*value_river
commonMistakes: Trying to reason about attention only abstractly without ever computing a concrete example -- the mechanism is much clearer once you've traced actual numbers through it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to walk through this calculation is a common, concrete interview exercise for roles touching transformer internals.

lessons.title: Transformers beyond text: vision & multimodal models
objectives: Explain how the transformer architecture extends beyond text
Explain how vision transformer changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: Vision transformers (ViT) apply the same self-attention mechanism to images, by splitting an image into patches and treating each patch like a token. Multimodal models combine text and image (or audio) understanding in one architecture, often using cross-attention so text tokens can attend to image patches and vice versa.
examples:
# Vision Transformer (ViT) intuition:
# split a 224x224 image into 16x16 patches -> 196 'tokens'
# feed these patch embeddings through the SAME kind of transformer
# encoder used for text -- attention works the same way, just on patches
commonMistakes: Assuming transformers only work for text -- the same core self-attention mechanism generalizes to images, audio, and combinations of modalities.
lessons.careerRelevance: Vision transformers and multimodal architectures are now common in production computer vision and generative AI systems.

lessons.title: What generative AI is
objectives: Define generative AI and name its major output types
Explain how generative vs discriminative changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect generative vs discriminative with content creation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Generative AI creates NEW content — text, images, audio, video — rather than just labeling or predicting a category on existing content. A spam filter is discriminative (sorts existing emails); an LLM writing an email, or a diffusion model painting an image from a text prompt, is generative (creates something new that didn't exist before).
examples:
# discriminative: given an email, predict spam/not-spam (a label for existing input)
# generative: given a prompt, produce a brand-new email/image/song that didn't exist before

lessons.title: Training vs inference, prompting & conditioning
objectives: Distinguish training-time and inference-time, and explain conditioning
Explain how training vs inference changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect training vs inference with conditioning and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Training is the (expensive, one-time-ish) process of learning the distribution from data. Inference is using the trained model to generate new outputs — cheap, per-request.
examples:
# training: learn from millions of (image, caption) pairs -- expensive, done once (or periodically)
# inference: 'generate an image of a red bicycle' -- cheap, done per request
# the caption/prompt is the CONDITIONING signal steering what gets generated
commonMistakes: Confusing fine-tuning (updating model weights, a training-time activity) with prompting (steering a fixed model at inference time, no weight changes) — they solve similar problems very.
lessons.careerRelevance: This distinction underlies every practical decision about cost, speed, and customization in a real generative AI product.

lessons.title: Risk: copyright, bias, privacy & misuse
objectives: Identify the major categories of risk generative AI systems raise
Explain how copyright provenance changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect copyright provenance with bias amplification and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Generative models trained on large scraped datasets raise real, unresolved questions: copyright (was training on this data legal/licensed, and who owns generated output that resembles it), bias (models reproduce and can amplify biases present in training data), privacy (models can sometimes memorize and regurgitate sensitive training examples).
examples:

# copyright -- training data provenance, output ownership
# bias -- reproducing/amplifying training-data biases
# privacy -- memorized sensitive training examples resurfacing
# misuse -- deepfakes, impersonation, disinformation at scale
commonMistakes: Treating these risks as someone else's problem ('the model vendor handles that') — anyone building a product on top of generative AI inherits real responsibility for how it's used and what.

lessons.explanation: A purely pretrained model (next-token prediction on raw internet text) is good at continuing text patterns, but not necessarily at being a HELPFUL assistant — it might continue a question with more questions rather than answering it.

lessons.title: Inference & decoding: greedy, sampling & temperature
objectives: Explain how a trained LLM turns probabilities into an actual generated response
Explain how greedy decoding changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: At each step, an LLM computes a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary for the next token. Greedy decoding always picks the single highest-probability token (deterministic, but can be repetitive/boring).
examples:
# temperature intuition:
# temperature -> 0: almost always picks the top token (deterministic, focused)
# temperature = 1: samples proportional to the model's real learned probabilities
# temperature > 1: flattens the distribution further, more random/surprising choices
commonMistakes: Using high temperature for tasks needing precise, factual, repeatable output (like structured data extraction) — that's exactly where LOW temperature (or greedy decoding) is the right.

lessons.explanation: Building on the Transformers track's explanation of WHY context windows are computationally expensive, this lesson is about the PRACTICAL side: everything you want the model to consider — system instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, the user's question — must fit within one finite token budget, competing with each other.
examples:
# a context budget is a competition for space:
# system prompt (500 tokens) + conversation history (variable) + retrieved docs (variable) + user question
# -- all must fit inside, say, an 8,000 token limit -- something has to be prioritized/trimmed
commonMistakes: Naively appending the full conversation history to every request with no trimming strategy — long conversations will eventually exceed the context limit or silently push out important.

lessons.explanation: LLMs generate plausible-sounding text based on learned patterns, with no built-in mechanism to verify factual truth — a confident, fluent, completely fabricated citation or statistic is not a rare glitch, it's an expected failure mode of how these models fundamentally work.
examples:
# a hallucination looks EXACTLY as confident and fluent as a correct answer --
# there's no built-in 'uncertainty flag' the model reliably surfaces on its own
# this is precisely the problem RAG (grounding in real retrieved documents) is designed to reduce
commonMistakes: Trusting an LLM's confident tone as a signal of factual accuracy — confidence and correctness are not correlated the way they are in human communication; fluency is not evidence of truth.
lessons.careerRelevance: Hallucination mitigation is one of the most consequential practical design decisions in any real LLM product, directly motivating the RAG track next.

objectives: Contrast open and closed model access models, and describe responsible-use basics

lessons.explanation: Closed models (accessed via an API, weights not available) are typically easier to use and stay current, but you depend entirely on the provider for availability, pricing, and policy changes. Open-weight models can be self-hosted, audited, and fine-tuned freely, at the cost of needing your own infrastructure and expertise to run well.
examples:
# closed (API-based): fast to start, provider handles infra, but you don't control the weights or guarantee availability
# open-weight: full control, can self-host and fine-tune freely, but you own the operational burden

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide between an open-source and a closed/API-based model for a given feature?
interviewPreparation.a: Data sensitivity (can this data leave your infrastructure at all), cost structure at your expected volume (per-request API cost vs. self-hosting infrastructure cost), and how much control you need over the model itself (fine-tuning, weight access) all factor in -- there's rarely a universally right answer, only the right tradeoff for this specific feature's constraints.

interviewPreparation.q: Why would you choose greedy decoding over sampling with temperature, or vice versa?
interviewPreparation.a: Greedy decoding (or low temperature) gives consistent, repeatable output, which matters for factual extraction or tasks needing the same answer every time. Higher temperature sampling introduces controlled randomness, useful for creative tasks where varied, less predictable output is actually desirable, not a defect.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you manage context as a conversation grows beyond what comfortably fits in the context window?
interviewPreparation.a: Options include truncating older history, summarizing it instead of keeping it verbatim, or using retrieval to pull back only what's relevant rather than keeping everything -- the right choice depends on whether older context is still likely to matter, and whether losing some fidelity is an acceptable tradeoff for staying within budget.

interviewPreparation.q: What would a good task-specific evaluation plan for an LLM feature actually include?
interviewPreparation.a: A real test set representative of what the feature will actually see in production, and explicit scoring criteria tied to what matters for this specific task -- not just running it against a generic benchmark, which may not reflect the feature's actual failure modes or success criteria at all.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you mitigate the risk of a model hallucinating in a specific feature, beyond a generic disclaimer?
interviewPreparation.a: Grounding the model's response in retrieved, verifiable source material (rather than relying purely on its internal knowledge) when factual accuracy matters, and being explicit in the interface about what's model-generated versus sourced -- a disclaimer alone doesn't reduce the actual rate of fabricated claims, it just describes the risk.

capstone.title: Build and defend a production-minded LLM feature, not just a working prompt

This is about the judgment layer around an LLM, not prompt-writing alone -- the same judgment a team would actually need before shipping this to real users.
deliverables: A specific LLM feature idea with a justified model choice (open vs. closed, and roughly what size/cost tier) tied to the feature's actual latency and cost constraints
A decoding strategy (temperature, sampling vs. greedy) chosen and justified for this specific task, not a default
An explicit context-budget strategy for how the feature behaves as input grows (truncation, summarization, or retrieval), not an assumption that everything always fits

blurb: Give LLMs real, current knowledge grounded in your own data.

lessons.title: The RAG pipeline
lessons.explain: RAG solves the LLM's stale/unknown-data problem: split your docs into chunks, embed them into vectors, store them, then for each query retrieve the most similar chunks and feed them to the LLM so its answer is grounded.
lessons.example:
docs -> chunk -> embed -> vector DB
query -> embed -> top-k similar -> LLM(query+chunks)

lessons.explanation: Before documents can be searched, they must be ingested (loaded from PDFs, web pages, databases) and chunked — split into smaller pieces, since embedding and retrieving an entire long document as one unit loses precision (you'd retrieve the whole thing even if only one paragraph is relevant).
examples:
# naive chunking: split every 500 characters, ignoring sentence/paragraph boundaries
# better: split on natural boundaries (paragraphs, sections), with some overlap between
# chunks so a fact split across a boundary isn't completely lost
commonMistakes: Chunking purely by a fixed character count with no regard for sentence or paragraph boundaries — this routinely splits a single coherent idea across two chunks, weakening retrieval for.
lessons.careerRelevance: Chunking strategy is one of the highest-leverage, most commonly tuned decisions in any real RAG system's quality.

lessons.title: Embeddings & vector databases
objectives: Explain how chunks become searchable by meaning, not just keywords

Explain how embeddings changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect embeddings with vector database and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Each chunk is converted into an embedding — a dense vector where semantically similar text ends up close together in vector space (as covered in the NLP track).
examples:
chunk_embedding = embed_model.encode(chunk_text)   # e.g. a 768-dimension vector
vector_db.insert(chunk_id, chunk_embedding, metadata={'source': doc_name})

lessons.title: Reranking & context construction
objectives: Explain why an initial retrieval pass is often reranked, and how final context is assembled
Explain how reranking changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect reranking with two-stage retrieval and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Initial similarity search (fast, approximate) often returns a broader set of candidate chunks than needed; a reranking step (using a slower but more accurate model) reorders these candidates by true relevance to the specific query, improving precision at the cost of some extra latency.
examples:
candidates = vector_search(query, top_k=50)     # fast, broad first pass
reranked = rerank_model(query, candidates)        # slower, more accurate reordering
final_context = format_top_n(reranked, n=5)        # assemble what actually goes in the prompt
commonMistakes: Sending all 50 initially-retrieved chunks directly to the LLM without reranking or trimming — this wastes context budget on lower-relevance chunks and can bury the truly relevant ones.
lessons.careerRelevance: The retrieve-then-rerank pattern is a standard, expected architecture in production-quality RAG systems.

lessons.explanation: Grounded generation explicitly instructs the model to answer ONLY using the retrieved context provided (not its general pretrained knowledge), and to say it doesn't know when the retrieved context doesn't contain the answer — directly fighting hallucination.

# If the context doesn't contain the answer, say you don't know. Cite the source for each claim.'
# -- without this explicit instruction, the model may blend in ungrounded pretrained knowledge

lessons.title: Retrieval & generation evaluation
objectives: Evaluate a RAG system's retrieval quality and final answer quality separately
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: Recall@K, MRR (mean reciprocal rank).
Explain how retrieval evaluation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect retrieval evaluation with generation evaluation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: RAG systems need TWO separate evaluations: retrieval evaluation (did we find the right chunks? measured with metrics like hit rate or recall against a labeled set of query-to-correct-document pairs) and generation evaluation (given good chunks, did the model produce a good, grounded, accurate answer?).
examples:
# retrieval eval: for 50 labeled test queries, does the retrieved set contain the KNOWN correct document?
# generation eval (given GOOD retrieved chunks): is the final answer accurate, grounded, and well-cited?
# -- always debug these two stages SEPARATELY, not as one combined 'is the answer good' check
commonMistakes: Debugging a bad RAG answer by only looking at the final output — always check whether retrieval found the right chunks FIRST, before assuming the problem is in generation.
lessons.careerRelevance: This two-stage evaluation discipline is exactly what separates a systematically-improvable RAG system from one tuned by guesswork. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Freshness, access control & common failure modes
objectives: Identify practical operational concerns and common RAG failure patterns
Explain how index freshness changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect index freshness with access control enforcement and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Real RAG systems need a plan for freshness (how often is the underlying document index updated as source documents change) and access control (a user should only ever retrieve chunks from documents they're actually permitted to see — a critical, easy-to-miss security requirement, not an afterthought).
examples:
# access control failure (serious): a shared vector index with no permission filtering means
# ANY user's query could retrieve chunks from documents they shouldn't have access to at all
# -- metadata filtering by user/team permissions must be enforced at retrieval time, always
commonMistakes: Building a shared vector index without permission-aware filtering baked into every retrieval call — this is a real, serious security gap, not a minor edge case.
lessons.careerRelevance: Access control in RAG systems is now a standard, explicit requirement in any enterprise-facing AI product review.

lessons.title: When RAG is (and isn't) the right approach
objectives: Decide when RAG genuinely solves the problem at hand
Explain how when to use RAG changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect when to use RAG with document-dependent answers and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: RAG is well-suited when answers depend on specific, current, or proprietary documents a model wasn't trained on. It's a poor fit when the task needs general reasoning rather than document lookup, or when the true answer isn't actually contained in any retrievable document -- RAG can't invent grounding that doesn't exist in the corpus.
examples:
# good RAG fit: 'What does OUR company's return policy say about X?'
# poor RAG fit: 'Write a creative poem about autumn'
# (nothing to retrieve -- this needs generation, not lookup)
commonMistakes: Reaching for RAG by default for every task, even ones that don't actually depend on retrievable documents at all.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly scoping when RAG applies (vs prompting alone, or an agent) is a real, practical architecture decision.

lessons.title: Hybrid Search: Combining Dense and Sparse Retrieval
objectives: Explain why combining dense (embedding-based) and sparse (keyword-based) retrieval catches more relevant results than either alone
Explain how hybrid search changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect hybrid search with dense retrieval and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Dense retrieval (embeddings + vector similarity) is good at capturing MEANING -- it can find a relevant passage even if it doesn't share exact wording with the query. But it can miss exact matches that matter, like a specific product ID, error code, or rare technical term, since embeddings represent overall semantic meaning, not precise token identity.
examples:
# Dense retrieval alone: might miss an exact match for a specific error code
# if the surrounding wording differs a lot from the query's phrasing

# Sparse (BM25) retrieval alone: would nail the exact error code match,
# but might miss a conceptually relevant passage that doesn't use the
# same words as the query

# Hybrid: run both retrievers, combine/rerank their results --
# catches the exact-match case AND the semantic-similarity case
commonMistakes: Assuming dense (embedding-based) retrieval alone is always sufficient -- it's genuinely weak at exact matches (IDs, codes, rare terms) precisely because embeddings capture overall meaning.
lessons.careerRelevance: Production RAG systems handling real, varied queries commonly use hybrid search specifically because relying on dense retrieval alone leaves a real, recurring class of queries poorly served.

description: Give LLMs real, current knowledge grounded in your own data.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is it important to evaluate retrieval and generation separately in a RAG system?
interviewPreparation.a: A bad answer could come from retrieving the wrong chunks (a retrieval failure) or from generating poorly despite having the right chunks (a generation failure) -- these need different fixes, and a single combined 'good/bad answer' judgment can't tell you which one actually happened, or where to focus effort.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you use hybrid search instead of pure dense (embedding-based) retrieval?
interviewPreparation.a: When query patterns include exact-match needs (specific IDs, error codes, rare technical terms) that embeddings tend to miss, since dense retrieval captures overall meaning rather than precise token identity -- combining it with keyword/BM25-style sparse retrieval catches both the semantic matches and the exact matches.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide on a chunking strategy for a new document set?
interviewPreparation.a: Base it on the actual document structure and how people will query it -- dense technical documents with numbered sections often benefit from larger, structure-aware chunks, while shorter, more atomic content might chunk well at a smaller size. There's no universal right chunk size, only one justified by the specific documents and queries.

interviewPreparation.q: A RAG system retrieves topically-related but unhelpful passages for a factual question. How do you diagnose this?
interviewPreparation.a: Check whether the chunking is fragmenting relevant information awkwardly, whether the embedding model captures the right kind of similarity for this domain, and whether metadata filtering or reranking could help surface more specific matches -- it's rarely one single cause, so isolating which stage is actually failing matters.

interviewPreparation.q: When is RAG NOT the right approach for a given problem?
interviewPreparation.a: When the task doesn't actually depend on document-grounded facts -- creative writing, general reasoning, or tasks where the model's own broad knowledge is sufficient don't benefit from retrieval, and adding RAG in those cases adds complexity and latency without solving a real problem.

careerApplications: A concrete, in-demand AI engineering skill beyond just prompting.

capstone.title: Build a production-minded RAG system, with a measured evaluation of retrieval and generation separately
capstone.description: Take a real document set and build a genuinely production-minded RAG pipeline: chunking justified by the document type, a retrieval strategy (dense, or hybrid if the query patterns call for it), reranking, grounded generation with real citations, and -- critically -- separate evaluation of retrieval quality and generation quality, since a good answer built on the wrong retrieved chunks is not the same success as a good answer built on the right ones. This assumes tokens, embeddings, and context windows are already understood -- the focus here is retrieval system design and measurement, not LLM fundamentals.
deliverables: A chunking strategy justified by the actual document type (not a default chunk size picked without reasoning)
A retrieval approach -- dense, or hybrid if you can justify why pure dense retrieval would miss real query patterns for this document set
Grounded generation with real citations pointing to the actual retrieved source, not fabricated or generic references
Separate evaluation of retrieval quality (are the right chunks being found) and generation quality (is the answer good given those chunks) -- not one combined 'does it work' judgment
A written account of one real failure mode you found (a topically-related-but-unhelpful retrieval, a stale index, or a case RAG genuinely isn't well suited for) and how you'd address or accept it
capstone.portfolioTips: Separating retrieval evaluation from generation evaluation is the single detail that most distinguishes a real RAG system from a demo -- it's the difference between 'the answer looked right' and being able to say specifically whether retrieval or generation is the actual bottleneck when something goes wrong.

lessons.title: The agent loop
lessons.explain: An agent is an LLM in a loop: it observes state, decides an action (often calling a tool), executes it, sees the result, and repeats until the task is done. Tools give it the ability to DO things, not just talk.
lessons.example:
while not done:
    action = llm(state, tools)
    result = run(action)
    state = update(state, result)

commonMistakes: Assuming an agent's tool-calling is guaranteed safe -- the model decides which tool to call, but the code executing it must still validate and gate risky actions.

lessons.title: Tool use & function calling
objectives: Explain how an LLM invokes external tools via function calling
Explain how function calling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect function calling with tool definitions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Tool use is what turns an LLM from 'a text generator' into 'a system that can act.' Function calling gives the model a defined list of available tools (name, description, expected arguments) and lets it choose to output a structured request to call one — your code executes the actual function and returns the result back to the model for the next step.
commonMistakes: Assuming the model directly executes actions itself — it only ever outputs a structured REQUEST to call a tool; your application code is what actually performs the action, which is exactly.
lessons.careerRelevance: Function calling is the specific mechanism underlying essentially every real AI agent product today.

lessons.explanation: Short-term memory is simply the current conversation/task context within the active context window — it disappears once the session ends.
examples:

# long-term: 'this user has consistently preferred bullet points across the last 20 sessions'
# -- stored externally, retrieved and injected into context when a new session starts
commonMistakes: Assuming an agent 'remembers' anything between separate sessions without an explicit external memory system — without one, every new session starts with a genuinely blank context.
lessons.careerRelevance: Memory design is a core, practical architecture decision in any agent meant to improve over repeated use, not a solved default.

lessons.title: Planning, reflection & verification
objectives: Explain how agents break down goals into steps and check their own work
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: ReAct reasoning-and-action pattern.
Explain how planning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect planning with reflection and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Planning is breaking a high-level goal ('book me the cheapest flight under $500') into a concrete sequence of steps (search flights, filter by price, check availability, confirm).
examples:
# planning: goal -> [search_flights(), filter(price<500), sort(cheapest), confirm_with_user()]
# reflection: after search_flights() returns results, agent checks 'do these actually match the constraints?'
# before proceeding, rather than blindly trusting the first result
commonMistakes: Skipping reflection entirely for cost/speed and just chaining steps blindly — this works fine for simple, low-stakes tasks but is risky for anything where an intermediate error could.
lessons.careerRelevance: Planning and reflection quality is exactly what separates a genuinely useful agent from one that confidently takes a wrong action. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Human approval, permissions & least privilege
objectives: Design appropriate human-approval gates and permission scoping for an agent
Explain how human-in-the-loop approval changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect human-in-the-loop approval with least privilege and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Not every agent action should execute automatically — high-stakes or irreversible actions (sending an email, making a purchase, deleting data) should typically require human approval before executing, especially early in a system's deployment.
examples:
# a research agent needs: web search, document read access
# a research agent does NOT need: ability to send emails, delete files, or make purchases
# -- scope its tool access to exactly what the task requires, nothing more
commonMistakes: Giving an agent broad tool access 'to be flexible for future tasks' — this directly increases the blast radius of any single agent mistake or adversarial prompt injection.
lessons.careerRelevance: Approval gates and least-privilege scoping are the most important practical safety controls in any real production agent system.

lessons.title: Error handling, recovery & agent evaluation
objectives: Design error recovery for agent tool failures and evaluate agent performance
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: agent task-completion rate, agent latency and tool-call observability.
Explain how error recovery changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect error recovery with retry/fallback strategies and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Tool calls fail — APIs time out, return unexpected data, or reject invalid input — and an agent needs an explicit strategy: retry, fall back to an alternative approach, or surface the failure clearly rather than silently proceeding with bad data.
commonMistakes: Letting an agent silently continue after a failed tool call as if it had succeeded — this can compound into a confidently wrong final action built on a foundation that already failed.
lessons.careerRelevance: Robust error handling is what separates a demo-quality agent from one trustworthy enough for real production use. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: Tool calls fail — APIs time out, return unexpected data, or reject invalid input — and an agent needs an explicit strategy: retry, fall back to an alternative approach, or surface the failure clearly rather than silently proceeding with bad data.

lessons.title: Security risks & when not to use agents
objectives: Identify agent-specific security risks and recognize when a simpler system is the better choice
Explain how injection-driven tool misuse changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect injection-driven tool misuse with blast radius of tool access and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Agents introduce risks beyond a normal LLM call: prompt injection can hijack an agent's tool-use decisions (not just its text output), and a compromised or confused agent with real tool access can take real, damaging actions — not just generate bad text.
examples:
# a task that ALWAYS does: fetch data -> transform -> save --
# with no real decisions or branching needed -- is better as a simple script,
# NOT an agent; agents earn their complexity cost when genuine judgment/adaptation is needed
concepts: when a script beats an agent
commonMistakes: Defaulting to an agentic architecture for any automation task, regardless of whether real decision-making is actually involved — this adds cost, latency, and failure surface for no real.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing when NOT to use an agent is just as valuable an architecture skill as knowing how to build one well, and is a common senior-level interview distinction.
lessons.explain: Agents introduce risks beyond a normal LLM call: prompt injection can hijack an agent's tool-use decisions (not just its text output), and a compromised or confused agent with real tool access can take real, damaging actions — not just generate bad text.

lessons.title: When an agent is the right tool
objectives: Decide when agent overhead is actually justified
Explain how when to use an agent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect when to use an agent with fixed script vs dynamic decisions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An agent is justified when a task genuinely requires multiple dynamic steps, tool calls, and decisions that can't be predetermined in a fixed script. For tasks with a known, fixed sequence of steps, a simple deterministic script is more reliable, cheaper, and easier to debug than an agent.
examples:
# good agent fit: 'research this topic, decide which sources are credible,
# then summarize' -- the STEPS aren't knowable in advance
# poor agent fit: 'always run steps A, B, then C in that exact order' --
# just write a script; an agent adds cost and unpredictability with no benefit
commonMistakes: Building an agent for a task with a known, fixed sequence of steps, when a simple deterministic script would be more reliable and far cheaper.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly scoping when agent overhead is justified is a genuinely important, practical architecture decision.
lessons.explain: An agent is justified when a task genuinely requires multiple dynamic steps, tool calls, and decisions that can't be predetermined in a fixed script. lessons.title: MCP: why it exists & host/client/server architecture
objectives: Explain how MCP standardizes connections between LLM applications and external context/tools.
Explain how MCP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MCP with host and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Model Context Protocol separates an AI host application, MCP clients managed by that host, and MCP servers that expose capabilities. The protocol reduces one-off integration code by standardizing discovery and invocation of tools, resources, prompts, and client-side features.
lessons.explain: Model Context Protocol separates an AI host application, MCP clients managed by that host, and MCP servers that expose capabilities. The protocol reduces one-off integration code by standardizing discovery and invocation of tools, resources, prompts, and client-side features.
examples:
architecture={"host":"assistant app","client":"MCP connection","server":"calendar/files service"}
print(architecture)
lessons.example:
architecture={"host":"assistant app","client":"MCP connection","server":"calendar/files service"}
print(architecture)
commonMistakes: Calling MCP “a model” or “an agent” confuses the protocol layer with the application and reasoning layers built on top of it.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Base protocol, JSON-RPC, lifecycle & capabilities
objectives: Trace initialization and capability negotiation before normal requests begin.
Explain how JSON-RPC changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect JSON-RPC with initialize and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP messages use JSON-RPC 2.0 and a defined lifecycle. Client and server initialize the connection, exchange protocol versions and capability declarations, then perform capability-specific requests.
lessons.explain: MCP messages use JSON-RPC 2.0 and a defined lifecycle. Client and server initialize the connection, exchange protocol versions and capability declarations, then perform capability-specific requests.
examples:
message={"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"current"}}
print(message["method"])
lessons.example:
message={"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"current"}}
print(message["method"])
commonMistakes: Sending tool or resource requests before initialization/capability negotiation can make implementations fail unpredictably across clients.

lessons.title: Transports: stdio & Streamable HTTP
objectives: Choose a transport based on local process versus remote service boundaries.
Explain how stdio changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect stdio with Streamable HTTP and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP can run over transports such as stdio for a locally launched server process or Streamable HTTP for networked services. Stdio is simple and keeps credentials in the local process environment; HTTP introduces network authentication, server discovery, scaling, and failure concerns.
lessons.explain: MCP can run over transports such as stdio for a locally launched server process or Streamable HTTP for networked services. Stdio is simple and keeps credentials in the local process environment; HTTP introduces network authentication, server discovery, scaling, and failure concerns.
examples:

lessons.example:
transports={"local":"stdio","remote":"Streamable HTTP"}

lessons.title: Tools: schemas, discovery & safe invocation
objectives: Expose model-invokable actions with clear schemas and application-controlled safety.
Explain how tools changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tools with JSON schema and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP tools are server capabilities that models may discover and request to invoke. A tool definition needs a precise name, description, and input schema so the model can construct valid arguments.
lessons.explain: MCP tools are server capabilities that models may discover and request to invoke. A tool definition needs a precise name, description, and input schema so the model can construct valid arguments.
examples:
tool={"name":"get_weather","inputSchema":{"type":"object","required":["city"]}}
print(tool)
lessons.example:
tool={"name":"get_weather","inputSchema":{"type":"object","required":["city"]}}
print(tool)
commonMistakes: Trusting model-generated tool arguments without server-side validation can turn a harmless-looking tool call into an invalid or unsafe operation.

lessons.explanation: Resources provide application-controlled contextual data such as files, database records, repository history, or documentation. Servers can expose concrete resource URIs and templates for parameterized resources.
lessons.explain: Resources provide application-controlled contextual data such as files, database records, repository history, or documentation. Servers can expose concrete resource URIs and templates for parameterized resources.

lessons.title: Client features: sampling, roots & elicitation
objectives: Explain capabilities that servers may request from the client/host side.
Explain how sampling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect sampling with roots and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP is bidirectional: clients can expose features to servers. Sampling lets a server request model generation through the host under host/user controls; roots describe filesystem or URI boundaries the client makes available; elicitation lets a server request additional user information.
lessons.explain: MCP is bidirectional: clients can expose features to servers. Sampling lets a server request model generation through the host under host/user controls; roots describe filesystem or URI boundaries the client makes available; elicitation lets a server request additional user information.

client_caps={"sampling":True,"roots":["file:///workspace"],"elicitation":True}
print(client_caps)
lessons.example:
client_caps={"sampling":True,"roots":["file:///workspace"],"elicitation":True}

commonMistakes: A server should never assume a client supports sampling, roots, or elicitation unless the capability was negotiated.

lessons.title: Authorization for remote MCP servers
objectives: Explain the authorization boundary for HTTP-based MCP without token passthrough.
Explain how OAuth 2.1 changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect OAuth 2.1 with authorization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Remote MCP authorization follows modern OAuth-based patterns. The client discovers authorization metadata, obtains an access token intended for the specific MCP resource, and sends it in the Authorization header.
lessons.explain: Remote MCP authorization follows modern OAuth-based patterns. The client discovers authorization metadata, obtains an access token intended for the specific MCP resource, and sends it in the Authorization header.
examples:
request={"resource":"https://mcp.example.com","scope":"orders.read","header":"Authorization: Bearer <token>"}
print(request["resource"],request["scope"])
lessons.example:
request={"resource":"https://mcp.example.com","scope":"orders.read","header":"Authorization: Bearer <token>"}
print(request["resource"],request["scope"])
commonMistakes: Token passthrough to an unrelated downstream API can expose credentials to the wrong audience and violates the intended authorization boundary.

lessons.title: MCP security, consent & trust boundaries
objectives: Design MCP integrations assuming server data and tool descriptions can be untrusted.
Explain how consent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect consent with tool safety and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP enables data access and code-execution paths, so hosts need explicit consent, clear capability visibility, least privilege, input/output validation, and isolation for risky operations. Resource content or tool descriptions may contain malicious or misleading instructions; the host should not treat server-provided text as trusted policy.
lessons.explain: MCP enables data access and code-execution paths, so hosts need explicit consent, clear capability visibility, least privilege, input/output validation, and isolation for risky operations. Resource content or tool descriptions may contain malicious or misleading instructions; the host should not treat server-provided text as trusted policy.
examples:
policy={"read_docs":True,"delete_files":False,"send_email":"requires_approval"}
print(policy)
lessons.example:
policy={"read_docs":True,"delete_files":False,"send_email":"requires_approval"}
print(policy)
commonMistakes: Connecting a server and automatically approving every tool invocation turns interoperability into an unnecessarily large security blast radius.

lessons.title: Errors, progress, cancellation, logging & protocol tests
objectives: Build observable MCP integrations that fail cleanly and can be tested without manual clicking.

lessons.explanation: Production protocol integrations need predictable errors, cancellation, timeouts, progress signals, logs, and compatibility tests. JSON-RPC errors should distinguish invalid requests from application failures, long-running operations should respect cancellation, and logs must not corrupt transport streams or expose secrets.
lessons.explain: Production protocol integrations need predictable errors, cancellation, timeouts, progress signals, logs, and compatibility tests. JSON-RPC errors should distinguish invalid requests from application failures, long-running operations should respect cancellation, and logs must not corrupt transport streams or expose secrets.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an agent from a chatbot?
options: it's faster
it takes actions via tools
it's smaller
it needs no LLM

options: train-test
observe-think-act
map-reduce
fetch-render

quiz.q: In function calling, who actually executes the tool?
options: the LLM itself
your application code, based on the model's structured request
the user manually
the vector database

quiz.q: Least privilege for an agent means:
options: giving it every tool available just in case
scoping its tool access to only what its task actually requires
disabling all tool use
giving it admin access to simplify development

quiz.q: An agent is LESS appropriate than a simple deterministic script when:
options: the task requires real judgment and adaptation
the task is a fixed, predictable sequence with no real decisions needed
the task involves multiple tools
the task changes based on context

quiz.q: What does 'the model decides, code executes' describe in function calling?
options: the model directly executes code itself
the model decides WHICH tool to call and with what arguments, while separate code actually performs the action
code decides which model to call
this describes training, not inference

quiz.q: What is a tool definition, in an agent system?
options: the agent's training data
a description of an available action (name, parameters, purpose) the model can choose to invoke
a synonym for a prompt template
the agent's memory storage

quiz.q: What is short-term memory in an agent system?
options: permanent storage across all sessions ever
context retained within the current task/session, typically lost once it ends
a synonym for long-term memory
irrelevant to agent behavior

quiz.q: What is long-term memory in an agent system?
options: memory that lasts only one step
information persisted across sessions, often via external storage, so it's available in future interactions
a synonym for short-term memory
never used in real agent systems

quiz.q: Why does long-term memory typically require external persistence?
options: it doesn't require anything special
without saving state outside the model's own transient context, information wouldn't survive between separate sessions
external storage is never necessary for long-term memory
models retain everything permanently by default

quiz.q: What does reflection mean in an agentic workflow?
options: ignoring past actions entirely
having the agent evaluate its own previous output or reasoning to catch mistakes before proceeding
a synonym for planning
only relevant for image-generating agents

quiz.q: What is self-verification in agent systems?
options: skipping all verification for speed
the agent checking its own work against expected criteria before considering a step complete
a synonym for human-in-the-loop approval
only used during training, never inference

quiz.q: What distinguishes a multi-agent system from a single-agent workflow?
options: there's no real difference
multiple specialized agents collaborate, each often handling a distinct role, versus one agent handling everything
multi-agent systems never communicate with each other
single-agent workflows always perform better

quiz.q: What is coordination overhead in multi-agent systems?
options: a benefit with no downsides
the added complexity and cost of managing communication and hand-offs between multiple agents
a synonym for memory persistence
only relevant for single-agent systems

quiz.q: Why include human-in-the-loop approval for certain agent actions?
options: approval steps are always unnecessary friction
some actions are irreversible or high-stakes enough that a human check before execution reduces real risk
human approval only applies to low-stakes actions
this concept doesn't apply to real agent systems

quiz.q: What does 'least privilege' mean for an agent's tool access?
options: giving an agent access to every possible tool
granting only the minimum permissions/tools actually needed for its task, limiting potential damage from mistakes or misuse
least privilege means no tools at all
privilege level has no security relevance

quiz.q: Why gate irreversible actions (like deleting data) more strictly than reversible ones?
options: irreversible actions need no special handling
a mistake on an irreversible action can't simply be undone, so extra caution (like approval) reduces real, permanent harm
all actions carry identical risk
gating irreversible actions is only relevant for financial systems

quiz.q: What is a retry/fallback strategy in agent error handling?
options: ignoring all errors permanently
having a defined response when a step fails, like retrying, trying an alternative approach, or escalating to a human
a synonym for planning
only relevant during training

quiz.q: Why is end-to-end task evaluation important for agents, not just per-step correctness?
options: per-step correctness is always sufficient
an agent can execute each individual step 'correctly' yet still fail to accomplish the actual overall goal
end-to-end evaluation is never practical for agents
this only matters for single-step tasks

quiz.q: What is injection-driven tool misuse?
options: a hardware failure
malicious input tricking an agent into misusing its available tools in unintended, potentially harmful ways
a synonym for reflection
only a risk for agents with no tool access

quiz.q: What does 'blast radius of tool access' refer to?
options: the physical location of a server
how much potential damage an agent could cause given the tools and permissions it has access to
a synonym for context window
irrelevant to agent security

quiz.q: When does 'a script beat an agent'?
options: scripts are never a better choice than agents
when the task follows a fixed, predictable sequence of steps that doesn't require dynamic, model-driven decisions
scripts always underperform agents regardless of task
this comparison doesn't apply in practice

quiz.q: What is the agent loop, at a high level?
options: a single one-shot model call with no iteration
a repeating cycle of observing state, deciding an action (often via a tool), executing it, and incorporating the result before deciding the next step
a synonym for training loop specifically for language models
only relevant for image-generating systems

quiz.q: What does 'planning' mean in an agentic system?

the agent determining a sequence of steps likely to accomplish a goal before or while acting
a synonym for memory
only relevant for multi-agent systems

quiz.q: Why might an agent need to dynamically re-plan mid-task?
options: re-planning is never necessary

title: Docker
description: Containers, images, Dockerfiles, and Compose for reproducible environments.
blurb: Containers, images, Dockerfiles, and Compose for reproducible environments.
careerApplications: 'It works on my machine' is a real, common failure mode Docker exists to eliminate — expected baseline knowledge for most SWE roles.

beginner: Basic docker CLI (run, ps, stop, logs)

lessons.title: Why containers exist
objectives: State the problem containers solve
Distinguish a container from a VM
Explain how container changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect container with virtual machine and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: 'It works on my machine' happens because your machine has different OS versions, library versions, and config than the server. A container packages your app WITH its exact dependencies into one portable unit that runs identically anywhere Docker is installed.
examples:
# Without Docker: 'runs fine locally, breaks in prod'
# because prod has Python 3.9 and your machine has 3.12

# With Docker: the container HAS Python 3.9 baked in,
# identical everywhere
commonMistakes: Thinking a container IS a lightweight VM — it isn't; it shares the host kernel, which is exactly why it's fast but also why it isn't as isolated as a real VM.
lessons.careerRelevance: Virtually every modern deployment pipeline assumes your app is containerized.

lessons.title: Images vs containers
objectives: Define image and container precisely
Explain the relationship between them
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: container registry.
lessons.explanation: An image is a read-only template — your app plus its dependencies, frozen as a set of layered files. A container is a running instance of that image, with its own writable layer on top.
examples:
docker images        # list images (the templates)
docker ps             # list running containers (instances)
docker run python:3.11  # spins up a NEW container from the python:3.11 image
commonMistakes: Confusing 'stopping a container' with 'deleting the image' — stopping just pauses the running instance; the image (template) is untouched.
lessons.careerRelevance: This class/object mental model is exactly how you'll reason about containers day to day. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: An image is a read-only template — your app plus its dependencies, frozen as a set of layered files. A container is a running instance of that image, with its own writable layer on top.

lessons.title: Basic docker CLI
objectives: Run, list, stop, and inspect containers from the command line
Explain how docker run changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect docker run with docker ps and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A small set of commands covers most day-to-day container use: `docker run` starts a new container from an image, `docker ps` lists running containers, `docker stop` gracefully stops one, and `docker logs` shows its output — essential for debugging.
examples:
docker run -d --name myapp -p 8000:8000 myimage
docker ps
docker logs myapp
docker stop myapp
commonMistakes: Forgetting `-p` (port mapping) and then wondering why the app 'isn't responding' — the container is running, but nothing outside it can reach the port.
lessons.careerRelevance: You'll run these commands dozens of times a day once containers are part of your workflow.

lessons.title: Writing a Dockerfile
objectives: Write a Dockerfile that builds a working image
Explain each common instruction
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: HEALTHCHECK.
lessons.explanation: A Dockerfile is a recipe for building an image: FROM picks a base image, COPY brings in your code, RUN executes setup commands (like installing dependencies) at build time, and CMD specifies what runs when the container starts.
examples:
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
commonMistakes: Copying all your code BEFORE installing dependencies — this busts the build cache on every code change, since Docker rebuilds every layer after the first one that changed.
lessons.careerRelevance: Writing a correct, efficient Dockerfile is a common practical task in backend/SWE interviews and onboarding. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Volumes & persisting data
objectives: Explain why container data is ephemeral by default
Use a volume to persist data
Explain how volume changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect volume with ephemeral storage and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed — anything your app wrote (a database file, uploaded images) is gone too, unless you use a volume: a directory managed by Docker (or mounted from the host) that survives container restarts and removal.
examples:
docker run -v mydata:/app/data myimage
# 'mydata' volume persists even if the container is deleted and recreated
commonMistakes: Storing a database's data files inside the container with no volume — a routine `docker rm` silently wipes the database.
lessons.careerRelevance: Any containerized service with real data (a database, file uploads) needs volumes to be production-safe.
lessons.explain: A container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed — anything your app wrote (a database file, uploaded images) is gone too, unless you use a volume: a directory managed by Docker (or mounted from the host) that survives container restarts and removal.

lessons.title: Docker Compose for multi-container apps
objectives: Read and write a docker-compose.yml for a multi-service app
Explain how docker-compose.yml changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect docker-compose.yml with services and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Real apps are rarely one container — a web app + a database + a cache is typical. Docker Compose lets you define all of them, plus how they connect, in one YAML file, and bring the whole stack up or down with a single command.
examples:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on: [db]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
commonMistakes: Assuming `depends_on` waits for the database to be READY (accepting connections) — it only waits for the container to START, which is not the same thing; apps often need their own retry.
lessons.careerRelevance: Local development environments for most real projects are defined with Compose.

lessons.title: Multi-Stage Builds & Image Optimization
objectives: Use multi-stage builds to keep production images small and free of build-time dependencies
Explain how multi-stage build changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect multi-stage build with build stage and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A naive Dockerfile often ships the whole build toolchain (compilers, dev dependencies, source maps) inside the final image, even though none of that is needed to actually RUN the app -- this bloats image size and increases attack surface.
examples:
# Stage 1: build
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: run -- only the compiled output ships, not node_modules or source
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
commonMistakes: Shipping the entire build stage (compilers, dev dependencies, source files) in the final image because it's simpler than setting up a second stage -- this can make images several times.
lessons.careerRelevance: Multi-stage builds are the standard, expected way to keep production images lean in any real containerized deployment -- an interviewer will notice if a candidate ships an unoptimized image without knowing why it matters.
lessons.explain: A naive Dockerfile often ships the whole build toolchain (compilers, dev dependencies, source maps) inside the final image, even though none of that is needed to actually RUN the app -- this bloats image size and increases attack surface.
lessons.example:
# Stage 1: build
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: run -- only the compiled output ships, not node_modules or source
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

lessons.title: Container Networking & Environment Configuration
objectives: Configure containers with environment variables and understand how containers reach each other over Docker's network
Explain how environment variable changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect environment variable with env-file and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Environment variables (passed via `docker run -e KEY=value` or an `--env-file`, or the `environment:` section in Compose) let the same image behave differently across environments -- a database URL, an API key, a feature flag -- without baking those values into the image itself, which also keeps secrets out of version control.
examples:
docker run -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/app -e DEBUG=false my-app

# in docker-compose.yml, a Flask service reaching a Redis service:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    environment:
      - REDIS_HOST=redis   # service name, NOT localhost
  redis:
    image: redis:7
commonMistakes: Using `localhost` to reach another container -- from inside a container, localhost refers to that container itself, not the host machine or a sibling service; use the other service's name on.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly configuring environment variables and inter-container networking is what separates a container that works on one machine from a deployable, environment-agnostic service.

interviewPreparation.q: Why would you use a multi-stage build instead of a single-stage Dockerfile?
interviewPreparation.a: A single-stage build often ships build tools, dev dependencies, and source files that aren't needed to run the app, bloating the image and increasing attack surface. A multi-stage build compiles or installs in an early stage, then copies only the finished artifacts into a fresh, minimal final stage -- meaningfully smaller and cleaner images.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does a container exit immediately if its main process finishes, unlike a virtual machine?
interviewPreparation.a: A container's lifecycle is tied directly to its main process (the CMD/ENTRYPOINT) -- there's no separate 'OS' running underneath that keeps going. A VM keeps running its guest OS regardless of any single process; a container IS essentially that one process, so when it exits, the container exits with it.

interviewPreparation.q: How do two containers in the same Docker Compose project actually reach each other?
interviewPreparation.a: By service name, over the shared bridge network Compose creates automatically -- not by localhost or a hardcoded IP. A web service reaches a database service at `db:5432`, for example, because Compose's internal DNS resolves service names to the right container.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you handle configuration (like a database URL or API key) that differs between dev, staging, and production?
interviewPreparation.a: Environment variables, injected at run time (via `-e`, an env file, or Compose's environment section) rather than baked into the image -- the same image should work across environments, with only its configuration changing, and secrets specifically should never be committed into the image or version control.

interviewPreparation.q: A container works fine on your machine but fails in a teammate's environment. What would you check?
interviewPreparation.a: Whether the failure is actually environment-specific config (missing env vars, a different port already in use) versus something baked into the image that assumed your local setup -- `docker logs` and comparing exact environment variables between the two setups usually narrows it down quickly.

capstone.title: Package and deploy your Backend + API system with Docker
capstone.description: Take the backend service and API you already built (from the Backend and APIs capstones, or equivalents) and make them genuinely deployable: multi-stage Dockerfiles that keep images lean, a Compose setup that wires the service to its real dependencies (a database, a cache), environment-based configuration instead of hardcoded values, and a documented account of at least one real container failure you hit and how you debugged it. This capstone isn't about building new backend logic -- it's about proving you can package and run what you already built reliably.
deliverables: A multi-stage Dockerfile for the service, with a documented before/after image size comparison
A docker-compose.yml wiring the service to at least one real dependency (database and/or cache) via service-name networking, not hardcoded IPs
Configuration driven by environment variables (e.g. database URL, debug flag) -- nothing environment-specific hardcoded into the image
A short written account of one real container failure you hit while building this (a crash, a networking issue, a build cache problem) and exactly how you diagnosed and fixed it
Volumes correctly used for anything that needs to persist across container restarts (e.g. database data)
capstone.portfolioTips: The image-size comparison and the real debugging story are the two things that make this capstone distinct from 'I wrote a Dockerfile' -- they're concrete, specific evidence that you understand why multi-stage builds and container lifecycle matter, not just the syntax.

lessons.title: Tokenizers in practice
objectives: Use a Hugging Face tokenizer's practical output correctly

lessons.explanation: You already know conceptually why sub-word tokenization exists (from the Transformers and LLMs tracks) -- this lesson is about using the actual tokenizer object. Calling a tokenizer returns input_ids (the token IDs the model expects) and an attention_mask (marking real tokens vs padding, so the model ignores padded positions).
examples:
tokenizer(['Hi', 'A much longer sentence here'], padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors='pt')
# input_ids:      padded token ID sequences, same length across the batch
# attention_mask:  1s for real tokens, 0s for padding -- tells the model what to ignore
commonMistakes: Forgetting padding=True when tokenizing a batch of different-length sequences -- this causes a shape-mismatch error, since the model needs every sequence in a batch to be the same length.

lessons.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: LoRA and QLoRA
objectives: Explain LoRA and QLoRA conceptually, and choose between full fine-tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA for a given constraint
Explain how LoRA (rank, alpha, target modules, dropout) changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect LoRA (rank, alpha, target modules, dropout) with QLoRA (quantized-base training) and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Full fine-tuning updates every parameter in a model -- expensive in memory and compute, and requires storing a full new copy of the model per fine-tuned variant.
examples:
# the core trade-off, without matrix derivations:
# full fine-tuning: EVERY parameter trains -- most capacity, most memory/compute cost
# LoRA: base model FROZEN, small adapter matrices train -- far less memory, a
# small extra file saved separately from the (unchanged) base model
# QLoRA: LoRA's adapter training, but the FROZEN base model is also quantized
# during training specifically to fit in less memory -- this is TRAINING-time
# quantization of the base, not the same as quantizing a model for inference only
commonMistakes: Assuming QLoRA and inference-time quantization are the same technique -- QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model specifically to make TRAINING fit in less memory, while inference quantization.
lessons.careerRelevance: LoRA and QLoRA are now the standard, default way most real fine-tuning work is actually done in practice, given how much cheaper they are than full fine-tuning for most use cases.

# why label masking matters -- training on the WRONG tokens changes the task:
