exercises.hint: CAP's trade-off only applies DURING a network partition -- when the network is healthy, a well-designed system can offer both consistency and availability

exercises.title: Pick the right consistency model
exercises.prompt: For a live view-counter on a video (shown publicly, briefly stale is fine) versus an account balance (must never show a stale, too-high number a user could act on) -- which consistency model fits each?
exercises.hint: view counter: eventual consistency is fine. Account balance: needs strong consistency, since a stale read could let a user overdraw

exercises.title: Diagnose a silent failure
exercises.prompt: A service wraps every downstream call in a try/except that logs nothing and returns a default value on any error. Weeks later, a critical downstream outage went completely unnoticed. What's the actual root cause here, and what should change?
exercises.hint: the silent catch-and-ignore itself is the root cause -- it should log the error clearly (and likely alert) even while still returning a safe default, rather than hiding the failure entirely

exercises.title: Design an idempotency key
exercises.prompt: A client submits an order twice due to a lost response (same order, retried). What would you use as the idempotency key, and where should the server check it before processing?
exercises.hint: a client-generated unique ID sent with the request (e.g. a UUID); the server checks it BEFORE processing, and if already seen, returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate order

exercises.title: Trace exponential backoff
exercises.prompt: With base_delay=1 and doubling each retry, what are the wait times before attempts 2, 3, and 4?
exercises.hint: 1, 2, 4 -- doubling from the base delay each time

exercises.title: Trace a circuit breaker's states
exercises.prompt: A circuit breaker has failure_threshold=2. It sees: fail, fail, (circuit opens), a request comes in immediately after (before the cooldown), then after the cooldown a test request succeeds. What state is the circuit in after each event?
exercises.hint: CLOSED, CLOSED->OPEN (2nd failure hits threshold), still OPEN (rejected, cooldown not done), HALF-OPEN then CLOSED (test request succeeds)

exercises.title: Diagnose a split-brain risk
exercises.prompt: A leader-elected system re-elects a new leader after 5 seconds of no heartbeat, but the old leader (just slow, not actually dead) resumes normal operation 6 seconds later, unaware a new leader was elected. What's the risk, and what should the system check before acting as leader again?
exercises.hint: both nodes might now believe they're the leader (split brain); the old leader should check whether a newer leader term/epoch exists before resuming leader actions, and step down if so

exercises.title: Diagnose a distributed lock bug
exercises.prompt: Node A acquires a distributed lock with a 10-second expiry, then pauses (garbage collection) for 15 seconds. What happens to the lock, and what's the resulting risk?
exercises.hint: the lock expires while node A is paused; another node can correctly acquire it; when node A resumes, it still believes it holds the lock -- now two nodes both think they have exclusive access

exercises.title: Choose direct call or message queue
exercises.prompt: A checkout flow needs to send a confirmation email after payment succeeds. Should this be a direct synchronous call, or published to a queue? Why?
exercises.hint: a queue -- the email service being temporarily down shouldn't fail or delay the actual checkout; the message can wait in the queue and be sent once the email service recovers

exercises.title: Explain a message-ordering gotcha
exercises.prompt: A team assumes their message queue delivers all messages in the exact order they were published, globally. What's the likely gap in this assumption, and how would you verify it for their specific queue?
exercises.hint: most real queues (for scalability) only guarantee ordering per-partition/per-key, not globally across all partitions -- check the specific queue's documentation and partition/key strategy

exercises.title: Explain async I/O's benefit at scale
exercises.prompt: A service needs to handle 5,000 concurrent slow network calls. Explain, in your own words, why a small thread pool with async I/O handles this better than one thread per connection.
exercises.hint: one-thread-per-connection means 5,000 threads mostly sitting idle waiting, with real memory/context-switching overhead; async I/O lets a small number of threads juggle many in-flight operations, resuming each only when its result is ready

exercises.title: Decide whether to use a coordination service
exercises.prompt: A team is about to hand-write their own leader-election logic from scratch for a new service. What would you ask them before they start, and what would you suggest instead?
exercises.hint: ask whether they've considered using an existing coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul) instead -- leader election is a genuinely hard, easy-to-get-wrong problem that's already been solved and heavily tested elsewhere

exercises.title: Explain why a trace ID matters
exercises.prompt: A request is slow, and it touched 6 different microservices. Without a shared trace ID, why is this hard to debug -- and what does the trace ID actually fix?
exercises.hint: each service's logs are separate with no way to connect them into one request's story; a shared trace ID logged by every service lets you reconstruct exactly which service in the chain caused the delay

exercises.title: Apply the failure-first mindset
exercises.prompt: You're designing a new service that calls two downstream APIs. Before writing the happy-path code, list at least 3 concrete failure modes you should design for first.
exercises.hint: examples: either downstream API times out or errors (need retries/circuit breakers), a request gets duplicated by a client retry (need idempotency), one downstream API is slow but not failed (need a sane timeout so it doesn't block everything)

exercises.title: Diagnose an availability vs consistency choice
exercises.prompt: During a network partition, a shopping cart service chooses to keep accepting adds-to-cart on every node, resolving conflicts later, rather than rejecting requests it can't verify are consistent. Which side of the CAP trade-off did it choose, and is that a reasonable choice for a shopping cart specifically?
exercises.hint: it chose availability (AP) over strict consistency; reasonable for a shopping cart, since a temporarily-inconsistent cart that gets reconciled later is a much smaller problem than rejecting a user's ability to add items during a partition

exercises.title: Combine idempotency with retries
exercises.prompt: A client uses exponential backoff to retry a failed payment request up to 4 times. Without an idempotency key, what could go wrong even with well-designed backoff?
exercises.hint: backoff controls WHEN retries happen, not WHETHER they're safe -- without an idempotency key, if an earlier attempt actually succeeded server-side but the response was lost, a well-spaced retry can still duplicate the charge

projects.title: Consistent hash ring simulator
projects.desc: Build a simulator showing key-to-node assignment on a hash ring, and demonstrate that adding/removing a node reassigns only a minority of keys.

projects.title: Retry-and-circuit-breaker client wrapper
projects.desc: Wrap an unreliable (simulated) API call with exponential backoff and a circuit breaker, demonstrating all three circuit states under sustained failure and recovery.

projects.title: Idempotent request processor
projects.desc: Build a request handler that deduplicates retried requests using an idempotency key, with a test suite proving duplicate requests never double-process.

projects.title: Simplified leader election simulator
projects.desc: Implement the bully algorithm across a set of simulated nodes, correctly handling leader failure and re-election.

projects.title: Event-driven order pipeline (simulated)
projects.desc: Design a simulated order-processing pipeline where services communicate via published events rather than direct calls, demonstrating that a temporarily-down consumer doesn't block the producer.

interviewPreparation.q: Explain the CAP theorem precisely -- what exactly does it claim, and what's the most common way people misstate it?
interviewPreparation.a: During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response, even if possibly stale) -- it can't guarantee both simultaneously during that partition. The most common misreading treats this as a permanent, all-the-time trade-off, when it specifically only applies during partition conditions; a well-designed system can offer both when the network is healthy.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does an idempotency key matter for a payment API specifically?
interviewPreparation.a: Networks can lose a response even after the server successfully processed a request. Without an idempotency key, a client's retry (believing the original attempt failed) would cause the server to process the same payment a second time. The idempotency key lets the server recognize the retry and return the original result instead of duplicating the charge.

interviewPreparation.q: Walk through what a circuit breaker does and why immediate, unlimited retries can make an outage worse.
interviewPreparation.a: A circuit breaker tracks consecutive failures; once a threshold is hit, it moves to OPEN and rejects requests immediately without adding more load to the struggling downstream service, then cautiously tests recovery via a HALF-OPEN state before fully resuming. Without this, every caller retrying immediately and repeatedly floods an already-overloaded service with even more traffic, which can turn a partial slowdown into a full outage.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is consistent hashing preferred over naive hash(key) % N partitioning in a system that will scale up or down?
interviewPreparation.a: Naive modulo hashing reassigns almost every key when the node count changes, since the modulo result shifts for nearly all keys. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a conceptual ring, so adding or removing a node only reassigns the keys between it and its neighbor -- a minority of keys, not nearly all of them.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between a message queue and a direct API call, in terms of failure behavior?
interviewPreparation.a: A direct call fails immediately if the receiving service is down. A message queue decouples the two -- the message waits in the queue until a consumer is available, meaning a temporarily-down consumer doesn't cause the sender to fail at all, at the cost of not getting an immediate confirmation that the work is fully done.

capstone.title: Design and Simulate a Fault-Tolerant Distributed Service
capstone.description: Design a small distributed service (e.g. a simplified order-processing system) that explicitly handles replication, partitioning, retries with backoff, a circuit breaker, idempotent request handling, and leader election for a coordinator role -- then simulate at least 3 realistic failure scenarios and show the system behaving correctly (or explain precisely what it sacrifices and why).
deliverables: An architecture diagram showing replication, partitioning strategy, and where a coordinator/leader role is needed

A working simulation of at least 3 failure scenarios: a node failure requiring leader re-election, a downstream service becoming unavailable (triggering circuit-breaker behavior), and a duplicated client request (proving idempotent handling)
A written explanation of which consistency model was chosen for which piece of data, and why -- tied to CAP trade-offs specific to this system
Test cases proving idempotent handling actually prevents duplicate processing
A short section explicitly stating what this design deliberately sacrifices (e.g. some staleness window, or added latency) and why that trade-off was chosen
capstone.portfolioTips: Explicitly stating what your design SACRIFICES (not just what it achieves) is exactly the kind of trade-off-aware thinking senior system-design interviews are testing for -- most candidates only describe the happy path.

industryUsage.usage: DynamoDB uses consistent hashing for partitioning and offers tunable consistency (strong or eventual) per request -- a direct, production example of nearly every concept in this course.
Popularized the circuit-breaker pattern (via their Hystrix library) specifically to prevent cascading failures across their large microservices architecture.
Requires an idempotency key on payment-creation API calls specifically to make retries after a lost response safe -- one of the clearest real-world idempotency examples in production use.

careerApplications: Used by backend, platform, cloud, and infrastructure engineers to design reliable services across multiple machines, including replication, consistency, coordination, retries, queues, and failure handling.

title: Model & App Deployment
blurb: Run applications and models reliably in production: service boundaries, configuration, health, artifacts, observability, scaling, and runtime safety.

intermediate: Serving an ML model as an API

lessons.title: From local code to a production service
lessons.explain: Deployment turns local code into a reliable service other people or systems can call. Define a stable service interface, package the runtime, externalize configuration, expose health signals, and verify startup/shutdown behavior.
objectives: Turn local code into a callable service
Identify runtime requirements separate from CI/CD automation
Explain how service interface changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect service interface with runtime packaging and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Deploying code that works locally without accounting for environment differences (dependencies, config) between local and production.
lessons.explanation: Deployment turns local code into a reliable service other people or systems can call. Define a stable service interface, package the runtime, externalize configuration, expose health signals, and verify startup/shutdown behavior.

lessons.title: Service contracts, health checks & readiness
objectives: Separate liveness from readiness
Design health endpoints that do not lie about dependencies
Explain how liveness changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect liveness with readiness and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A deployed service needs a clear contract and health signals. Liveness answers whether the process is alive; readiness answers whether it can safely receive traffic.
commonMistakes: Returning “healthy” before required startup work is complete can send real traffic to a service that cannot serve it.
lessons.explain: A deployed service needs a clear contract and health signals. Liveness answers whether the process is alive; readiness answers whether it can safely receive traffic.

lessons.title: Deployment Prerequisites: Containers & Configuration
objectives: Explain what a container provides
Explain how container changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect container with portable and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before continuing in Deployment, you should already be comfortable with what's covered in the Docker course: a container packages an application together with its dependencies and runtime, making it portable across machines -- this is exactly why "it works on my machine" becomes less of a problem.
examples:
# Deployment assumes you can already do this from Docker:
# - write a Dockerfile and build an image
# - run docker-compose for a multi-service local setup
# - configure environment variables and container networking
#
# If any of this is unfamiliar, review the Docker course first --
# Deployment picks up from here: shipping that container safely.
commonMistakes: Skipping straight into CI/CD and release strategy without solid Docker fundamentals -- Deployment assumes containerization is already comfortable, and gaps there make the actual Deployment.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing what you're expected to already know is as useful as the content itself -- this checkpoint exists so the rest of Deployment can focus entirely on what it actually owns.
lessons.explain: Before continuing in Deployment, you should already be comfortable with what's covered in the Docker course: a container packages an application together with its dependencies and runtime, making it portable across machines -- this is exactly why "it works on my machine" becomes less of a problem.

lessons.title: Environment variables & configuration
objectives: Use environment variables to separate configuration from code
Explain how environment variables changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect environment variables with configuration and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Environment variables store configuration (API keys, database URLs, feature flags) OUTSIDE the codebase itself, so the same code can run differently in development, staging, and production just by changing the environment it runs in -- without ever hardcoding secrets or environment-specific values directly into source code.
examples:
import os
database_url = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')
api_key = os.environ.get('API_KEY')
# the SAME code runs against different databases/keys per environment
commonMistakes: Hardcoding a secret or environment-specific value (like a production database URL) directly into source code -- this leaks into version control and can't differ across environments.
lessons.careerRelevance: Separating configuration from code via environment variables is a basic, expected practice in any real deployed application.
lessons.explain: Environment variables store configuration (API keys, database URLs, feature flags) OUTSIDE the codebase itself, so the same code can run differently in development, staging, and production just by changing the environment it runs in -- without ever hardcoding secrets or environment-specific values directly into source code.
lessons.example:
import os
database_url = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')
api_key = os.environ.get('API_KEY')
# the SAME code runs against different databases/keys per environment

lessons.title: Artifacts, model loading & startup lifecycle
objectives: Version runtime artifacts
Load large artifacts once at startup
Fail fast when required artifacts are invalid
lessons.explanation: Production services often depend on model weights, indexes, templates, or other versioned artifacts. Load expensive immutable artifacts during startup rather than once per request, validate their version/checksum, and make startup fail clearly if a required artifact is missing or incompatible.
examples:
from pathlib import Path
MODEL = Path('model.bin')
if not MODEL.exists():
    raise RuntimeError('required model artifact missing')
# load once during startup, then reuse for requests
commonMistakes: Loading a large model or index on every request destroys latency and can exhaust memory under concurrency.
lessons.explain: Production services often depend on model weights, indexes, templates, or other versioned artifacts. Load expensive immutable artifacts during startup rather than once per request, validate their version/checksum, and make startup fail clearly if a required artifact is missing or incompatible.

lessons.title: Logging in production
objectives: Explain why structured, leveled logging matters in production
Explain how logging changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect logging with log levels and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Once code is running in production, you can't attach a debugger to it the way you can locally -- logging is often your only window into what actually happened.
examples:
import logging
logging.info('Order %s processed successfully', order_id)
logging.error('Payment failed for order %s: %s', order_id, error_message)
commonMistakes: Relying only on print statements in a deployed production system -- these aren't leveled, searchable, or aggregable the way real logging is.
lessons.careerRelevance: Production-quality logging is what makes a real deployed system's problems actually debuggable after the fact.
lessons.explain: Once code is running in production, you can't attach a debugger to it the way you can locally -- logging is often your only window into what actually happened.
lessons.example:
import logging
logging.info('Order %s processed successfully', order_id)
logging.error('Payment failed for order %s: %s', order_id, error_message)

lessons.title: Monitoring & alerting
objectives: Explain what monitoring and alerting provide in production
Explain how monitoring changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect monitoring with alerting and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Monitoring continuously tracks a system's health (error rates, response times, resource usage) so problems can be noticed proactively, rather than only when a user complains.
examples:
# example alert rule:
# if error_rate > 5% for more than 2 minutes -> page the on-call engineer
# without this, the team might not notice until customers start complaining
commonMistakes: Having no automated alerting and relying on customers or manual dashboard-checking to notice real production problems.
lessons.careerRelevance: Monitoring and alerting are what let a real engineering team respond to production issues quickly, not just eventually.
lessons.explain: Monitoring continuously tracks a system's health (error rates, response times, resource usage) so problems can be noticed proactively, rather than only when a user complains.
lessons.example:

# if error_rate > 5% for more than 2 minutes -> page the on-call engineer

lessons.title: Scaling workers, concurrency & resource limits
objectives: Choose a worker/concurrency model
Set explicit resource limits
Recognize CPU-bound vs I/O-bound serving constraints
lessons.explanation: Scaling is not just adding replicas. Decide how many requests one process can safely handle, whether work is CPU-bound or I/O-bound, how much memory each worker consumes, and when horizontal replicas are safer than increasing concurrency inside one process.
examples:
workers = 4
memory_per_worker_mb = 700
print('estimated memory MB:', workers * memory_per_worker_mb)
commonMistakes: Increasing worker count without measuring memory or CPU can make a service slower or cause out-of-memory restarts.
lessons.explain: Scaling is not just adding replicas. Decide how many requests one process can safely handle, whether work is CPU-bound or I/O-bound, how much memory each worker consumes, and when horizontal replicas are safer than increasing concurrency inside one process.

lessons.title: Timeouts, graceful shutdown & runtime failure
objectives: Use timeouts around external calls
Stop accepting new work during shutdown
Let in-flight work finish or cancel safely
lessons.explanation: Production processes are restarted, rescheduled, and terminated. External calls need timeouts so requests cannot hang forever, and shutdown should stop new work before releasing resources.
examples:
# shutdown sequence, conceptually:
# 1. mark readiness = false
# 2. stop accepting new requests
# 3. wait briefly for in-flight work
# 4. close clients/files and exit
commonMistakes: Ignoring termination signals can drop in-flight requests and leave external resources in an uncertain state.
lessons.explain: Production processes are restarted, rescheduled, and terminated. External calls need timeouts so requests cannot hang forever, and shutdown should stop new work before releasing resources.

lessons.title: Post-deploy smoke tests & runtime validation
objectives: Verify a deployed service through its public boundary
Check critical dependencies and one realistic request
Separate deployment validation from the CI pipeline itself
lessons.explanation: After a service starts, validate the actual deployed runtime: call the health/readiness endpoints, send one realistic request through the public interface, verify a critical dependency, and confirm logs/metrics appear. CI/CD decides how a release is delivered; smoke validation proves the running instance actually works.
examples:
# conceptual smoke checks
checks = ['GET /health -> 200', 'GET /ready -> 200', 'POST /predict sample -> valid schema', 'metric emitted']
for check in checks:
    print('verify:', check)
commonMistakes: Treating “the deployment command succeeded” as proof the application is usable misses startup, dependency, and routing failures.
lessons.explain: After a service starts, validate the actual deployed runtime: call the health/readiness endpoints, send one realistic request through the public interface, verify a critical dependency, and confirm logs/metrics appear. CI/CD decides how a release is delivered; smoke validation proves the running instance actually works.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between blue-green deployment and canary release, and when would you choose one over the other?
interviewPreparation.a: Blue-green switches all traffic at once between two full environments, with instant rollback by switching back -- simple, but a bad release still affects 100% of users the moment it's live. Canary ramps gradually (5%, 25%, 100%), catching problems while only a fraction of users are affected, at the cost of more complexity and a slower rollout. Canary is usually preferred when the blast radius of a bad release matters more than rollout speed.

interviewPreparation.q: How do feature flags change the relationship between deploying and releasing?
interviewPreparation.a: They decouple the two: code can be deployed to production dark (present but inactive) and released to users separately, gradually, or instantly reverted by flipping the flag off -- no new deploy needed. This means a bad feature can be turned off in seconds instead of requiring a rollback deploy.

interviewPreparation.q: A canary release looked healthy the whole time but a bad version still reached all users. What would you investigate?
interviewPreparation.a: Whether the health checks and canary duration actually matched the failure mode -- a canary that only runs for a minute won't catch a slow memory leak or a failure that only appears under sustained load. The canary process needs to run long enough, and check the right signals, for the specific ways this deploy could actually fail.

interviewPreparation.q: Why might 'the server responds to a health check' not be a sufficient signal that a release is actually healthy?
interviewPreparation.a: A server can respond to a basic ping while a specific endpoint is broken, a downstream dependency is failing, or error rates are elevated on real traffic -- a shallow health check only proves the process is running, not that it's doing its job correctly. Real health checks should reflect the actual behavior you care about, not just process liveness.

interviewPreparation.q: What makes a rollback plan trustworthy versus just theoretical?
interviewPreparation.a: Having actually exercised it -- triggered a real rollback in a non-production or staging environment and confirmed the previous version came back correctly, rather than assuming it would work because the steps are documented. A rollback procedure that's never been tested is one of the most common things that fails exactly when you need it most.

careerApplications: Turns a working model/app into something a company can actually ship.

capstone.title: Ship a safe, observable release pipeline for your deployed system
capstone.description: Take the system you've already deployed to the cloud (from the Cloud Computing capstone, or equivalent) and build the release layer on top of it: an automated CI pipeline that tests and deploys on merge, a release strategy that limits blast radius (blue-green or canary), health checks that can actually catch a bad release, and a documented rollback you've genuinely exercised. This capstone is deliberately NOT about containerizing, provisioning cloud infrastructure, or writing unit tests -- those are already covered by Docker, Cloud Computing, and Testing. It's specifically about the safety and observability of shipping changes to something already running.
deliverables: A CI pipeline (e.g. GitHub Actions) that runs tests and deploys automatically on merge to main -- not a manual deploy
A release strategy limiting blast radius (blue-green or a canary ramp), not a straight 100% cutover
Health checks specific enough to actually catch a bad release, not just 'the server responds to a ping'
Structured logging and at least one real alert configured on a meaningful signal (error rate, latency), not just 'server is up/down'
A rollback you've actually exercised (not just described) -- a written account of triggering it and confirming the previous version was genuinely restored
capstone.portfolioTips: Actually exercising the rollback -- not just writing that you 'could' roll back -- is the single most convincing piece of evidence here. Anyone can claim a rollback plan exists; showing you actually triggered one and it worked is a different, much stronger signal.

industryUsage.usage: Pioneered much of the industry's thinking on canary releases and automated health-check-driven rollouts, given the cost of a bad release reaching its full user base directly and immediately.
Uses feature flags extensively to decouple deploying code from releasing features to users, letting code ship dark and get turned on gradually or instantly reverted without a new deploy.

Operates release pipelines at a scale where blast-radius control (canary rollouts, staged releases) is a practical necessity, not a nice-to-have, given how many users a single bad release could otherwise reach immediately.

lessons.title: Deployments & ReplicaSets
objectives: Explain how a Deployment manages replicas and enables safe rollouts
Explain how Deployment changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: You rarely create bare pods directly in production -- a Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which ensures a specified number of identical pod replicas are running at all times, automatically replacing any that crash or get deleted.
examples:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: my-app:2.0
commonMistakes: Manually creating and managing individual pods instead of a Deployment -- you lose automatic replacement on crash, easy scaling, and safe rolling updates, all of which a Deployment gives you.
lessons.careerRelevance: Deployments are the single most commonly used Kubernetes object in real production workloads.

lessons.title: Services: stable networking for pods
objectives: Explain why Services exist and the main Service types
Explain how Service changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Service with ClusterIP and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pods are ephemeral -- they get replaced constantly, and each replacement gets a new IP address. A Service provides a single, stable IP address and DNS name that automatically routes traffic to whichever healthy pods currently match its label selector, so other parts of your system never need to track individual pod IPs directly.
examples:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-app-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-app
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
commonMistakes: Hardcoding a pod's IP address anywhere in application config -- pod IPs change constantly as pods are replaced; always target a Service's stable address instead.
lessons.careerRelevance: Services are how literally everything in a real Kubernetes cluster actually talks to everything else.

lessons.explanation: A ConfigMap holds non-sensitive configuration (URLs, feature flags, config files) as key-value data that can be injected into pods as environment variables or mounted files -- keeping config separate from the container image so the same image works across environments.

lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly separating config/secrets from container images is expected practice in any real deployment pipeline.

lessons.title: Namespaces: organizing a cluster
objectives: Use namespaces to isolate resources within a shared cluster
Explain how namespace changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect namespace with namespace-scoped resources and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A namespace is a way to divide a single cluster into multiple virtual clusters -- useful for separating environments (dev/staging/prod) or teams sharing one physical cluster. Most resources are namespace-scoped (a Service in namespace A can't be found by name alone from namespace B), while some cluster-wide resources (like nodes) are not namespaced at all.
examples:
kubectl get pods -n staging
kubectl create namespace staging
# a Service 'my-app' in namespace 'staging' is reached at:
# my-app.staging.svc.cluster.local from elsewhere in the cluster
commonMistakes: Forgetting to specify -n <namespace> and assuming kubectl commands operate cluster-wide -- most commands default to the 'default' namespace, silently missing resources that live elsewhere.
lessons.careerRelevance: Namespace-based organization is standard practice in any real multi-team or multi-environment cluster.

lessons.explanation: A LoadBalancer Service works, but provisioning one per application gets expensive and doesn't handle path/host-based routing well.
examples:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: my-ingress}
spec:
  rules:
  - host: myapp.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: {name: my-app-service, port: {number: 80}}
commonMistakes: Provisioning a separate LoadBalancer Service for every single application -- this is expensive and doesn't scale; Ingress lets many applications share one entry point with routing rules.

lessons.title: Scaling & the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
objectives: Explain manual and automatic scaling of pod replicas

lessons.explanation: Scaling a Deployment manually (kubectl scale) is simple but requires you to notice load changes yourself.
examples:
kubectl scale deployment my-app --replicas=5

# or, automatically:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {kind: Deployment, name: my-app}
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70}}
commonMistakes: Setting no maxReplicas ceiling on an HPA -- an unexpected traffic spike (or a bug causing runaway load) could then scale far beyond what your cluster's actual capacity or budget can handle.
lessons.careerRelevance: Autoscaling is a standard, expected capability in any production Kubernetes deployment handling variable traffic.

lessons.explanation: When a rollout goes wrong, kubectl rollout undo instantly reverts a Deployment to its previous working revision.
examples:
kubectl rollout status deployment/my-app
kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app   # revert to the previous revision

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between a Deployment and a bare Pod?
interviewPreparation.a: A bare Pod, if it crashes or is deleted, is simply gone -- nothing recreates it. A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet that continuously ensures a specified number of pod replicas exist, automatically replacing any that fail, and also manages safe rolling updates when you change the image version.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you debug a pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff?
interviewPreparation.a: Start with kubectl describe pod to check the Events section for the real cause, then kubectl logs --previous to see the crashed container's actual output. Common causes include a misconfigured command, a missing environment variable/config the app expects, or the app failing its own startup health check.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret?
interviewPreparation.a: Both externalize configuration from the container image, but a Secret is intended for sensitive data. By default a Secret is only base64-encoded, not encrypted -- real protection requires enabling encryption at rest or using an external secrets manager, which is a common point of confusion.

interviewPreparation.q: Why would you use Ingress instead of just a LoadBalancer Service for every app?
interviewPreparation.a: A LoadBalancer Service typically provisions a real external cloud load balancer per Service, which gets expensive and doesn't support host/path-based routing well. Ingress lets many applications share a single entry point (and often a single LoadBalancer) with routing rules based on hostname and path.

interviewPreparation.q: How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decide when to scale?
interviewPreparation.a: It continuously watches a specified metric (commonly CPU utilization) against a target value, and adjusts the replica count up or down within a configured min/max range to keep the metric near that target -- growing under load and shrinking back down as load drops.

interviewPreparation.q: What would you do if a deployment you just rolled out started causing errors in production?
interviewPreparation.a: Run kubectl rollout undo immediately to revert to the last known-good revision -- it's fast, safe, and doesn't require improvising a manual fix under pressure. Investigate the actual root cause afterward, with the system already stable again.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical benefit of using Helm instead of raw kubectl apply with YAML files?
interviewPreparation.a: A real application often needs many coordinated, environment-specific YAML files. Helm packages these as one templated, versioned chart, so installing, upgrading, and rolling back the entire application is a single command instead of manually tracking and editing many separate files.

lessons.explanation: 'The cloud' is just someone else's data center, rented by the hour (or the second), accessed over the internet through an API instead of you racking physical servers. Instead of buying a machine, you request compute/storage/networking on demand from a provider (AWS, GCP, Azure), and pay only for what you use.

# Cloud: request a VM via an API call, pay per second, delete it when done
commonMistakes: Thinking 'the cloud' is one magic thing rather than a rentable version of the same servers/storage/networking you'd otherwise buy yourself.

# Block storage: the disk backing your Postgres VM -> EBS

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between what a security group controls and what IAM controls?
interviewPreparation.a: A security group is network-level -- it controls what traffic can even reach a resource. IAM is action-level -- it controls what a principal (user, service, role) is allowed to DO once it has access, regardless of the network path. A service can have a perfectly locked-down security group and still be a major security risk if its IAM permissions are far broader than it actually needs.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide between a VM, a managed container service, and serverless for a given workload?
interviewPreparation.a: Serverless fits spiky, infrequent, short-lived workloads well since you pay only for actual execution time, but has cold-start latency and execution time limits. Managed containers fit steady, longer-running services well. A raw VM makes sense when you need full control over the environment that a managed service doesn't give you. The deciding factors are traffic pattern, acceptable latency, and how much operational control you actually need.

interviewPreparation.q: What does 'designing for failure' actually mean in a cloud architecture?
interviewPreparation.a: Assuming any single component -- a VM, an availability zone, even a whole region -- can fail at any time, and architecting so the system survives it: redundancy across availability zones, auto-scaling to replace failed instances, load balancers routing around unhealthy nodes. It's a mindset shift from 'prevent failure' to 'assume failure and survive it.'

interviewPreparation.q: Why is the principle of least privilege important in cloud IAM specifically?
interviewPreparation.a: Cloud credentials and roles are attached to automated services, not just humans, and a single leaked key or a bug in automated code can be exploited immediately at scale. Scoping permissions to exactly what's needed limits the blast radius of any single compromised credential or buggy deployment, rather than one mistake having full account-wide consequences.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you design an auto-scaling policy for a web application, and what could go wrong with a poorly chosen one?
interviewPreparation.a: Pick a metric that actually reflects load (CPU, request count, queue depth) and thresholds with enough margin to react before users are affected, plus a reasonable cooldown so it doesn't thrash. A poorly chosen policy either scales too slowly (users see degraded performance before new capacity arrives) or too aggressively (rapid scale up/down cycles that waste cost and can even destabilize the service).

This capstone answers a genuinely different question than Docker's: not 'can you package this,' but 'can you deploy and operate this in an environment designed for real traffic and real failure.'

lessons.explanation: Architecture isn't about following rules for their own sake -- it's about making a codebase cheaper to CHANGE over time. A poorly structured system might work fine on day one, but every new feature gets slower to add, every bug fix risks breaking something unrelated, and onboarding a new engineer takes weeks instead of days.

# the real question architecture answers:

# BUT: 'when the requirements change next month (they will), how much of

lessons.title: Coupling & cohesion
objectives: Explain coupling and cohesion, and why you want LOW coupling but HIGH cohesion
Explain how coupling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect coupling with cohesion and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Coupling measures how much one piece of code depends on the internal details of another -- high coupling means changing one module frequently breaks or requires changing another. Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities WITHIN a single module are -- high cohesion means a module does one clear job, not several unrelated ones.
examples:
# recognizing the two independently:
# HIGH coupling: changing the database schema also requires editing the UI code directly
# LOW cohesion: a single 'Utils' class handles date formatting, network calls, AND email sending
# the goal: modules with ONE clear job (high cohesion), that don't reach into each other's internals (low coupling)
commonMistakes: Assuming coupling and cohesion are the same idea -- they're independent properties; a module CAN be low-coupled but still low-cohesion (unrelated responsibilities that just happen not to.
lessons.careerRelevance: Nearly every principle covered later (SRP, dependency inversion, clean architecture) is really just a specific technique for improving coupling and cohesion in a particular situation.

objectives: State the Single Responsibility Principle precisely, and distinguish it from 'a class should be small'

lessons.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle states that a class should have only ONE reason to change -- not that it should be short, and not that it should do only one literal action.
examples:
# NOT about size -- about REASONS TO CHANGE:
# UserRepository: reason to change = how users are stored (database schema, ORM version)
# UserEmailFormatter: reason to change = how emails are worded/templated
# these are genuinely DIFFERENT reasons -- which is exactly why they belong in separate classes
commonMistakes: Treating SRP as 'keep classes small' -- a class can be small and still violate SRP (if its few lines serve two unrelated purposes), and a class can be somewhat large while still honoring SRP.
lessons.careerRelevance: SRP violations are one of the most commonly cited issues in real code review -- 'this class is doing too many unrelated things' is a direct, practical application of this principle.

lessons.explanation: The Open/Closed Principle states that code should be open for EXTENSION (you can add new behavior) but closed for MODIFICATION (you shouldn't need to edit existing, already-tested code to do it).
examples:
# violation: a growing if/elif chain
# def calculate_discount(customer_type, price):
#     if customer_type == 'regular': return price
#     elif customer_type == 'vip': return price*0.9

#
# fix: each customer type is its own class implementing discount() --
# adding 'Employee' means writing a NEW class, touching nothing existing

lessons.title: Liskov Substitution & Interface Segregation
objectives: Explain both principles with the classic Square/Rectangle example and a 'fat interface' example

lessons.explanation: The Liskov Substitution Principle says a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without breaking correctness -- the classic violation is a Square inheriting from Rectangle but breaking any code that sets width and height independently (since a square can't honor that).
examples:
# LSP violation: Square(Rectangle) breaks code that expects independent width/height setting
# ISP violation: a 'Worker' interface with work(), eat(), sleep() forces a Robot
# implementation to awkwardly implement eat() and sleep(), which make no sense for it
# fix (ISP): split into separate, focused interfaces -- Workable, Eatable, Sleepable
commonMistakes: Forcing an inheritance relationship because it 'seems similar' (like Square/Rectangle) -- similarity isn't the same as a genuine is-a relationship that holds for EVERY operation the parent.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the same Liskov concept covered in the Distributed Systems course's leader-election lesson (a Square inheriting Rectangle) -- this lesson gives it the fuller, dedicated treatment alongside its sibling principle.

lessons.title: Dependency Inversion & dependency injection

lessons.explanation: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level code (business logic) shouldn't depend directly on low-level details (a specific database, a specific email provider) -- both should depend on an abstraction (an interface) instead.
examples:
# without DI: class OrderService: def __init__(self): self.db = PostgresDB()  # hard-coded, can't swap
# with DI:    class OrderService: def __init__(self, db): self.db = db  # injected
#             # tests can now pass in a FakeDB() instead of a real PostgresDB()

lessons.careerRelevance: Nearly every popular backend framework (Spring, NestJS, ASP.NET Core) is built around dependency injection specifically because of how much easier it makes testing and swapping implementations.

lessons.explanation: The Strategy pattern lets you swap an ALGORITHM at runtime by wrapping each variant in its own class implementing a shared interface -- e.g. different discount calculations, different sorting approaches, different payment-processing rules, selected based on context.

# cart.strategy = PercentOff(20)  # or NoDiscount(), or BuyOneGetOne()
# cart.total(100)  # uses whichever strategy is currently set
#
# Factory: centralize OBJECT CREATION
# shape = shape_factory('circle', radius=2)  # caller doesn't need to know it's a Circle class

lessons.title: Adapter & Facade patterns
objectives: Distinguish Adapter (make incompatible interfaces work together) from Facade (simplify a complex interface)
Explain how Adapter pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Adapter pattern with Facade pattern and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: The Adapter pattern lets two pieces of code with INCOMPATIBLE interfaces work together, by wrapping one so it exposes the interface the other expects -- e.g. a third-party payment library with its own method names, wrapped so your code can call it through your OWN standard payment interface.
examples:
# Adapter: bridge an INCOMPATIBLE interface
# ThirdPartyPayment has charge_customer(amount, token) -- your code expects pay(amount)
# PaymentAdapter.pay(amount) internally calls third_party.charge_customer(amount, self.token)
#
# Facade: SIMPLIFY a complex subsystem
# checkout.complete(cart)  # internally coordinates inventory, payment, shipping, notification --
# calling code only ever sees this one simple method
commonMistakes: Confusing Adapter with Facade because both 'wrap' something -- Adapter exists because two interfaces are INCOMPATIBLE and need bridging; Facade exists because an interface is too COMPLEX and.
lessons.careerRelevance: Adapters show up constantly when integrating third-party libraries or legacy code that doesn't match your codebase's own conventions -- a genuinely common real-world need.

lessons.title: Singleton -- and why it's controversial
objectives: Explain what Singleton guarantees, and articulate the real, specific reasons it's often considered an anti-pattern
Explain how Singleton pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Singleton pattern with hidden global state and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: The Singleton pattern guarantees a class has exactly ONE instance, globally accessible from anywhere in the code. It's genuinely useful for things like a single shared configuration object or a single connection pool.
examples:
# Singleton: guarantees exactly one instance, globally reachable
# config = AppConfig.get_instance()  # same instance everywhere, anywhere in the codebase
#
# the real critique: this is genuinely hard to unit-test, since a test can't easily
# substitute a fake AppConfig -- code reaches for the SAME global instance no matter what.
# often, passing the config explicitly (dependency injection) solves the same problem more testably.
commonMistakes: Reaching for Singleton by default whenever 'there should only be one of something' -- often, achieving the SAME practical guarantee via dependency injection (create one instance, pass it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to articulate SPECIFIC, concrete reasons Singleton is controversial (not just 'it's bad') is exactly the kind of nuanced judgment senior engineering interviews look for.

lessons.title: Clean architecture & layering
objectives: Explain the core idea behind clean/layered architecture: dependencies point inward, toward business logic
Explain how clean architecture changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect clean architecture with layered architecture and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Clean (or layered, or hexagonal) architecture organizes code so business logic sits at the CENTER, with no dependency on outer layers like the database, the web framework, or the UI -- those outer layers depend ON the business logic, never the reverse.
examples:
# dependency direction is the whole idea:
# Web framework -> Business logic -> Database interface <- Database implementation
# (arrows point TOWARD business logic, never away from it)
# business logic never imports or knows about Flask, Postgres, or React specifically --
# it just knows about its OWN interfaces, which outer layers implement
commonMistakes: Assuming clean architecture means 'more files and more folders' -- the actual test is the DIRECTION dependencies point; adding layers without enforcing that direction doesn't achieve any of.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is precisely why well-architected backend systems can swap databases or add a new API layer (GraphQL alongside REST) without rewriting business logic -- a genuine, valuable payoff of this approach.

lessons.title: Refactoring & code smells
objectives: Recognize the most common named code smells and the refactoring each typically calls for

lessons.explanation: A code smell is a surface-level sign that a design problem likely exists underneath -- not a bug, but a pattern that USUALLY indicates one.
examples:
# recognizing smells by their SYMPTOM, then applying the matching refactor:
# 'this method is 200 lines and does five different things' -> extract smaller methods
# 'this exact block appears in four places' -> extract shared function/class
# 'this method mostly reads and writes ANOTHER class's fields' -> move it to that class (feature envy)
commonMistakes: Refactoring without any tests in place first -- refactoring is specifically supposed to preserve behavior; without tests confirming that, you can't actually verify the refactor didn't.

lessons.explanation: A monolith is a single deployable unit containing all of an application's functionality -- simpler to develop, test, and deploy initially, but can become harder to scale specific parts independently as it grows.
examples:
# the honest trade-off, not a one-sided pitch:

lessons.explanation: Reviewing code for DESIGN (not just correctness) means asking a specific, repeatable set of questions: does this class have one clear reason to change (SRP)? Would adding a new case require editing this existing logic (OCP)?
examples:
# a genuinely useful design-review checklist, applied while reading real code:
# 1. does this class have ONE clear reason to change?
# 2. would a new case require editing existing, working logic?
# 3. does this depend on a concrete implementation it could depend on an interface instead?
# 4. is there duplicated logic anywhere nearby that should be extracted?
commonMistakes: Reviewing only for correctness ('does this work') and skipping design entirely -- design issues compound over time in ways correctness bugs usually don't; a working-but-poorly-structured.

lessons.title: When NOT to apply a pattern
objectives: Explain the real cost of unnecessary abstraction, and articulate a rule of thumb for when a pattern is premature

lessons.explanation: Every pattern in this course adds a layer of indirection -- worthwhile when it genuinely reduces future cost, but a real cost (more files, more abstraction to trace through, more to understand) when applied somewhere that will never actually need the flexibility it provides.
examples:
# the honest cost/benefit check before adding a pattern:
# 'I'm adding a Strategy interface for discount calculation' --
# do we have (or clearly will have) MULTIPLE discount strategies? if yes, worth it.
# if there's genuinely only ever going to be one, a plain function is simpler and just as correct.
commonMistakes: Adding a pattern 'in case we need it later' with no concrete evidence that need is coming -- this is precisely the over-engineering this lesson warns against; patterns should follow real.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing when to simplify (remove unnecessary abstraction) is just as valued in real engineering as knowing the patterns themselves -- and often more of a signal of genuine seniority.

exercises.title: Identify a Liskov violation
exercises.prompt: A `ReadOnlyList` inherits from `List` but throws an exception on `append()`. Code that works correctly with any `List` (calling append freely) breaks when given a `ReadOnlyList`. What's happening, and what's the real fix?
exercises.hint: a genuine LSP violation -- ReadOnlyList can't honor everything List promises; the real fix is not making ReadOnlyList inherit from List at all (composition or a separate, smaller interface instead)

exercises.title: Fix a fat interface
exercises.prompt: A `Worker` interface requires `work()`, `eat()`, and `sleep()`. A `RobotWorker` class must implement all three, but `eat()` and `sleep()` make no sense for it. What ISP-based fix would you apply?
exercises.hint: split into separate, focused interfaces (e.g. Workable, Eatable, Sleepable); RobotWorker only implements Workable, without being forced into meaningless eat()/sleep() implementations

exercises.title: Apply dependency injection
exercises.prompt: A class hard-codes `self.db = PostgresDB()` inside its constructor. Rewrite this using dependency injection, and explain the specific testing benefit.
exercises.hint: change the constructor to accept db as a parameter (self.db = db); tests can now inject a FakeDB() instead of needing a real Postgres connection

exercises.title: Choose Strategy or Factory
exercises.prompt: You need to (a) select which shipping-cost algorithm applies based on region, and (b) create the correct Shape subclass based on a string name. Which pattern fits each, and why?
exercises.hint: (a) Strategy -- swapping the ALGORITHM used at runtime; (b) Factory -- centralizing which concrete class gets CREATED

exercises.title: Design an Observer scenario
exercises.prompt: When an order is placed, three unrelated things must happen: send a confirmation email, update analytics, and adjust inventory. Design this with the Observer pattern -- what's the subject, and what are the observers?
exercises.hint: the order-placement event is the subject; email sender, analytics tracker, and inventory updater are three independent observers, each notified without the subject needing to know about them specifically

exercises.title: Avoid a Decorator subclass explosion
exercises.prompt: A coffee-ordering system has Coffee, MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee, MilkSugarCreamCoffee... explain why this is a problem and how Decorator fixes it.
exercises.hint: this is a combinatorial explosion -- N optional add-ons require up to 2^N subclasses; Decorator fixes it by wrapping a base Coffee with independent decorator layers (MilkDecorator, SugarDecorator) that combine freely without needing a subclass per combination

exercises.title: Distinguish Adapter from Facade
exercises.prompt: You're integrating a third-party payment library with different method names than your codebase uses. Separately, you also want one simple method that coordinates inventory, payment, and shipping for checkout. Which pattern is which?
exercises.hint: the payment-library integration is Adapter (bridging incompatible interfaces); the coordinated checkout method is Facade (simplifying a complex multi-part subsystem)

exercises.title: Critique a Singleton use case
exercises.prompt: A team uses a Singleton for their application's database connection pool, accessed globally throughout the codebase. What's a concrete testing problem this creates, and what alternative would you suggest?
exercises.hint: tests can't easily substitute a fake connection pool, since code reaches for the one global Singleton instance directly; suggest passing the pool explicitly via dependency injection instead

exercises.title: Trace a dependency direction
exercises.prompt: In a clean-architecture design, does the business logic layer import the specific database library (e.g. psycopg2), or does the database layer import an interface defined by the business logic? Explain why.
exercises.hint: the database layer implements an interface DEFINED by the business logic (e.g. an OrderRepository interface); business logic never imports the specific database library directly -- dependencies point inward, toward the business logic

exercises.title: Identify a code smell
exercises.prompt: A method is 220 lines long and handles validation, database saving, email sending, and logging all in one function. Name the smell and the refactor.
exercises.hint: a 'long method' smell (likely also an SRP violation); refactor by extracting each concern (validation, saving, emailing, logging) into its own well-named method or class

exercises.title: Spot feature envy
exercises.prompt: A method on `OrderPrinter` reads five different fields directly from a `Customer` object to format an address, and doesn't use any of OrderPrinter's own data. What smell is this, and where should the logic likely move?
exercises.hint: feature envy -- the method uses Customer's data far more than OrderPrinter's own; the address-formatting logic likely belongs on Customer (or a dedicated AddressFormatter) instead

exercises.title: Weigh monolith vs microservices honestly
exercises.prompt: A 5-person startup with one small product is considering microservices from day one. What would you advise, and why?
exercises.hint: likely advise starting with a monolith -- microservices' operational complexity and distributed-systems costs (network calls, partial failure) usually aren't worth paying at this size; the trade-off makes more sense at larger scale/team size

exercises.title: Run a design-focused review checklist
exercises.prompt: Given a class that both validates user input AND persists it to a database, walk through at least 2 of the design-review checklist questions from this course against it.
exercises.hint: e.g. 'does this have one reason to change?' -- no, validation rules and storage details are two separate reasons; 'is there duplicated logic nearby?' -- worth checking if similar validation exists elsewhere and should be extracted

exercises.title: Recognize premature abstraction
exercises.prompt: A developer adds a Strategy interface with a plugin-style architecture for a discount calculation that will only ever have one implementation, 'in case we need more later.' Evaluate this decision.
exercises.hint: likely premature abstraction (over-engineering) -- with no concrete evidence of multiple real implementations needed, a plain function would be simpler and equally correct; the pattern should follow demonstrated variation, not speculation

exercises.title: Diagnose an Open/Closed AND SRP violation together
exercises.prompt: A `ReportGenerator` class has a `generate(format)` method with an if/elif chain for 'pdf', 'csv', and 'html', and ALSO handles saving the file and emailing it. Identify both violations and propose a fix.
exercises.hint: OCP violation: adding a new format means editing the existing if/elif; SRP violation: format generation, saving, and emailing are three separate reasons to change. Fix: separate format-specific generator classes (OCP), plus separate FileSaver and EmailSender classes (SRP)

exercises.title: Choose composition over inheritance for a DI-friendly design
exercises.prompt: Design a `NotificationService` that can send via email OR SMS, decided at construction time, and is easy to unit test. Sketch the class relationships (in words, not code) using concepts from this course.
exercises.hint: use dependency injection: NotificationService accepts a Sender interface (Strategy pattern) in its constructor; EmailSender and SMSSender each implement Sender; tests inject a FakeSender to verify behavior without real email/SMS calls

interviewPreparation.q: Explain the Single Responsibility Principle with a concrete example, not just the definition.
interviewPreparation.a: A class should have only one reason to change. For example, a class that both saves a user to a database AND formats a user for an email has two separate reasons to change: a storage-format change, or an email-template change. These should be split into two focused classes so each concern can change independently without touching the other.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between Dependency Inversion and dependency injection?
interviewPreparation.a: Dependency Inversion is the design principle: high-level code should depend on abstractions, not concrete low-level details. Dependency injection is the specific technique that typically achieves this: instead of a class creating its own dependency internally, the dependency is passed in from outside, allowing real or fake implementations to be swapped in -- which is exactly why DI makes unit testing significantly easier.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose Strategy over a simple if/else, and when would the if/else actually be the better choice?
interviewPreparation.a: Strategy is worth the extra indirection when there are multiple real (or near-certain future) variations of a behavior that need to be swapped independently. If there are only two stable cases that will essentially never grow, a simple if/else is simpler and just as correct -- adding Strategy there would be premature abstraction with no real payoff.

interviewPreparation.q: What are the genuine, specific costs of microservices compared to a monolith -- not just the commonly cited benefits?
interviewPreparation.a: Function calls that used to be simple, reliable in-process calls become network calls, introducing real distributed-systems complexity: partial failure, retries, timeouts, and consistency concerns. Microservices also add significant operational overhead -- more deployments to manage, more services to monitor, more points of failure. These are genuine costs, not just complexity for complexity's sake, which is why many successful systems remain monoliths.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is Singleton often considered an anti-pattern despite being useful?
interviewPreparation.a: It creates hidden global state that any code, anywhere, can read or modify, making behavior harder to reason about. It also makes unit testing meaningfully harder, since tests can't easily substitute a fake instance -- code reaches for the same global Singleton directly. Often, achieving the same 'exactly one instance' guarantee via dependency injection (creating one instance and passing it explicitly) provides the same benefit without these specific costs.

capstone.title: Refactor a Poorly Designed System, With Evidence
capstone.description: Given (or designing your own) a small system with multiple real design violations -- SRP, OCP, tight coupling, hard-coded dependencies -- identify each violation explicitly, apply the appropriate principle or pattern to fix it, and prove with tests that behavior didn't change during the refactor.
deliverables: A written list of at least 4 specific design violations found, each naming the principle or smell it violates
The refactored code applying an appropriate fix for each violation (e.g. splitting an SRP-violating class, introducing dependency injection, replacing an if/elif chain with Strategy or polymorphism)
A test suite proving the refactored code behaves identically to the original for the same inputs
A short written justification for each pattern used -- specifically citing the concrete evidence of variation or coupling that justified it, not just 'this seemed like a good pattern to use'
At least one explicit note about a place you deliberately did NOT apply a pattern, and why the simpler approach was the right call there
capstone.portfolioTips: That last deliverable -- explicitly justifying where you did NOT add abstraction -- is exactly the kind of judgment that distinguishes a strong architecture portfolio piece from one that just lists patterns applied for their own sake.

industryUsage.usage: Both frameworks are built entirely around dependency injection as a first-class feature, specifically because of how much easier it makes testing and swapping implementations at scale.

Both are frequently cited examples of large-scale microservices architectures -- and both have also publicly discussed the real operational complexity that came with that choice, illustrating the honest trade-off covered in this course.

The SOLID principles and named code smells in this course are the direct, everyday vocabulary used in real pull-request review comments across the industry -- 'this violates SRP' or 'this looks like feature envy' are genuine, common review feedback, not just textbook terms.

careerApplications: Used by senior software engineers and technical leads to define service boundaries, interfaces, data flow, failure behavior, scalability, maintainability, and trade-offs before large implementations.

title: CI/CD: Continuous Integration & Deployment
blurb: How code actually gets from a commit to production safely, automatically, and repeatedly -- pipelines, deployment strategies, and rollback.
description: Pipelines, automated testing, deployment strategies (rolling, blue-green, canary), rollback, and the operational judgment to ship safely and often.

lessons.title: Why CI/CD exists
objectives: Explain the real problems CI/CD solves, in terms of what manual deployment actually costs a team
Explain how Continuous Integration changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Continuous Integration with Continuous Deployment and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before CI/CD, deploying code meant a person manually running builds, manually running tests, and manually copying files to a server -- slow, error-prone, and something people naturally avoid doing often (since it's risky and tedious).
examples:
# the vicious cycle CI/CD breaks:
# manual deploys are risky -> teams deploy less often -> each deploy bundles more changes
# -> each deploy becomes even riskier -> teams deploy even LESS often (cycle repeats)
#
# CI/CD's actual fix: make deploying so automated and routine that doing it OFTEN
# is exactly what makes each individual deploy SAFER, not riskier
commonMistakes: Treating CI/CD as just 'automation for its own sake' -- the real point is breaking the cycle where infrequent, risky deploys reinforce each other; frequency and safety are connected, not.
lessons.careerRelevance: Deployment frequency is one of the most cited metrics (alongside lead time, change failure rate, and recovery time) that distinguishes high-performing engineering teams in real industry research.

lessons.title: The anatomy of a pipeline
objectives: Name the typical pipeline stages in order, and explain why order matters
Explain how pipeline stages changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pipeline stages with build and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A CI/CD pipeline is a sequence of automated stages a code change passes through: typically build (compile/package the code), test (run automated tests), and deploy (ship it somewhere) -- often with additional stages like lint (style/quality checks) or security scanning in between.
examples:
# typical stage order, cheapest/fastest checks first:
# lint (seconds) -> build (compile/package) -> test (run automated tests) -> deploy
# if lint fails, the pipeline stops immediately -- no time wasted running build/test/deploy
# on code that already has an obvious style violation
commonMistakes: Running expensive stages before cheap ones -- ordering cheap, fast checks FIRST means failures are caught (and the pipeline stops) as early and cheaply as possible, saving real time on every.
lessons.careerRelevance: Reading and reasoning about a pipeline's stage order (and why a step is placed where it is) is a very common, practical part of working with CI/CD in any real engineering job.

lessons.title: Continuous Integration in practice
objectives: Explain what makes integration 'continuous,' and the real problem it solves compared to long-lived branches
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: branch protection, required status checks.
Explain how Continuous Integration changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Continuous Integration with integration hell and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Continuous Integration means developers merge their changes into a shared branch FREQUENTLY (multiple times a day, ideally), with an automated build and test run on every merge.
examples:
# integration hell (long-lived branch) vs continuous integration:
# long-lived branch: 3 weeks of changes, merge conflict with 40 files at once,
# unclear WHICH of hundreds of commits actually broke something
# continuous integration: merge every few hours, if something breaks it's
# obvious which small, recent change caused it
commonMistakes: Letting a feature branch live for weeks before merging -- the LONGER a branch diverges from the shared branch, the more painful and conflict-prone the eventual merge becomes; this is exactly.
lessons.careerRelevance: Trunk-based development (frequent merges to a shared main branch) is the CI practice most strongly associated with high-performing engineering teams in real industry studies. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Automated testing in the pipeline
objectives: Explain the test pyramid concept and where each test type typically runs in a pipeline
Explain how test pyramid changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect test pyramid with unit tests and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pipelines typically run several LAYERS of automated tests: unit tests (fast, test one small piece in isolation, run on every commit), integration tests (slower, test how pieces work together, e.g. with a real database), and end-to-end tests (slowest, test the whole system as a user would experience it, often run less frequently).
examples:
# the test pyramid, by SPEED and QUANTITY:
# many unit tests (seconds each, run on every commit)
# fewer integration tests (tens of seconds, run on every commit or merge)
# very few end-to-end tests (minutes each, often run before a deploy, not every commit)
commonMistakes: Relying mostly on slow, flaky end-to-end tests instead of a broad base of fast unit tests -- this inverts the test pyramid, making the pipeline slow and unreliable, and is a common.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the same 'Testing' course content applied specifically to CI -- how test types map onto WHEN and HOW OFTEN they run in an automated pipeline.

lessons.title: Build artifacts & versioning
objectives: Explain why you build an artifact ONCE and promote the SAME artifact through environments, rather than rebuilding for each
Explain how build artifact changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect build artifact with build once, promote everywhere and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A build artifact is the packaged, deployable output of the build stage -- a Docker image, a compiled binary, a zip of built assets. A critical, easy-to-miss principle: build the artifact ONCE, then promote that EXACT SAME artifact through dev, staging, and production -- never rebuild separately for each environment.
examples:
# the risk of rebuilding per environment:
# build for staging -> tests pass -> build AGAIN for production (different day, maybe a
# dependency version shifted) -> production artifact is SUBTLY DIFFERENT from what was tested
#
# the fix: build ONCE, tag it (e.g. app:a1b2c3), and promote that EXACT tagged artifact
# through every environment -- what you tested is EXACTLY what ships
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the application separately for each environment -- this breaks the guarantee that what was tested is exactly what gets deployed, reintroducing the very risk automated testing was.
lessons.careerRelevance: "Build once, deploy everywhere" is one of the most consistently emphasized real CI/CD best practices, specifically because violating it has caused real, hard-to-diagnose production incidents.

lessons.title: Environments & promotion
objectives: Explain the typical dev/staging/production environment chain and what 'promotion' means
Explain how environment chain changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect environment chain with staging and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Most pipelines move a build through a chain of environments with increasing similarity to production and increasing caution: development (fast feedback, may be unstable), staging (a close mirror of production, used for final verification), and production (real users, real consequences).
examples:
# a typical promotion chain:
# dev (fast feedback, engineers verify basic functionality)
# -> staging (mirrors production config/scale, final automated + manual checks)
# -> production (real users -- often gated by an explicit human approval step)
# the SAME artifact moves through all three -- never rebuilt along the way
commonMistakes: Assuming a fully automated pipeline means NO human ever approves a production deploy -- many real, mature CI/CD setups deliberately keep a manual gate before production specifically.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this environment chain and where manual gates typically sit is directly relevant to how release processes are actually structured at most companies.
