lessons.title: Tensors & basic operations in TensorFlow
objectives: Create and manipulate TensorFlow tensors
Explain how tensor changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tensor with eager execution and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: TensorFlow tensors work much like PyTorch's or NumPy's arrays: multi-dimensional, typed, and shape-checked.
examples:
import tensorflow as tf
x = tf.constant([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
print(x.shape)             # (2, 2)
y = tf.matmul(x, x)        # eager execution -- runs immediately, prints real values
commonMistakes: Assuming TensorFlow still requires building an explicit static graph before running anything, as in TF1 — TF2's eager-by-default execution is deliberately much closer to normal.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing the eager-vs-graph distinction (even if you rarely touch graph mode directly today) explains a lot of TensorFlow's history and design in interviews.

lessons.title: Building a model with the Keras Sequential API
objectives: Define a simple model by stacking layers with the Sequential API
Explain how Sequential API changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Sequential API with layer stacking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Sequential API is the simplest way to build a model: a straight stack of layers, each feeding directly into the next, declared in order. It's fast to write and read, but only fits models with a single input, single output, and no branching or shared layers — for anything more complex, the Functional API (next lesson) is needed.
examples:
from tensorflow import keras
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu', input_shape=(784,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax'),
])
commonMistakes: Trying to force a model with multiple inputs or a skip-connection into the Sequential API — this API genuinely can't express that; recognize when you need the Functional API instead.
lessons.careerRelevance: Sequential models cover a large fraction of straightforward real tasks and are the fastest way to prototype an idea.
lessons.explain: The Sequential API is the simplest way to build a model: a straight stack of layers, each feeding directly into the next, declared in order. It's fast to write and read, but only fits models with a single input, single output, and no branching or shared layers — for anything more complex, the Functional API (next lesson) is needed.
lessons.example:
from tensorflow import keras
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu', input_shape=(784,)),

])

lessons.title: The Keras Functional API for flexible architectures
objectives: Build a model with multiple inputs, outputs, or branching using the Functional API
Explain how Functional API changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Functional API with multi-input/output models and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Functional API treats layers as callable functions applied to explicit tensor inputs, letting you build graphs Sequential can't express: multiple inputs, multiple outputs, or branches that merge back together (like a skip connection).
examples:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(784,))
x = keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu')(inputs)
outputs = keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)
commonMistakes: Defaulting to the Functional API's added complexity for a simple single-path model — Sequential is simpler and sufficient whenever your architecture genuinely has no branching.
lessons.careerRelevance: Real production architectures (multiple input types, auxiliary outputs) very often need the Functional API's flexibility, not just Sequential.
lessons.explain: The Functional API treats layers as callable functions applied to explicit tensor inputs, letting you build graphs Sequential can't express: multiple inputs, multiple outputs, or branches that merge back together (like a skip connection).

lessons.title: tf.data pipelines for real datasets
objectives: Build an efficient input pipeline with tf.data
Explain how tf.data.Dataset changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tf.data.Dataset with shuffle/batch/map/prefetch and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: `tf.data.Dataset` builds an efficient, composable input pipeline: load data, apply transformations (shuffle, batch, map a preprocessing function, prefetch), and feed it to training — designed so data loading/preprocessing can overlap with GPU computation instead of blocking it, which matters a lot for real dataset sizes.
examples:
dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((images, labels))
dataset = dataset.shuffle(1000).batch(32).map(preprocess_fn).prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
for batch_images, batch_labels in dataset: ...
commonMistakes: Loading and preprocessing an entire large dataset eagerly into memory up front instead of building a lazy tf.data pipeline — this doesn't scale to real dataset sizes and wastes the overlap.
lessons.careerRelevance: tf.data pipelines are the standard, expected way real TensorFlow training scales past toy-sized datasets.
lessons.explain: `tf.data.Dataset` builds an efficient, composable input pipeline: load data, apply transformations (shuffle, batch, map a preprocessing function, prefetch), and feed it to training — designed so data loading/preprocessing can overlap with GPU computation instead of blocking it, which matters a lot for real dataset sizes.

lessons.title: Training with model.fit and custom training loops
objectives: Train a Keras model with model.fit, and know when a custom training loop is needed instead
Explain how model.compile/fit changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model.compile/fit with tf.GradientTape and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: For standard cases, `model.compile()` (specifying optimizer, loss, metrics) followed by `model.fit()` handles the entire training loop for you — batching, gradient updates, validation, all in one call.
examples:
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
history = model.fit(train_dataset, validation_data=val_dataset, epochs=10)

# custom loop, when fit() isn't flexible enough:
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    predictions = model(x, training=True)
    loss = loss_fn(y, predictions)
grads = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(grads, model.trainable_variables))
commonMistakes: Reaching for a custom GradientTape loop by default 'for control' when model.fit() with callbacks would handle the case perfectly well — the built-in loop covers the large majority of real.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing both the high-level (fit) and low-level (GradientTape) paths, and when each is appropriate, is a mark of real TensorFlow fluency.
lessons.explain: For standard cases, `model.compile()` (specifying optimizer, loss, metrics) followed by `model.fit()` handles the entire training loop for you — batching, gradient updates, validation, all in one call.

lessons.title: Debugging TensorFlow models
objectives: Apply a systematic checklist when a TensorFlow model isn't training correctly
Explain how shape debugging changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: The same debugging discipline from the PyTorch track applies here: check shapes explicitly at each step, try to overfit a tiny subset of data first (if that fails, the bug is in your code), and inspect actual data batches rather than assuming preprocessing worked.
examples:
# same 'overfit 10 examples' test as PyTorch:
# if the model can't drive loss near zero on 10 examples, the bug is in your code
# (wrong loss, bad labels, frozen layers) -- not dataset difficulty or model capacity
commonMistakes: Assuming a non-learning model just needs more epochs or a bigger model before ruling out an actual bug with the fast small-subset overfit test.
lessons.careerRelevance: This debugging method transfers directly between PyTorch and TensorFlow, since the underlying causes of training bugs are largely framework-agnostic.

lessons.title: Callbacks & training monitoring
objectives: Use Keras callbacks to monitor and control training automatically
Explain how EarlyStopping changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect EarlyStopping with ModelCheckpoint and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Callbacks hook into the training loop at specific points (end of each epoch, when a metric stops improving) without you writing manual loop logic: EarlyStopping halts training when validation loss stops improving (fighting overfitting automatically), ModelCheckpoint saves the best-performing version seen so far.
examples:
callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=3, restore_best_weights=True),
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint('best_model.keras', save_best_only=True),
]
model.fit(train_dataset, validation_data=val_dataset, epochs=50, callbacks=callbacks)
commonMistakes: Manually watching a training log and stopping by hand when it looks like it's overfitting — EarlyStopping automates exactly this, more reliably and reproducibly.
lessons.careerRelevance: Using callbacks well is what separates a quick prototype training script from a robust, unattended training pipeline.
lessons.explain: Callbacks hook into the training loop at specific points (end of each epoch, when a metric stops improving) without you writing manual loop logic: EarlyStopping halts training when validation loss stops improving (fighting overfitting automatically), ModelCheckpoint saves the best-performing version seen so far.

    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=3, restore_best_weights=True),
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint('best_model.keras', save_best_only=True),
]

lessons.title: Saving, exporting & deploying a TensorFlow model
objectives: Save a trained model and describe TensorFlow's deployment paths
Explain how model.save/load_model changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model.save/load_model with TensorFlow Serving and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: TensorFlow's native format saves the full model (architecture AND weights) in one step, simpler than PyTorch's weights-only convention.
examples:
model.save('my_model.keras')                       # full model: architecture + weights
loaded = keras.models.load_model('my_model.keras')   # ready to use immediately, no need to redefine the class

# deployment targets:
# TensorFlow Serving -> standard server API
# TensorFlow Lite    -> mobile/edge
# TensorFlow.js      -> in-browser
commonMistakes: Assuming every deployment target needs the same model format/optimizations — mobile (Lite) and browser (.js) deployment typically need additional conversion and often.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing which deployment path fits a given target (server, mobile, browser) is a practical, real architecture decision, not just a technical footnote.

lessons.explanation: A useful requirement describes observable behavior, not a preferred implementation. User stories can capture who needs what and why, but acceptance criteria make the request testable by defining examples, boundaries, and failure behavior.
lessons.explain: A useful requirement describes observable behavior, not a preferred implementation. User stories can capture who needs what and why, but acceptance criteria make the request testable by defining examples, boundaries, and failure behavior.

lessons.explanation: Functional requirements describe behavior such as creating an order or searching a catalog. Non-functional requirements describe qualities and constraints such as latency, availability, privacy, capacity, auditability, and accessibility.
lessons.explain: Functional requirements describe behavior such as creating an order or searching a catalog. Non-functional requirements describe qualities and constraints such as latency, availability, privacy, capacity, auditability, and accessibility.

lessons.title: Design docs, ADRs & practical UML
objectives: Write a concise design decision with context, alternatives, and consequences.
Choose the lightest diagram that answers the team’s actual design question.
Use class, sequence, component, activity, and state diagrams to communicate structure, interactions, workflows, and lifecycle behavior.
lessons.explanation: Start from the question the diagram needs to answer. Use a class diagram for structure, a sequence diagram for interactions over time, a component diagram for major system parts, an activity diagram for workflow, and a state diagram for an object's states and transitions. Keep only the detail needed to explain the design.
lessons.explain: Start from the question the diagram needs to answer. Use a class diagram for structure, a sequence diagram for interactions over time, a component diagram for major system parts, an activity diagram for workflow, and a state diagram for an object's states and transitions. Keep only the detail needed to explain the design.
commonMistakes: Treating UML as paperwork or trying to draw every possible detail makes diagrams noisy and stale.
lessons.careerRelevance: Engineers use lightweight design docs, ADRs, sequence/component/state diagrams, and similar architecture sketches during feature design, code review, incident analysis, onboarding, and cross-team communication. The valuable skill is choosing the right artifact for the question and keeping it tied to the real system.

Explain how API contract changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect API contract with schema and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An interface contract includes inputs, outputs, errors, side effects, ordering, and compatibility expectations. Once other code or users depend on that contract, changing it becomes a coordination problem.
lessons.explain: An interface contract includes inputs, outputs, errors, side effects, ordering, and compatibility expectations. Once other code or users depend on that contract, changing it becomes a coordination problem.

lessons.explanation: A test strategy connects risks to evidence. Unit tests give fast feedback on isolated logic, integration tests verify boundaries such as databases and APIs, and end-to-end tests cover a few critical user journeys.
lessons.explain: A test strategy connects risks to evidence. Unit tests give fast feedback on isolated logic, integration tests verify boundaries such as databases and APIs, and end-to-end tests cover a few critical user journeys.

title: Classical AI: Search, Reasoning & Planning
blurb: Search, heuristics, CSPs, games, logic, knowledge representation, planning, uncertainty and MDPs.
description: A certification-style classical AI foundation aligned to NPTEL/IIT search and knowledge-representation curricula, with hands-on Python models and problem-formulation practice.

lessons.title: Intelligent agents & problem formulation
objectives: Formulate a real problem as states, actions, goals, and costs.
Explain how agent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect agent with state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Classical AI begins by choosing a representation that makes reasoning possible. An agent observes an environment and chooses actions; a search problem specifies an initial state, possible actions, transition model, goal test, and path cost.
lessons.explain: Classical AI begins by choosing a representation that makes reasoning possible. An agent observes an environment and chooses actions; a search problem specifies an initial state, possible actions, transition model, goal test, and path cost.
examples:
problem={"start":"A","goal":"G","actions":{"A":["B","C"],"B":["G"],"C":[]}}
print(problem["start"],"->",problem["goal"])
lessons.example:
problem={"start":"A","goal":"G","actions":{"A":["B","C"],"B":["G"],"C":[]}}
print(problem["start"],"->",problem["goal"])
commonMistakes: Choosing a state representation that omits information needed for future decisions can make the correct solution impossible to express.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: State spaces, graphs & search trees
objectives: Distinguish the underlying state graph from the search tree generated by an algorithm.
Explain how state space changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect state space with search tree and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A state space is the set of possible configurations and transitions. A search tree is the algorithm’s unfolding of that space from the start state, so the same world state may appear many times through different paths.
lessons.explain: A state space is the set of possible configurations and transitions. A search tree is the algorithm’s unfolding of that space from the start state, so the same world state may appear many times through different paths.
commonMistakes: Treating every search-tree node as a new world state can cause exponential repeated work in cyclic or converging graphs.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Breadth-first & depth-first search
objectives: Choose BFS or DFS based on solution depth, memory, and completeness.
Explain how BFS changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect BFS with DFS and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Breadth-first search expands the shallowest frontier first and is complete on finite branching graphs; with equal step costs it finds a shortest path in number of edges. Depth-first search follows one branch deeply using little frontier memory but can waste time down an unhelpful path and needs cycle handling.
lessons.explain: Breadth-first search expands the shallowest frontier first and is complete on finite branching graphs; with equal step costs it finds a shortest path in number of edges. Depth-first search follows one branch deeply using little frontier memory but can waste time down an unhelpful path and needs cycle handling.
commonMistakes: Using DFS when the search space can contain an infinite branch can prevent the algorithm from ever reaching a nearby solution elsewhere.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Uniform-cost search & path cost
objectives: Find the least-cost path when actions have different costs.
Explain how uniform-cost search changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect uniform-cost search with priority queue and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Uniform-cost search expands the frontier node with the lowest accumulated path cost g(n). With non-negative step costs, the first time a goal is removed from the priority queue its cost is optimal.
lessons.explain: Uniform-cost search expands the frontier node with the lowest accumulated path cost g(n). With non-negative step costs, the first time a goal is removed from the priority queue its cost is optimal.
examples:
import heapq
frontier=[(0,"A")]
heapq.heappush(frontier,(5,"C")); heapq.heappush(frontier,(2,"B"))
print(heapq.heappop(frontier))
lessons.example:
import heapq
frontier=[(0,"A")]
heapq.heappush(frontier,(5,"C")); heapq.heappush(frontier,(2,"B"))
print(heapq.heappop(frontier))
commonMistakes: Marking a node permanently visited when it is first generated rather than when its best cost is established can discard a cheaper path found later.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Heuristics & greedy best-first search
objectives: Design a heuristic and understand what information it adds to search.
Explain how heuristic changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect heuristic with greedy best-first and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost from a state to a goal. Greedy best-first search expands the state with the smallest heuristic estimate, often reaching a goal quickly but without considering the cost already paid.
lessons.explain: A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost from a state to a goal. Greedy best-first search expands the state with the smallest heuristic estimate, often reaching a goal quickly but without considering the cost already paid.
examples:
heuristic={"A":6,"B":2,"C":4,"G":0}
print(min(["B","C"], key=heuristic.get))
lessons.example:
heuristic={"A":6,"B":2,"C":4,"G":0}
print(min(["B","C"], key=heuristic.get))
commonMistakes: A heuristic that looks intuitive but systematically overvalues the wrong feature can make informed search worse than a simpler baseline.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: A* search, admissibility & consistency
objectives: Explain why A* balances known path cost with estimated remaining cost.
Explain how A* changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect A* with admissible heuristic and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A* orders states by f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining the cost already paid with an estimate of the cost remaining. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost; consistency adds a triangle-inequality-style condition across edges and makes graph-search behavior cleaner.
lessons.explain: A* orders states by f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining the cost already paid with an estimate of the cost remaining. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost; consistency adds a triangle-inequality-style condition across edges and makes graph-search behavior cleaner.
commonMistakes: Using a heuristic because it “usually seems close” without checking its admissibility can silently remove the optimality guarantee.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Local search: hill climbing & simulated annealing
objectives: Use local search when the path is irrelevant and only a good final state matters.
Explain how hill climbing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect hill climbing with local optimum and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Local search keeps one or a small number of candidate states and improves an objective rather than constructing a path from start to goal. Hill climbing moves to a better neighbor but can become trapped on local optima, ridges, or plateaus.
lessons.explain: Local search keeps one or a small number of candidate states and improves an objective rather than constructing a path from start to goal. Hill climbing moves to a better neighbor but can become trapped on local optima, ridges, or plateaus.
examples:
scores=[3,5,7,6,9]
best=scores[0]
for s in scores[1:]:
    if s>best: best=s
print("best observed",best)
lessons.example:
scores=[3,5,7,6,9]
best=scores[0]
for s in scores[1:]:
    if s>best: best=s
print("best observed",best)
commonMistakes: Assuming hill climbing found the global optimum because no immediate neighbor is better confuses local optimality with global optimality.

lessons.title: Constraint satisfaction & backtracking
objectives: Model a problem as variables, domains, constraints, and a systematic search.
Explain how CSP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CSP with variable and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Constraint Satisfaction Problems separate representation from search: variables must receive values from domains while satisfying constraints. Backtracking assigns one variable at a time and reverses choices when a constraint fails.
lessons.explain: Constraint Satisfaction Problems separate representation from search: variables must receive values from domains while satisfying constraints. Backtracking assigns one variable at a time and reverses choices when a constraint fails.
examples:
colors=["R","G","B"]
solutions=[(a,b) for a in colors for b in colors if a!=b]
print(solutions)
lessons.example:
colors=["R","G","B"]
solutions=[(a,b) for a in colors for b in colors if a!=b]
print(solutions)
commonMistakes: Generating complete assignments before checking constraints throws away the main advantage of backtracking: pruning impossible partial solutions early.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Constraint propagation, MRV & arc consistency
objectives: Reduce CSP search by propagating constraints before making more guesses.
Explain how MRV changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MRV with forward checking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Constraint propagation removes domain values that cannot participate in a valid solution. Forward checking prunes neighbors after an assignment; arc consistency repeatedly ensures each value of one variable has compatible support in a connected variable.
lessons.explain: Constraint propagation removes domain values that cannot participate in a valid solution. Forward checking prunes neighbors after an assignment; arc consistency repeatedly ensures each value of one variable has compatible support in a connected variable.
commonMistakes: Propagation must preserve only logically impossible values; over-pruning can delete valid solutions and make the solver appear fast but incorrect.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Adversarial search & minimax
objectives: Choose an action assuming an opponent also acts rationally.
Explain how minimax changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect minimax with MAX and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Adversarial search models environments where another agent actively tries to reduce your outcome. Minimax alternates MAX nodes, which choose the highest utility, and MIN nodes, which choose the lowest utility from MAX’s perspective.
lessons.explain: Adversarial search models environments where another agent actively tries to reduce your outcome. Minimax alternates MAX nodes, which choose the highest utility, and MIN nodes, which choose the lowest utility from MAX’s perspective.
examples:
children=[3,-2,5]
print("MAX chooses",max(children),"MIN chooses",min(children))
lessons.example:
children=[3,-2,5]
print("MAX chooses",max(children),"MIN chooses",min(children))
commonMistakes: Evaluating only your own best next move ignores the opponent’s response and produces plans that fail immediately against rational play.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Alpha-beta pruning & evaluation functions
objectives: Prune game-tree branches that cannot affect the minimax decision.
Explain how alpha-beta pruning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect alpha-beta pruning with evaluation function and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Alpha-beta pruning computes the same minimax choice while skipping branches proven irrelevant to the final result. Alpha tracks MAX’s best guaranteed value so far; beta tracks MIN’s.
lessons.explain: Alpha-beta pruning computes the same minimax choice while skipping branches proven irrelevant to the final result. Alpha tracks MAX’s best guaranteed value so far; beta tracks MIN’s.
commonMistakes: A fast evaluation function with poor correlation to winning can make deeper search confidently choose bad moves.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Propositional logic & knowledge bases
objectives: Represent facts and rules with precise truth conditions.
Explain how proposition changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect proposition with logical connective and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Propositional logic represents statements that are true or false and combines them with NOT, AND, OR, implication, and equivalence. A knowledge base is a set of sentences; entailment asks whether every model that satisfies the knowledge base also satisfies a query.
lessons.explain: Propositional logic represents statements that are true or false and combines them with NOT, AND, OR, implication, and equivalence. A knowledge base is a set of sentences; entailment asks whether every model that satisfies the knowledge base also satisfies a query.
examples:
rain=True; umbrella=True
print("protected from rain:", (not rain) or umbrella)
lessons.example:
rain=True; umbrella=True
print("protected from rain:", (not rain) or umbrella)
commonMistakes: Treating implication P→Q as if it also means Q→P is the classic converse error and produces invalid conclusions.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Logical inference, entailment & resolution
objectives: Derive conclusions using sound inference rather than intuition.
Explain how entailment changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect entailment with resolution and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Inference algorithms transform or inspect a knowledge base to prove consequences. Resolution works conveniently with clauses in conjunctive normal form and proves a query by showing that adding its negation leads to contradiction.
lessons.explain: Inference algorithms transform or inspect a knowledge base to prove consequences. Resolution works conveniently with clauses in conjunctive normal form and proves a query by showing that adding its negation leads to contradiction.
examples:
facts={"cloudy", "cloudy->rain"}
if "cloudy" in facts and "cloudy->rain" in facts: print("derive: rain")
lessons.example:
facts={"cloudy", "cloudy->rain"}
if "cloudy" in facts and "cloudy->rain" in facts: print("derive: rain")
commonMistakes: Using a plausible real-world belief that was never encoded in the knowledge base is not logical inference from the represented facts.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: First-order logic & unification
objectives: Represent objects, relations, variables, and quantified rules.
Explain how first-order logic changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect first-order logic with predicate and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: First-order logic extends propositional logic with objects, predicates, functions, variables, and quantifiers. Instead of a separate proposition for every person, a rule can state that all humans satisfy some property.
lessons.explain: First-order logic extends propositional logic with objects, predicates, functions, variables, and quantifiers. Instead of a separate proposition for every person, a rule can state that all humans satisfy some property.
examples:
rule=("parent", "X", "Y")
fact=("parent", "Ada", "Byron")
substitution={rule[1]:fact[1],rule[2]:fact[2]}
print(substitution)
lessons.example:
rule=("parent", "X", "Y")
fact=("parent", "Ada", "Byron")
substitution={rule[1]:fact[1],rule[2]:fact[2]}
print(substitution)
commonMistakes: Confusing existential “there exists” with universal “for all” changes the meaning of a rule completely.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Knowledge representation: rules, frames & ontologies
objectives: Choose a representation that exposes the relationships an inference task needs.
Explain how knowledge representation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect knowledge representation with ontology and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Knowledge representation is the engineering decision about how concepts, categories, attributes, relations, defaults, and rules are encoded. Rule systems are good for explicit implications, graph/ontology representations are good for typed entities and relationships, and structured frames can group properties around concepts.
lessons.explain: Knowledge representation is the engineering decision about how concepts, categories, attributes, relations, defaults, and rules are encoded. Rule systems are good for explicit implications, graph/ontology representations are good for typed entities and relationships, and structured frames can group properties around concepts.
examples:
knowledge={"Ada":{"type":"Person","skills":{"math","programming"}}}
print("programming" in knowledge["Ada"]["skills"])
lessons.example:
knowledge={"Ada":{"type":"Person","skills":{"math","programming"}}}
print("programming" in knowledge["Ada"]["skills"])
commonMistakes: A representation that stores facts but cannot express the relationships needed by the reasoning task forces complex, brittle application code later.

lessons.title: Reasoning under uncertainty & Bayes networks
objectives: Represent uncertain dependencies and update beliefs from evidence.
Explain how Bayes network changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Bayes network with conditional probability and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Real environments rarely provide complete certainty. Bayesian networks represent random variables as a directed acyclic graph whose edges capture conditional dependencies; local conditional probability tables define the joint distribution compactly when independences hold.
lessons.explain: Real environments rarely provide complete certainty. Bayesian networks represent random variables as a directed acyclic graph whose edges capture conditional dependencies; local conditional probability tables define the joint distribution compactly when independences hold.
examples:
prior=0.01; sensitivity=0.9; false_positive=0.05
p_pos=prior*sensitivity + (1-prior)*false_positive
posterior=prior*sensitivity/p_pos
print(round(posterior,3))
lessons.example:
prior=0.01; sensitivity=0.9; false_positive=0.05
p_pos=prior*sensitivity + (1-prior)*false_positive
posterior=prior*sensitivity/p_pos
print(round(posterior,3))
commonMistakes: Interpreting P(test positive | disease) as P(disease | test positive) ignores the base rate and is a common probabilistic reasoning error.

lessons.title: Planning with actions, preconditions & effects
objectives: Represent a goal-directed plan as actions that transform symbolic state.
Explain how planning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect planning with precondition and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Classical planning separates action definitions from the specific problem instance. An action has preconditions that must be true before it can execute and effects that change the state.
lessons.explain: Classical planning separates action definitions from the specific problem instance. An action has preconditions that must be true before it can execute and effects that change the state.
commonMistakes: Allowing an action to execute without checking its preconditions creates impossible plans that look valid only because state transitions were under-specified.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Plan-space, hierarchical & partial-order planning
objectives: Reason about plans without forcing every action into a fixed total order too early.
Explain how partial-order planning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect partial-order planning with hierarchical planning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Some planning problems are easier when the system commits only to ordering constraints that are necessary. Partial-order planning can leave independent actions unordered, while hierarchical planning decomposes abstract tasks into smaller methods and actions.
lessons.explain: Some planning problems are easier when the system commits only to ordering constraints that are necessary. Partial-order planning can leave independent actions unordered, while hierarchical planning decomposes abstract tasks into smaller methods and actions.
examples:

lessons.example:

lessons.title: Markov Decision Processes as a bridge to RL
objectives: Model sequential decisions where actions have uncertain outcomes.
Explain how MDP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MDP with transition probability and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A Markov Decision Process specifies states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and a discount factor. Unlike deterministic planning, an action may lead to several next states with different probabilities.
lessons.explain: A Markov Decision Process specifies states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and a discount factor. Unlike deterministic planning, an action may lead to several next states with different probabilities.
examples:

lessons.example:

print(transitions)
commonMistakes: Choosing the action with the largest immediate reward can be worse over time when it leads to poor future states.

lessons.title: Choosing the right AI formulation & evaluating search
objectives: Select search, CSP, logic, planning, probability, or learning based on problem structure.
Explain how problem formulation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect problem formulation with baseline and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Near-mastery is the ability to recognize the structure before reaching for an algorithm. If you need a path, use search; if you need a consistent assignment, consider CSP; if you need provable symbolic consequences, use logic; if actions achieve symbolic goals, use planning; if uncertainty matters, use probabilistic models or MDPs.
lessons.explain: Near-mastery is the ability to recognize the structure before reaching for an algorithm. If you need a path, use search; if you need a consistent assignment, consider CSP; if you need provable symbolic consequences, use logic; if actions achieve symbolic goals, use planning; if uncertainty matters, use probabilistic models or MDPs.

lessons.title: The reinforcement-learning interaction loop
objectives: Explain how an RL agent learns from interaction rather than labeled targets.
Explain how agent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect agent with environment and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Reinforcement learning studies sequential decisions. At each step an agent observes state or observation, chooses an action, receives a reward, and reaches a new state.
lessons.explain: Reinforcement learning studies sequential decisions. At each step an agent observes state or observation, chooses an action, receives a reward, and reaches a new state.
examples:
trajectory=[("s0","right",0),("s1","right",0),("goal","stop",1)]
print("return",sum(r for _,_,r in trajectory))
lessons.example:
trajectory=[("s0","right",0),("s1","right",0),("goal","stop",1)]
print("return",sum(r for _,_,r in trajectory))
commonMistakes: Treating reward as a label for each action ignores delayed effects and can encourage behavior that looks locally good but fails the long-term task.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: MDPs, states, actions & the Markov property
objectives: Specify an RL task as an MDP and identify when the observation is not truly Markov.
Explain how MDP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MDP with state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An MDP formalizes states, actions, transition probabilities, reward function, and discount factor. The Markov property says the current state contains the information needed to predict the distribution of the next state given an action; history should not add information once state is known.
lessons.explain: An MDP formalizes states, actions, transition probabilities, reward function, and discount factor. The Markov property says the current state contains the information needed to predict the distribution of the next state given an action; history should not add information once state is known.
examples:
mdp={"states":[0,1,2],"actions":["left","right"],"gamma":0.99}
print(mdp)
lessons.example:
mdp={"states":[0,1,2],"actions":["left","right"],"gamma":0.99}
print(mdp)
commonMistakes: Calling any sensor reading “the state” can violate the Markov assumption if past information is required to predict what happens next.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Returns, discounting & reward design
objectives: Compute discounted return and reason about reward design incentives.
Explain how return changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect return with discount factor and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The return is the cumulative future reward an agent tries to maximize. Discounting with gamma gives nearer rewards more weight and keeps infinite-horizon sums well behaved.
lessons.explain: The return is the cumulative future reward an agent tries to maximize. Discounting with gamma gives nearer rewards more weight and keeps infinite-horizon sums well behaved.
examples:
rewards=[0,1,2]; gamma=.9
G=sum((gamma**t)*r for t,r in enumerate(rewards))
print(round(G,3))
lessons.example:
rewards=[0,1,2]; gamma=.9
G=sum((gamma**t)*r for t,r in enumerate(rewards))
print(round(G,3))
commonMistakes: Adding a convenient shaping reward can create reward hacking where the agent maximizes the proxy instead of the real objective.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Value functions: V(s) and Q(s,a)
objectives: Interpret value functions as expected future return under a policy.
Explain how state value changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect state value with action value and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Vπ(s) is the expected return starting from state s and following policy π. Qπ(s,a) additionally conditions on taking action a first.
lessons.explain: Vπ(s) is the expected return starting from state s and following policy π. Qπ(s,a) additionally conditions on taking action a first.
examples:
Q={"safe":1.2,"risky":0.8}
print("greedy action",max(Q,key=Q.get))
lessons.example:
Q={"safe":1.2,"risky":0.8}
print("greedy action",max(Q,key=Q.get))
commonMistakes: A value estimate is not an immediate reward; it summarizes expected future return and therefore depends on downstream behavior.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Bellman equations & bootstrapping
objectives: Explain how values relate recursively to reward plus next-state value.
Explain how Bellman equation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Bellman equation with bootstrapping and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Bellman equations express value as immediate reward plus discounted expected value of what follows. This recursive structure enables dynamic programming and temporal-difference learning.
lessons.explain: Bellman equations express value as immediate reward plus discounted expected value of what follows. This recursive structure enables dynamic programming and temporal-difference learning.
examples:
reward=1; gamma=.9; next_value=4
value=reward+gamma*next_value
print(value)
lessons.example:
reward=1; gamma=.9; next_value=4
value=reward+gamma*next_value
print(value)
commonMistakes: Bootstrapping from a badly biased value target can spread that bias through many states, so stability and target construction matter.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Dynamic programming: policy evaluation & iteration
objectives: Solve small known MDPs when transition and reward models are available.
Explain how policy evaluation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect policy evaluation with policy improvement and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Dynamic programming repeatedly applies Bellman backups using a known environment model. Policy evaluation estimates values for a fixed policy; policy improvement chooses better actions using those values; policy iteration alternates both.
lessons.explain: Dynamic programming repeatedly applies Bellman backups using a known environment model. Policy evaluation estimates values for a fixed policy; policy improvement chooses better actions using those values; policy iteration alternates both.
commonMistakes: Dynamic programming assumes access to transition probabilities and rewards; applying it directly to an unknown real environment is usually impossible.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo learning
objectives: Estimate values from complete sampled episodes without an environment model.
Explain how Monte Carlo changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Monte Carlo with episode and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Monte Carlo methods wait until an episode ends, compute the observed return, and use it as a target. They do not bootstrap and need no transition model, making them conceptually simple and unbiased with enough representative samples.
lessons.explain: Monte Carlo methods wait until an episode ends, compute the observed return, and use it as a target. They do not bootstrap and need no transition model, making them conceptually simple and unbiased with enough representative samples.
examples:
returns=[3,5,4,6]
print("MC estimate",sum(returns)/len(returns))
lessons.example:
returns=[3,5,4,6]
print("MC estimate",sum(returns)/len(returns))
commonMistakes: Treating one noisy episode return as a reliable value estimate produces unstable learning; Monte Carlo relies on averaging many samples.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Temporal-difference learning
objectives: Update a value estimate before an episode finishes.
Explain how TD learning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect TD learning with TD error and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Temporal-difference learning combines sampling with bootstrapping. TD(0) updates V(s) toward r + γV(s′) after each transition, using the TD error as the learning signal.
lessons.explain: Temporal-difference learning combines sampling with bootstrapping. TD(0) updates V(s) toward r + γV(s′) after each transition, using the TD error as the learning signal.
examples:
V=2.0; reward=1; next_v=3; gamma=.9; alpha=.1
td=reward+gamma*next_v-V
V += alpha*td
print(V)
lessons.example:
V=2.0; reward=1; next_v=3; gamma=.9; alpha=.1
td=reward+gamma*next_v-V
V += alpha*td
print(V)
commonMistakes: Using too large a learning rate can make bootstrapped value estimates oscillate or diverge instead of settling.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: SARSA & Q-learning
objectives: Contrast on-policy and off-policy TD control.
Explain how SARSA changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SARSA with Q-learning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: SARSA updates Q using the next action actually chosen by the current behavior policy, so it is on-policy. Q-learning updates toward the maximum next-action value, learning a greedy target policy while behavior may still explore, so it is off-policy.
lessons.explain: SARSA updates Q using the next action actually chosen by the current behavior policy, so it is on-policy. Q-learning updates toward the maximum next-action value, learning a greedy target policy while behavior may still explore, so it is off-policy.
examples:
q_sa=1; r=0; gamma=.9; q_next_actual=.5; q_next_best=1.2
print("SARSA target",r+gamma*q_next_actual,"Q target",r+gamma*q_next_best)
lessons.example:
q_sa=1; r=0; gamma=.9; q_next_actual=.5; q_next_best=1.2
print("SARSA target",r+gamma*q_next_actual,"Q target",r+gamma*q_next_best)
commonMistakes: Assuming on-policy and off-policy methods behave identically can hide important safety differences in environments where exploration has consequences.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Exploration: ε-greedy, schedules & uncertainty
objectives: Balance gathering information with using the best-known action.
Explain how exploration changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect exploration with epsilon-greedy and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An RL agent must explore because current value estimates may be wrong. ε-greedy chooses a random action with probability ε and the greedy action otherwise; schedules often reduce ε as knowledge improves.
lessons.explain: An RL agent must explore because current value estimates may be wrong. ε-greedy chooses a random action with probability ε and the greedy action otherwise; schedules often reduce ε as knowledge improves.
examples:
import random
actions=["left","right"]; epsilon=.1
choice=random.choice(actions) if random.random()<epsilon else "right"
print(choice)
lessons.example:
import random
actions=["left","right"]; epsilon=.1
choice=random.choice(actions) if random.random()<epsilon else "right"
print(choice)
commonMistakes: Decaying exploration too quickly can lock the agent into a mediocre policy based on early noisy experience.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Function approximation & neural value models
objectives: Generalize value estimates to large or continuous state spaces.
Explain how function approximation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect function approximation with generalization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Tabular values require a separate entry for every state-action pair, which is impossible in large spaces. Function approximation predicts values or policies from features using linear models or neural networks.
lessons.explain: Tabular values require a separate entry for every state-action pair, which is impossible in large spaces. Function approximation predicts values or policies from features using linear models or neural networks.
examples:
def q(features,weights): return sum(x*w for x,w in zip(features,weights))
print(q([1,.5],[.4,1.2]))
lessons.example:
def q(features,weights): return sum(x*w for x,w in zip(features,weights))
print(q([1,.5],[.4,1.2]))
commonMistakes: A function approximator can generalize in the wrong direction, so lower training loss does not automatically mean a better policy.

lessons.title: Deep Q-Networks: replay & target networks
objectives: Explain the two major stability mechanisms in DQN.
Explain how DQN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DQN with replay buffer and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: DQN uses a neural network to approximate Q values. Consecutive environment transitions are correlated, so replay buffers randomize training batches and reuse experience.
lessons.explain: DQN uses a neural network to approximate Q values. Consecutive environment transitions are correlated, so replay buffers randomize training batches and reuse experience.
commonMistakes: Training only on the newest transition couples updates strongly to recent trajectory order and can destabilize the network.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Policy gradients & REINFORCE
objectives: Optimize policy parameters directly using sampled returns.
Explain how policy gradient changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect policy gradient with REINFORCE and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Policy-gradient methods parameterize the action distribution and adjust parameters to increase the log-probability of actions that produced high return. REINFORCE is the basic Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimator.
lessons.explain: Policy-gradient methods parameterize the action distribution and adjust parameters to increase the log-probability of actions that produced high return. REINFORCE is the basic Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimator.
examples:
advantages=[1.2,-.4,.7]
log_probs=[-.2,-1.0,-.5]
loss=-sum(a*lp for a,lp in zip(advantages,log_probs))
print(round(loss,3))
lessons.example:
advantages=[1.2,-.4,.7]
log_probs=[-.2,-1.0,-.5]
loss=-sum(a*lp for a,lp in zip(advantages,log_probs))
print(round(loss,3))
commonMistakes: Using raw returns without normalization or a baseline can produce very noisy gradients that require many trajectories.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Actor-critic methods & advantage estimation
objectives: Use a learned critic to reduce policy-gradient variance.
Explain how actor-critic changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect actor-critic with critic and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Actor-critic methods learn a policy actor and a value critic together. The critic estimates expected return and the actor updates using an advantage signal that compares an action’s outcome with what was expected.
lessons.explain: Actor-critic methods learn a policy actor and a value critic together. The critic estimates expected return and the actor updates using an advantage signal that compares an action’s outcome with what was expected.
examples:
q=5.0; v=3.8
advantage=q-v
print("advantage",advantage)
lessons.example:
q=5.0; v=3.8
advantage=q-v
print("advantage",advantage)
commonMistakes: A poor critic can provide misleading advantages and push the policy in the wrong direction even when the policy optimizer is implemented correctly.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: PPO: clipped policy optimization
objectives: Explain how PPO limits destructive policy updates while reusing sampled data.
Explain how PPO changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect PPO with importance ratio and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: PPO compares the probability of sampled actions under the new and old policies using an importance ratio. Its clipped objective limits the incentive to move the ratio too far from 1, reducing the chance that one optimization phase destroys the policy.
lessons.explain: PPO compares the probability of sampled actions under the new and old policies using an importance ratio. Its clipped objective limits the incentive to move the ratio too far from 1, reducing the chance that one optimization phase destroys the policy.
examples:
ratio=1.35; eps=.2
clipped=min(max(ratio,1-eps),1+eps)
print("ratio",ratio,"clipped",clipped)
lessons.example:
ratio=1.35; eps=.2
clipped=min(max(ratio,1-eps),1+eps)
print("ratio",ratio,"clipped",clipped)
commonMistakes: Treating PPO as automatically stable and ignoring KL divergence, reward curves, or entropy can allow silent policy collapse.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Offline RL & distribution shift
objectives: Reason about learning from a fixed dataset without collecting new interaction.
Explain how offline RL changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect offline RL with behavior policy and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Offline RL learns from transitions collected by a behavior policy and cannot correct mistakes by immediately gathering new data. The major challenge is distribution shift: the learned policy may choose actions that are poorly represented in the dataset, where value estimates are unreliable.
lessons.explain: Offline RL learns from transitions collected by a behavior policy and cannot correct mistakes by immediately gathering new data. The major challenge is distribution shift: the learned policy may choose actions that are poorly represented in the dataset, where value estimates are unreliable.
examples:
dataset_actions={"safe":900,"risky":3}
print("coverage",dataset_actions)
lessons.example:
dataset_actions={"safe":900,"risky":3}

lessons.explanation: Behavior cloning treats expert state-action pairs as supervised learning examples. lessons.title: How to interview
lessons.explain: Interviewers score your PROCESS, not just the answer. Clarify the problem, state your approach out loud, start with brute force, then optimize, and communicate trade-offs.
lessons.example: Clarify → approach out loud → brute force → optimize → test → discuss
objectives: Communicate your reasoning clearly while solving a problem live
Explain how think aloud changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect think aloud with clarify and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Staying silent while thinking during a live interview, leaving the interviewer no way to follow your reasoning or help.
lessons.explanation: Interviewers score your PROCESS, not just the answer. Clarify the problem, state your approach out loud, start with brute force, then optimize, and communicate trade-offs.

lessons.title: Behavioral interviews & the STAR method
objectives: Structure a behavioral answer using the STAR method
Explain how STAR method changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect STAR method with situation/task/action/result and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Behavioral interviews probe past experience to predict future behavior ('tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate'). The STAR method structures a clear answer: Situation (brief context), Task (what needed to happen), Action (what YOU specifically did), Result (the outcome, ideally with a concrete measure).
examples:
# STAR in practice:
# Situation: 'Our team's deploy pipeline was failing intermittently'
# Task: 'I needed to find the root cause before the next release'
# Action: 'I added logging, isolated it to a race condition, and fixed it'
# Result: 'Deploy failures dropped from 15% to under 1%'
commonMistakes: Describing what 'the team' did throughout a STAR answer instead of specifically what YOU did — interviewers are evaluating your individual judgment and actions, not the team's.
lessons.careerRelevance: STAR-structured answers are the expected format in virtually every behavioral interview round across company types.
lessons.explain: Behavioral interviews probe past experience to predict future behavior ('tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate'). # STAR in practice:
# Situation: 'Our team's deploy pipeline was failing intermittently'
# Task: 'I needed to find the root cause before the next release'
# Action: 'I added logging, isolated it to a race condition, and fixed it'
# Result: 'Deploy failures dropped from 15% to under 1%'

lessons.title: Technical interviews: what's actually being evaluated
objectives: Understand what a technical interviewer is really scoring beyond 'right answer'
Explain how process over pure output changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect process over pure output with communicated reasoning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A technical interview scores more than just reaching a correct final answer: how you clarify the problem before coding, whether you communicate your reasoning as you go, how you handle hints or pushback, and whether you test/verify your own solution.
examples:
# what's actually being scored:
# - clarifying questions before diving in
# - reasoning communicated OUT LOUD, not just silent typing
# - responding well to hints, not getting defensive
# - testing your own solution before declaring it done
commonMistakes: Treating a technical interview as a silent exam to be solved alone — interviewers are actively evaluating your communication and collaboration throughout, not just grading a final answer.
lessons.careerRelevance: This process-focused framing directly connects to the Problem Solving track's think-aloud practice.

lessons.title: Whiteboard & live problem-solving interviews
objectives: Apply a structured approach to solving a problem live, under observation
Explain how narrated problem-solving changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect narrated problem-solving with managing observation pressure and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Live problem-solving (whiteboard or shared editor) rewards the same method as the Problem Solving track: restate the problem, work a small example, identify the pattern, start with brute force, then optimize — done OUT LOUD, in front of the interviewer, rather than silently in your head.
examples:
# live problem-solving flow, narrated out loud:
# 'Let me make sure I understand -- so we want the longest subarray where...'
# 'Let me try a small example: [1,2,3] would give...'
# 'I'll start with a brute-force approach, then see if we can optimize'
commonMistakes: Going silent for long stretches while thinking — even when stuck, narrating your current thinking ('I'm considering whether a hash map helps here') keeps the interviewer engaged and gives.
lessons.careerRelevance: Comfort with being watched while thinking is a distinct, practicable skill separate from raw problem-solving ability.

lessons.title: System design interviews
objectives: Structure a system design interview answer
Explain how requirements clarification first changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect requirements clarification first with high-level then deep-dive and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: System design interviews (common for more senior roles, sometimes appearing even at internship level) evaluate architectural judgment on open-ended problems ('design a URL shortener').
examples:
# system design flow:
# 1. clarify: how many users? read-heavy or write-heavy? latency requirements?
# 2. sketch high-level: client -> load balancer -> API -> database (+ cache)
# 3. go deep where the interviewer leans in, discussing trade-offs explicitly
commonMistakes: Jumping straight into deep technical detail on one component before clarifying scale and requirements — the 'right' design depends entirely on requirements that must be established first.
lessons.careerRelevance: System design interview structure directly reuses the System Design track's content, applied under live interview conditions.

lessons.title: Mock interview workflow
objectives: Design and run an effective mock interview practice routine
Explain how realistic simulation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect realistic simulation with specific actionable feedback and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An effective mock interview practice loop: simulate real conditions (timed, out loud, ideally with another person rather than silently in your head), get specific feedback (not just 'good job' but what exactly worked or didn't), and iterate — targeting the SPECIFIC weakness identified, not just repeating generic practice.
examples:
# mock interview loop:
# 1. simulate real conditions: timed, verbal, with a partner or recording
# 2. get SPECIFIC feedback ('you jumped to coding before clarifying constraints')
# 3. practice that SPECIFIC weakness deliberately before the next mock
# 4. repeat, tracking improvement over successive mocks
commonMistakes: Doing many mock interviews with no specific feedback loop or targeted improvement focus — repetition without a feedback loop plateaus quickly; targeted iteration on named weaknesses.
lessons.careerRelevance: A deliberate mock-interview practice discipline is one of the highest-leverage, most controllable parts of interview preparation.

lessons.title: Communication skills in interviews
objectives: Apply concrete communication habits that improve interview performance
Explain how deliberate pacing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect deliberate pacing with clarifying over guessing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Strong interview communication is learnable and concrete: pause briefly before answering rather than rushing to fill silence, ask clarifying questions rather than guessing at ambiguous prompts, and check in periodically ('does this approach make sense so far?') rather than talking uninterrupted for minutes.
examples:
# concrete communication habits:
# - a 2-3 second pause before answering beats a rushed, unclear answer
# - 'to make sure I understand correctly...' before diving into an ambiguous prompt
# - periodic check-ins during a long explanation, not one uninterrupted monologue
commonMistakes: Treating communication skill as fixed/innate rather than a practicable habit — these are concrete, learnable behaviors, not just personality traits.
lessons.careerRelevance: Communication quality is explicitly and separately scored in most structured interview rubrics, alongside technical correctness.

lessons.title: Salary negotiation basics
objectives: Apply basic, low-risk negotiation practices after receiving an offer
Explain how market research before negotiating changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect market research before negotiating with total package framing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Negotiation basics: let the company name a number first when possible, research a realistic market range beforehand (from public salary-data sources and your own network) so you have a concrete anchor, and negotiate the TOTAL package (base, equity, signing bonus, start date) not just base salary alone.
examples:
# a low-risk, low-drama negotiation script:
# 'Thank you for the offer, I'm excited about this. Based on my research and other
# conversations, I was hoping for something closer to $X -- is there flexibility here?'
commonMistakes: Accepting the very first offer immediately with no attempt to ask about flexibility — a polite, well-researched ask rarely costs anything and often yields at least a modest improvement.
lessons.careerRelevance: Negotiation directly affects real compensation outcomes and is a skill worth practicing deliberately, not avoiding out of discomfort.

lessons.title: Follow-up emails & closing the loop
objectives: Write an effective post-interview follow-up email
Explain how timely follow-up changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect timely follow-up with specific over generic and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A brief, genuine follow-up email within a day of each interview round — thanking the specific interviewer, referencing one real detail from the conversation, and reaffirming interest — is a small, low-cost signal of genuine engagement that a surprising number of candidates skip entirely.
examples:
# generic (weak): 'Thank you for your time today. I look forward to hearing from you.'
# specific (stronger): 'Thanks for walking me through the caching challenges your team is
# tackling -- our conversation about the trade-offs there really stuck with me.'
commonMistakes: Sending no follow-up at all, or a generic template identical to what you'd send any company — a brief, specific note costs little time and measurably signals genuine engagement.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is a small, easy, frequently-skipped habit with outsized signal value relative to its low effort cost.

lessons.title: Resume fundamentals: structure & content
objectives: Structure a resume that a recruiter can scan in under 10 seconds
Explain how scannable structure changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect scannable structure with outcome-focused bullets and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A resume gets scanned, not read, in the first pass — often under 10 seconds. Structure matters as much as content: a clear header, a tight skills section, and experience/projects described with concrete outcomes ('reduced query time by 40%') rather than vague duties ('worked on backend features').
examples:
# weak: 'Worked on the backend of a web application'
# strong: 'Built a REST API serving 10k+ daily requests, reducing average response time by 35%'
commonMistakes: Listing job duties instead of outcomes — 'responsible for X' tells a recruiter what you were assigned, not what you actually accomplished or how well you did it.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the single highest-leverage document in the entire job search — every other prep track feeds into what this document claims.

lessons.title: ATS optimization: passing the automated screen
objectives: Format and word a resume to survive automated screening
Explain how ATS parsing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect ATS parsing with keyword matching and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Many companies run resumes through an ATS (Applicant Tracking System) before a human ever sees them — software that parses text and often filters by keyword match against the job description.
examples:
# job description says: 'Experience with React.js and RESTful APIs required'
# resume should include those EXACT terms if true, not just close synonyms like 'frontend frameworks' and 'web services'
commonMistakes: Using a visually elaborate template with text boxes, columns, or icons that an ATS parser mangles into unreadable, out-of-order text — simpler, more standard formatting is safer for the.
lessons.careerRelevance: A resume that never survives the ATS never reaches a human, regardless of how strong the actual candidate is.

lessons.title: Portfolio creation: showing, not just telling

Explain how evidence over claims changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect evidence over claims with project curation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A resume CLAIMS skill; a portfolio (a personal site, deployed projects, a curated GitHub) PROVES it with evidence a reader can actually inspect.
examples:
# a portfolio entry that actually persuades:
# project name + one-line problem statement + live demo link + README covering
# key decisions and trade-offs + a screenshot -- not just a bare repo link
commonMistakes: Listing 15 half-finished tutorial-following projects with no individual context — quantity without depth or documentation reads as unfinished, not prolific.
lessons.careerRelevance: A portfolio is frequently what actually gets discussed in an interview, far more than the resume bullet points themselves.
