lessons.title: Building a strong GitHub profile
objectives: Curate a GitHub profile that reads well to a technical reviewer
Explain how pinned repositories changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pinned repositories with README quality and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A recruiter or engineer will often click through to GitHub before or during an interview loop — a profile with pinned, well-named repositories, clear READMEs, and a sensible commit history (from the Git & GitHub track) reads as someone who ships real, maintained work.
examples:
# pin your 4-6 BEST repos explicitly (GitHub lets you choose)
# make sure each pinned repo has: a real README, a working demo/screenshot if applicable,
# and reasonably recent, real commit activity -- not a single 'initial commit'
commonMistakes: Leaving GitHub's default repo ordering (most recently updated) instead of deliberately pinning your strongest work — a reviewer may see an old throwaway script before your best project.
lessons.careerRelevance: Technical interviewers frequently browse a candidate's GitHub directly, making it a real extension of the resume, not a side detail.

lessons.title: LinkedIn optimization
objectives: Optimize a LinkedIn profile for both recruiter search and human review
Explain how headline optimization changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect headline optimization with searchability vs readability and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: LinkedIn serves two audiences: recruiters SEARCHING by keyword (so your headline and skills section should include the exact terms you want to be found for) and humans actually READING your profile once found (so your About section should read like a coherent narrative, not a keyword dump).
examples:
# weak headline: 'Software Engineer'
# stronger: 'Backend Software Engineer | Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL | Building scalable APIs'
# -- searchable keywords AND a clear specialization, in one line
commonMistakes: Leaving a LinkedIn profile mostly blank or unchanged since account creation — an incomplete profile is directly filtered out of many recruiter searches before a human ever considers the.
lessons.careerRelevance: A significant share of real interview opportunities, especially for internships, originate from inbound recruiter outreach on LinkedIn, not just applications.

Explain how tailored emphasis changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A single generic resume sent everywhere underperforms a resume deliberately tailored per application — not rewritten from scratch each time, but with emphasis, keyword alignment, and bullet ordering adjusted to mirror what THIS specific job description prioritizes.
examples:
# job description emphasizes 'distributed systems' and 'API design' repeatedly
# -> reorder/reword your bullets to foreground exactly those experiences first,
# even if your resume also has other, less-relevant experience further down
commonMistakes: Sending the identical resume to every application regardless of role focus — small, targeted adjustments measurably improve response rates for a modest time cost per application.
lessons.careerRelevance: Tailoring is a repeatable, high-ROI habit that compounds across every application in a real job search.

objectives: Identify and fix the most frequent resume mistakes
Explain how typos/inconsistency changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect typos/inconsistency with length discipline and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: The most common, avoidable mistakes: typos and inconsistent formatting (a strong signal of carelessness to a reviewer), burying the most relevant experience below less relevant older material, resumes over 1-2 pages for early-career candidates, and vague buzzwords ('hardworking team player') with no concrete evidence behind them.
examples:
# vague, unsupported claim: 'Excellent problem solver and team player'
# fix: replace with a specific, evidenced example --
# 'Diagnosed and fixed a production memory leak, reducing server restarts by 90%'
commonMistakes: Treating buzzword-heavy language as a substitute for specific, evidenced accomplishments — reviewers routinely discount unsupported adjectives.
lessons.careerRelevance: Catching these mistakes before submission is entirely free — this lesson's checklist directly prevents avoidable rejections.

objectives: Apply a systematic final checklist before submitting a resume
Explain how pre-submission checklist changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pre-submission checklist with external review and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before submitting: does every bullet show an outcome, not just a duty? Does it mirror the target job description's key terms?
examples:
# a genuinely useful pre-submit checklist:
# [ ] every bullet has a measurable/concrete outcome
# [ ] key terms from the job description appear naturally
# [ ] simple, ATS-safe formatting
# [ ] zero typos (read aloud + a second reviewer)
# [ ] most relevant experience appears first
commonMistakes: Submitting a resume immediately after writing it with no second pass or outside reviewer — a fresh set of eyes catches errors and unclear phrasing the writer has become blind to.
lessons.careerRelevance: A consistent final-check habit is a small, repeatable discipline with an outsized effect on interview conversion rate.

lessons.title: Quantifying your achievements with real numbers
objectives: Turn vague resume claims into specific, quantified evidence
Explain how quantifying achievements changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect quantifying achievements with specific numbers and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: "Improved performance" is vague and unconvincing. "Reduced page load time by 40%, cutting bounce rate by 15%" is specific, verifiable-sounding, and memorable.
examples:

# quantified: 'Redesigned checkout flow, reducing cart abandonment from 68% to 51%'

lessons.careerRelevance: Quantified achievements are consistently what recruiters and hiring managers say they scan for first.

lessons.title: Researching companies before you apply

lessons.explanation: Real company research goes beyond the homepage: understand the actual product (use it if possible), recent news (funding, layoffs, launches — these shape interview mood and questions), engineering blog posts (reveal real technical priorities and stack), and what the interview process is known to look like (from company engineering blogs.

lessons.title: The FAANG-style interview process
objectives: Describe the typical structure of a large tech company's interview process
Explain how structured, multi-round process changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect structured, multi-round process with standardized rubrics and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Large tech companies (and companies that model their process similarly, sometimes called FAANG-style) typically run: an initial recruiter screen, one or more technical phone/video screens (often a live coding platform), an onsite or virtual loop with multiple rounds (coding, system design for more senior roles, behavioral).
examples:
# typical loop shape:
# recruiter screen -> 1-2 technical phone screens -> onsite loop
# (coding x2, system design, behavioral) -> hiring committee decision
# -- each round is often scored independently against a rubric, not just a gut call
commonMistakes: Assuming one strong round can compensate for a weak one, or that the interviewer alone makes the final call — many large companies use committee review across ALL round feedback, not a.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this structure specifically helps set realistic expectations and reduces anxiety about any single round feeling decisive.

lessons.explanation: Given limited interview time, the projects you bring up should map directly to what the target role and company actually need — a role emphasizing backend APIs is better served by discussing your Backend Development track projects in depth than a frontend side project, even if the latter is more polished.

lessons.title: Coding assessment strategies
objectives: Apply a systematic strategy for timed online coding assessments
Explain how assessment triage changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect assessment triage with brute-force-first under time pressure and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Timed coding assessments (OAs) reward strategy alongside raw ability: read ALL problems first and triage by difficulty/point value before diving in, don't get stuck on one problem burning all your remaining time, write and test the brute-force solution first if you're unsure of the optimal approach (partial credit usually beats no submission).
examples:
# OA time-management strategy:
# 1. skim ALL problems first, note relative difficulty/points
# 2. start with the one you're most confident about
# 3. get a working brute-force submission before attempting to optimize
# 4. reserve the last 10-15% of time for edge-case review across all problems
commonMistakes: Spending 70% of the available time perfecting the first problem and running out of time for the rest — triage and partial-credit strategy usually beats depth-first perfectionism on one.
lessons.careerRelevance: This strategic, time-aware approach is directly what separates candidates of similar raw skill in timed assessment outcomes.

lessons.title: Authority vs. Influence
objectives: Distinguish formal decision rights from the ability to move a decision
Explain how authority changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect authority with influence and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Authority is a formal right to decide -- a tech lead can approve a design, a manager can approve a hire.
examples:
# the distinction this whole course rests on:
# authority: 'I can approve this' -- a formal right, held by a specific role
# influence: 'I can help the person who approves this make a better decision'
# -- available to anyone, regardless of title, and the actual subject of this course
commonMistakes: Assuming influence requires becoming someone's manager first -- influence is available to any engineer immediately, built through credibility and how well you help the actual decision owner.
lessons.careerRelevance: Nearly every senior IC promotion at real companies explicitly credits this exact skill -- moving decisions forward without owning them.
lessons.explain: Authority is a formal right to decide -- a tech lead can approve a design, a manager can approve a hire.

lessons.title: Credibility and Trust
objectives: Explain how credibility is built and lost before any single conversation happens
Explain how credibility changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect credibility with trust and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Credibility is built cumulatively, before the specific conversation where you need it -- through a track record of being accurate (your claims turn out to be true), being fair (you represent other viewpoints honestly, not just your own case), and being consistent (you don't shift your position based on who's in the room).
examples:
# why identical proposals land differently:
# engineer A: has a track record of being right about risk estimates, and
# openly flagged their OWN proposal's downsides last time -- the room extends trust
# engineer B: is new, or has previously overstated a benefit that didn't pan out --
# the SAME proposal gets more scrutiny, not because of the idea's merit
commonMistakes: Treating credibility as something you can manufacture in the moment through confident delivery -- credibility is built over many prior interactions being accurate and fair, not created fresh.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is exactly why the same technical argument gets different receptions from different engineers on the same team -- a real, observable pattern, not an unfair mystery.
lessons.explain: Credibility is built cumulatively, before the specific conversation where you need it -- through a track record of being accurate (your claims turn out to be true), being fair (you represent other viewpoints honestly, not just your own case), and being consistent (you don't shift your position based on who's in the room).

objectives: Identify who actually owns a decision versus who merely has input
Explain how decision owner changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect decision owner with decision rights and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before trying to influence a decision, you need to know who actually owns it -- confusing an interested party for the decision owner wastes effort convincing the wrong person, or worse, makes the real owner feel bypassed.
examples:
# a common, avoidable mistake:
# spending a week convincing a skeptical peer engineer, only to learn
# the ACTUAL decision owner is the tech lead, who was never part of the conversation
# -- all that effort went toward someone who was never going to make the call
commonMistakes: Assuming the most vocal or most senior person in the room is automatically the decision owner -- decision rights depend on the actual structure of a specific decision, which isn't always the.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly identifying the real decision owner before investing effort is one of the highest-leverage, most overlooked skills in getting anything approved.
lessons.explain: Before trying to influence a decision, you need to know who actually owns it -- confusing an interested party for the decision owner wastes effort convincing the wrong person, or worse, makes the real owner feel bypassed.

lessons.title: Listening Before Persuading
objectives: Explain how genuine listening can change the proposal itself, not just how it's delivered

lessons.explanation: Listening before persuading isn't a delivery technique to make people feel heard before you convince them anyway -- done genuinely, it can change the actual proposal. A stakeholder's objection often contains real information (a constraint, a past incident, a dependency) that should legitimately change what you're proposing, not just how you pitch it.

# the real test of genuine listening:
# NOT: nodding along, then delivering the identical pitch anyway
# BUT: 'I hadn't considered that this migration would break your team's existing
# monitoring -- let me revise the plan to include a monitoring migration step first'
# -- the PROPOSAL itself changed because of what you heard, not just your delivery

lessons.careerRelevance: This distinction -- performed listening versus listening that changes the actual proposal -- is exactly what separates influence from a sales technique.

lessons.title: Framing for Different Audiences
objectives: Adapt the same technical fact for different audiences without changing or hiding the fact itself

lessons.explanation: Framing means presenting the same underlying facts in the way that addresses a specific audience's actual concern -- an engineer wants to know how it works and what could break; a product manager wants to know user and timeline impact; an executive wants risk and cost at a glance; a customer wants to know what changes for them.

# engineer: 'this requires a 4-hour maintenance window due to a schema lock'

# BOTH state the same 4-hour downtime fact -- neither hides or shrinks it

lessons.title: Influencing in Meetings and Design Reviews

lessons.explanation: A design review is where a proposal gets tested in real time -- preparing means anticipating the specific objections THIS specific audience is likely to raise (not a generic list), and having a clear, honest answer ready, including 'I don't know yet, here's how I'd find out' where genuinely true.
examples:
# actively inviting disagreement, rather than just defending:
# 'before I walk through the proposal, what's the concern you'd expect someone

# while it's still cheap to address, instead of discovering it after the room
# has already quietly decided against the idea

lessons.title: Handling Objections Without Defensiveness
objectives: Respond to a raised objection by acknowledging, clarifying, and offering evidence rather than becoming defensive
Explain how acknowledging concerns changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: A defensive response to an objection ('that's not going to happen' or immediately arguing back) tends to escalate rather than resolve, and damages the credibility the whole rest of this course depends on.

# defensive vs. constructive response to 'this is too risky':
# defensive: 'no it's not, I've already tested this' (dismisses the concern outright)
# constructive: 'that's a fair concern given our last incident -- here's what's
# different this time, and here's the rollback plan if I'm wrong'
# -- acknowledges, clarifies the assumption, and offers evidence/options

lessons.title: Productive Disagreement and Conflict
objectives: Distinguish disagreement from disrespect, and disagree while preserving the working relationship
Explain how disagreement vs. disrespect changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect disagreement vs. disrespect with psychological safety and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Disagreement is a normal, healthy part of technical work -- two reasonable engineers can look at the same facts and reach different conclusions, and treating disagreement itself as a problem to eliminate (rather than something to work through) tends to suppress genuinely useful pushback.
examples:
# disagreement (healthy) vs. disrespect (damaging):
# disagreement: 'I see this differently -- I think the caching layer adds more
# risk than it saves here, and here's why'
# disrespect: 'that's a naive suggestion' or refusing to explain why you disagree
# -- the first invites continued discussion; the second shuts it down and damages
# trust needed for future disagreements to go well
commonMistakes: Treating disagreement itself as something to avoid or suppress -- healthy technical disagreement, handled respectfully, is normal and valuable; the goal is disagreeing well, not avoiding.
lessons.careerRelevance: Teams with a strong track record of technical quality are frequently ones where disagreement is normalized and handled respectfully, not avoided.

lessons.title: Negotiating Scope, Deadlines and Technical Debt
objectives: Negotiate trade-offs honestly, recognizing that not every constraint can be maximized simultaneously
Explain how trade-off negotiation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect trade-off negotiation with coupled constraints and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Delivery date, feature scope, reliability, and technical debt are genuinely coupled -- you cannot maximize all of them simultaneously with fixed capacity, and pretending otherwise (agreeing to an unrealistic combination just to avoid conflict) just moves the actual failure to a worse, later moment.
examples:
# the trade-off, made visible instead of quietly ignored:
# 'ship all this scope, hit this date, AND maintain full reliability, with no
# extra staffing' is often not simultaneously achievable -- naming this honestly
# ('something has to give: less scope, more time, more people, or accepted risk')
# is more useful than agreeing to an impossible combination and failing later
commonMistakes: Agreeing to an unrealistic combination of scope, date, and reliability just to avoid a difficult conversation now -- this doesn't resolve the actual constraint, it just delays the failure to.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to name an infeasible combination of constraints honestly (rather than quietly overcommitting) is a hallmark of senior engineering judgment in real delivery negotiations.

lessons.title: Coalition Building and Cross-Functional Alignment
objectives: Build support across teams before a decision point, rather than only at the moment of decision
Explain how coalition building changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect coalition building with pre-alignment and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Coalition building means talking to key stakeholders individually BEFORE a decision meeting, understanding their specific concerns, and where possible addressing them ahead of time -- so the actual decision meeting is confirming alignment that already exists, rather than the first time anyone has heard the proposal or raised their concerns.
examples:
# genuine coalition building vs. manufactured consensus:
# genuine: talking to the security team a week before the review, learning their
# specific concern, and revising the proposal to address it BEFORE the meeting
# manufactured (NOT what this teaches): privately pressuring people to publicly
# agree regardless of their actual view, so the meeting just looks unanimous
commonMistakes: Confusing genuine coalition building (incorporating real feedback ahead of time) with manufacturing artificial consensus (pressuring people to appear aligned regardless of their actual view).
lessons.careerRelevance: Cross-functional alignment done well is frequently why some proposals sail through review while equally good ones stall -- the difference is often preparation, not idea quality.

lessons.title: Ethical Influence and a Repeatable Process
objectives: Synthesize the course into one repeatable process, stated honestly as improving decision quality, not guaranteeing agreement
Explain how repeatable influence process changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect repeatable influence process with improving decision quality and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every idea in this course fits into one repeatable process: (1) clarify the decision, (2) identify the decision owner, (3) map stakeholders, (4) listen for interests and constraints, (5) gather proportionate evidence, (6) frame the proposal honestly, (7) invite objections, (8) negotiate trade-offs.
examples:
# the repeatable process, and its honest limit:
# clarify -> identify owner -> map stakeholders -> listen -> gather evidence ->
# frame honestly -> invite objections -> negotiate -> escalate only if legitimate
# -> accept the final decision when appropriate
# this process improves decision QUALITY -- it does not guarantee AGREEMENT,
# and persisting past a legitimate 'no' is not a version of doing this well
commonMistakes: Treating a well-executed influence process as something that should always end in agreement -- a legitimate decision owner can hear a well-framed, well-evidenced case and still reasonably.
lessons.careerRelevance: This honest limit -- that good influence improves decisions without guaranteeing outcomes -- is exactly the maturity that distinguishes senior engineering judgment from simply being persuasive.

exercises.title: Map stakeholders for a database migration
exercises.prompt: A database migration affects the backend team, an adjacent analytics team, and a security reviewer. Identify each person's decision role, engagement requirement, and current stance.
exercises.hint: treat these as 3 independent fields per person -- e.g. the analytics team may have no formal decision right but needs to be consulted and currently feels resistant due to a past migration incident

exercises.title: Rewrite one argument for three audiences
exercises.prompt: Rewrite the fact 'this refactor requires 2 weeks and a temporary code freeze' for an engineer, a product manager, and an executive -- without changing or hiding the underlying fact.
exercises.hint: engineer: technical reason for the freeze; PM: timeline/feature impact; executive: risk and cost framing -- the 2-week freeze fact itself must appear, unchanged, in all three

exercises.title: Identify missing evidence in a proposal
exercises.prompt: A proposal claims 'this will improve performance significantly' with no supporting data. What evidence is missing, and what would be proportionate to add?
exercises.hint: missing: any metric or experiment supporting the performance claim; proportionate evidence would be a benchmark or a small controlled experiment, not just an opinion

exercises.title: Respond to a skeptical senior engineer
exercises.prompt: A senior engineer says 'I don't think this is worth the risk.' Draft a constructive response that acknowledges the concern without becoming defensive.
exercises.hint: acknowledge the concern as reasonable, clarify what specifically they're worried about, then offer evidence or a mitigation (e.g. a rollback plan) rather than dismissing the concern

exercises.title: Negotiate reduced scope with a product manager
exercises.prompt: A PM wants all planned features by the original date. Propose a scope reduction that preserves the most valuable parts while meeting the date.
exercises.hint: identify which features are highest-value vs. lowest-cost-to-defer, and propose deferring the lowest-value/highest-cost items to a follow-up phase rather than an across-the-board cut

exercises.title: Turn a vague complaint into an actionable proposal
exercises.prompt: A teammate says 'our deploys are always so stressful.' Turn this into a specific, actionable proposal.
exercises.hint: identify the specific pain point (e.g. no rollback plan, unclear deploy checklist) and propose one concrete, scoped fix rather than a vague 'improve deploys' goal

exercises.title: Choose the right action when decision ownership is unclear
exercises.prompt: You're unsure who actually owns a technical decision you want to influence. What should you do first: persuade, compromise, escalate, or accept?
exercises.hint: none of the above yet -- first clarify decision ownership itself before choosing an influence strategy; acting before knowing the real owner risks wasted effort

exercises.title: Choose the right action under severe timeline pressure
exercises.prompt: A deadline is in 2 days and your well-evidenced proposal hasn't been reviewed. What's the appropriate next step?
exercises.hint: likely a legitimate, direct request for a quick decision or a documented risk if the deadline passes without review -- not manufacturing urgency or going around the reviewer

exercises.title: Choose the right action after a final legitimate decision
exercises.prompt: The decision owner has heard your full case and decided against your proposal. What's the appropriate response?
exercises.hint: accept the decision -- continuing to push after a legitimate, informed decision has been made is not a version of good influence

exercises.title: Identify an unethical influence tactic
exercises.prompt: A colleague suggests: 'just tell them there's no time to discuss it further so they approve it now.' What's wrong with this, and what would you do instead?
exercises.hint: this is manufactured urgency, a tactic this course explicitly does not teach; instead, give an honest timeline and let the decision owner decide with accurate information

exercises.title: Write a follow-up after a disputed design meeting
exercises.prompt: A design review ended without a clear decision. Draft a follow-up message summarizing the disagreement and proposing next steps.
exercises.hint: summarize the specific point of disagreement accurately (not favoring your side), and propose a concrete next step (e.g. a small experiment to resolve the open question)

exercises.title: Distinguish legitimate escalation from going around someone
exercises.prompt: After a peer declines your proposal, is raising it with their manager always 'going around them'? Explain the distinction.
exercises.hint: legitimate escalation involves the peer knowing it's being raised further and generally uses an established channel; going around someone means bypassing them without their knowledge specifically to avoid their legitimate say

exercises.title: Map incentives behind an objection
exercises.prompt: A team lead objects to your proposal, citing 'not enough time.' What underlying incentive or constraint might actually be driving this?
exercises.hint: e.g. their team may already be over-committed this quarter to a different deliverable -- the stated objection ('not enough time') reflects a real, specific constraint, not necessarily disagreement with your idea's merit

exercises.title: Select proportionate evidence for a low-risk local change
exercises.prompt: You want to rename a poorly-named internal function. What evidence, if any, is proportionate here?
exercises.hint: minimal -- a quick explanation of the naming confusion is likely proportionate; a full experiment or extensive data would be disproportionate overkill for this size of change

exercises.title: Select proportionate evidence for a high-risk system-wide change
exercises.prompt: You want to replace the core database technology powering the whole product. What evidence would be proportionate here?
exercises.hint: a prototype or controlled experiment with real data, plus incident history motivating the change -- opinion alone is not proportionate for a costly, hard-to-reverse decision of this size

exercises.title: Revise a proposal after listening reveals a new constraint
exercises.prompt: While discussing your proposal, a stakeholder mentions a compliance requirement you hadn't considered. How should this change your proposal?
exercises.hint: genuinely incorporate the new constraint into a revised proposal (e.g. add a compliance step), rather than just acknowledging it verbally and proceeding with the original plan unchanged

exercises.title: Draft a trade-off table for a delivery negotiation
exercises.prompt: Draft a simple trade-off table showing how scope, date, and reliability investment relate for a delivery you're negotiating.
exercises.hint: a table with rows for each lever (scope/date/reliability/staffing) and columns showing what increasing one requires giving up elsewhere, making the coupling explicit rather than implied

exercises.title: Identify decision owner, advisors, and affected stakeholders in an ambiguous scenario
exercises.prompt: A cross-team API change has an unclear owner: the API team built it, the consuming teams depend on it, and a platform team sets API standards. Identify each party's likely role.
exercises.hint: likely: platform team or API team as decision owner (depending on org norms) -- must be clarified, not assumed; consuming teams as advisors/affected stakeholders needing consultation, not owners

quiz.q: What does a persuasive technical proposal do beyond describing the desired outcome?

options: They are the same thing

There is no meaningful distinction

quiz.q: What distinguishes healthy disagreement from disrespect?
options: Disagreement should always be avoided entirely
Disagreement engages with the technical substance; disrespect attacks the person or refuses to engage with their point
They are functionally identical
Disrespect is acceptable if the technical point is correct

quiz.q: Why can't delivery date, scope, reliability, and staffing all be maximized simultaneously with fixed capacity?
options: They can always be maximized together with enough effort
These constraints are genuinely coupled -- increasing one typically requires giving up elsewhere
This is only true for large projects
Technical debt is unrelated to these constraints

quiz.q: What distinguishes legitimate escalation from going around someone?
options: There is no real distinction
Legitimate escalation typically uses an established channel and doesn't hide the escalation from the person being escalated past
Escalation is always inappropriate
Going around someone is always the faster option

quiz.q: What distinguishes persuasion from manipulation?
options: They are the same technique with different names
Persuasion preserves informed choice with accurate information; manipulation relies on deception, hidden risk, or exploiting someone's position
Manipulation is simply more effective persuasion
Manipulation is acceptable if the underlying idea is correct

quiz.q: How can power differences affect how influence is experienced?
options: Power differences never matter in influence
A junior engineer raising a concern to someone senior may carry real risk that a peer-to-peer disagreement doesn't, which should be accounted for
Power differences only matter in salary negotiations
Only executives are affected by power differences

quiz.q: What is the appropriate response to a request to hide a material risk from stakeholders?
options: Comply if the requester is senior
Refuse, and use the appropriate reporting or escalation channel
Hide only the smaller risks
Wait until asked directly before disclosing anything

quiz.q: Why can a technically correct idea fail to be adopted?
options: Technically correct ideas are always adopted eventually
Organizational adoption also depends on timing, cost, trust, and competing priorities -- not technical correctness alone
Adoption is unrelated to any of these factors
This situation never actually happens in practice

projects.title: Rewrite a technical proposal for three audiences
projects.desc: Take one technical proposal and produce three honestly-framed one-page variants for an engineer, a product manager, and an executive, preserving all material facts.

projects.title: Build a stakeholder and decision-rights map
projects.desc: Produce a stakeholder map for a real or hypothetical technical change, using decision role, engagement requirement, and stance as independent dimensions for each person.

projects.title: Prepare a design-review influence plan
projects.desc: Prepare a meeting agenda and anticipated-objection list for a contested design review, including how you'll invite disagreement rather than only defend the proposal.

projects.title: Negotiate a delivery plan involving scope, risk, and technical debt
projects.desc: Produce a trade-off table and decision memo negotiating a realistic delivery plan across scope, date, reliability, and technical debt.

projects.title: Produce a complete cross-functional proposal package
projects.desc: Combine a stakeholder map, multi-audience framing, evidence plan, objection responses, and a written follow-up into one complete proposal package.

interviewPreparation.q: Tell me about a time you influenced a decision without owning it.
interviewPreparation.a: Describe a specific situation where you weren't the decision owner but helped shape the outcome -- name who the actual owner was, what evidence or framing you used, and the result. For structuring this as a full behavioral answer with STAR, see Interview Preparation.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you handle a senior engineer who disagrees with your proposal?
interviewPreparation.a: Acknowledge their concern as legitimate, clarify the assumption behind it, and offer evidence or options rather than becoming defensive -- disagreement from a credible senior engineer often contains real information worth incorporating, not just an obstacle to argue past.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you persuade a product manager to reduce scope for reliability?
interviewPreparation.a: Frame the trade-off in terms the PM actually cares about (user impact, timeline risk) rather than purely technical terms, and make the coupling between scope and reliability explicit rather than asking for reliability work 'on top of' the existing scope for free.

interviewPreparation.q: When should an engineer escalate a disagreement?
interviewPreparation.a: When a decision genuinely can't be resolved between the parties involved and something significant is at stake -- and escalation should go through a legitimate channel, transparently, rather than around the person being escalated past.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you build support for technical-debt work?
interviewPreparation.a: Connect the debt to a concrete, felt cost stakeholders already recognize (incident frequency, slow delivery) rather than arguing for 'code quality' in the abstract, and build alignment with affected teams before the work is formally proposed, not only at the proposal meeting.

capstone.title: Influence a Technical Change Across Multiple Stakeholders
capstone.description: Choose a realistic technical change (a database migration, API redesign, security improvement, observability investment, testing-strategy change, technical-debt reduction, architecture refactor, or model-safety improvement) and produce a complete influence plan for it, including one realistic outcome where the final answer remains no.
deliverables: Problem definition
Decision owner identification
Stakeholder map (decision role, engagement requirement, and stance for each person)
Incentives and constraints behind likely objections
An evidence plan proportionate to the size of the claim
An engineer-facing explanation of the change
A product-facing explanation of the change
An executive-facing summary of the change
A user-impact explanation
Anticipated objections and constructive responses
A trade-off table for scope, date, reliability, and technical debt
A meeting strategy for the decision point
A written follow-up after the meeting
A stated escalation boundary -- what would and would not justify escalating further
An ethical-risk check confirming no material risk is hidden or misrepresented
Success criteria for the change
One realistic outcome where, after the full process, the decision owner still says no -- and why accepting that is the right response
capstone.portfolioTips: The required 'still says no' outcome is the deliverable that most distinguishes genuine influence maturity from a persuasion checklist -- explaining why accepting that outcome is correct (not a failure) is exactly the judgment this course is built around.

industryUsage.usage: All explicitly evaluate cross-team influence without formal authority as a core criterion for senior/staff-level individual contributor promotion, distinct from management tracks.

The skills in this course (stakeholder mapping, honest framing, objection handling) are exactly what determines whether a technically sound proposal actually gets adopted in a real design review process.

careerApplications: Used by engineers working across teams to present evidence, negotiate trade-offs, write proposals, handle disagreement, and move technical decisions forward without relying on formal authority.

title: Embedded Systems & Microcontrollers
blurb: Microcontrollers, GPIO, sensors, timers, interrupts, firmware architecture, device communication, and Python-based simulation.
description: Learn embedded-system thinking with Python and MicroPython-style patterns while keeping browser practice safe and runnable.

lessons.title: Microcontrollers & the embedded mindset
objectives: Explain what a microcontroller contains
Reason about memory, timing, power, and hardware constraints
Explain how microcontroller changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect microcontroller with flash and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A microcontroller combines a CPU, flash, RAM, timers, communication peripherals, and GPIO on one device, usually under tighter memory, power, timing, and cost constraints than a desktop computer. Firmware often interacts directly with hardware registers or device drivers and may need predictable timing.
examples:
state = {"led": False, "temperature": 22.4}
print("boot", state)
commonMistakes: Designing as if the device has desktop-class memory, power, storage, and timing.
lessons.explain: A microcontroller combines a CPU, flash, RAM, timers, communication peripherals, and GPIO on one device, usually under tighter memory, power, timing, and cost constraints than a desktop computer. Firmware often interacts directly with hardware registers or device drivers and may need predictable timing.

lessons.title: GPIO: digital inputs & outputs
objectives: Model digital pin states safely
Explain pull-up logic
Debounce an input without blocking
lessons.explanation: GPIO pins can be configured as digital inputs or outputs. Inputs can float unless pull-up or pull-down resistors establish a known default level.
examples:
samples = [1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1]
stable = samples[-3:]
pressed = stable == [0, 0, 0]
print("pressed:", pressed)
commonMistakes: Reading a button or digital input without a defined pull-up/pull-down or debounce strategy, causing floating or repeated transitions to look like real events.
lessons.explain: GPIO pins can be configured as digital inputs or outputs. Inputs can float unless pull-up or pull-down resistors establish a known default level.

lessons.title: Timers, delays & interrupts
objectives: Replace long blocking delays
Model timer-driven work
Keep event handlers short
lessons.explanation: Timers provide hardware-based time measurement so firmware does not have to waste CPU cycles in long busy-wait loops. Interrupts let hardware signal that an event needs attention, but interrupt handlers should remain short because they can delay other time-sensitive work.
examples:
import asyncio

async def sample_sensor():
    for tick in range(3):
        print("sample", tick)
        await asyncio.sleep(0)

asyncio.run(sample_sensor())
commonMistakes: Using long blocking delays inside the main control loop, which prevents the device from responding to other events on time.
lessons.explain: Timers provide hardware-based time measurement so firmware does not have to waste CPU cycles in long busy-wait loops. Interrupts let hardware signal that an event needs attention, but interrupt handlers should remain short because they can delay other time-sensitive work.

lessons.title: ADC, PWM & analog signals
objectives: Interpret ADC resolution
Map sensor input to output
Explain PWM duty cycle
lessons.explanation: An ADC converts an analog voltage into a discrete digital number. Resolution determines how many distinct codes are available, while sampling rate determines how often the signal is measured.
examples:
raw = 2530
max_adc = 4095
volts = raw * (3.3 / max_adc)
duty = round(raw / max_adc * 100, 1)
print(volts, duty)
commonMistakes: Treating ADC readings and PWM output as perfectly exact analog values.
lessons.explain: An ADC converts an analog voltage into a discrete digital number. Resolution determines how many distinct codes are available, while sampling rate determines how often the signal is measured.

lessons.title: UART, I²C & SPI communication
objectives: Choose an appropriate bus
Explain addressing and clocking
Design a small device communication layer
lessons.explanation: UART, I²C, and SPI solve different communication needs. UART is asynchronous point-to-point serial communication.
commonMistakes: Mixing UART/I2C/SPI details directly into application logic.
lessons.explain: UART, I²C, and SPI solve different communication needs. UART is asynchronous point-to-point serial communication.

lessons.title: Sensors, actuators & device drivers
objectives: Build a driver boundary
Calibrate raw sensor values
Protect outputs with safe limits
lessons.explanation: A device driver translates application-level intent into the register operations or bus messages a specific sensor or actuator expects. Sensors often require calibration, scaling, unit conversion, and plausibility checks before raw readings become useful data.
commonMistakes: Using raw sensor values as trustworthy application data without calibration, unit conversion, range checks, timeout handling, or a defined safe response to device failure.
lessons.explain: A device driver translates application-level intent into the register operations or bus messages a specific sensor or actuator expects. Sensors often require calibration, scaling, unit conversion, and plausibility checks before raw readings become useful data.

lessons.title: Firmware architecture & state machines
objectives: Model device modes explicitly
Design deterministic transitions
Add a safe fault state
lessons.explanation: A state machine makes firmware behavior explicit by listing valid states, the events that cause transitions, and the actions performed on entry or transition. This is often safer than a collection of loosely related flags.
examples:
from enum import Enum
class State(Enum):
    IDLE = "idle"
    RUNNING = "running"
    FAULT = "fault"

state = State.IDLE
temperature = 82
state = State.FAULT if temperature > 70 else State.RUNNING
print(state.value)
commonMistakes: Representing modes with scattered booleans and implicit rules instead of explicit states and transitions, making impossible states and unsafe transitions hard to detect.
lessons.explain: A state machine makes firmware behavior explicit by listing valid states, the events that cause transitions, and the actions performed on entry or transition. This is often safer than a collection of loosely related flags.

lessons.title: Embedded testing & debugging
objectives: Unit-test hardware-independent logic
Use logs effectively
Plan simulation and hardware tests
lessons.explanation: Embedded testing combines ordinary unit tests with hardware-aware techniques. Logic can often be tested on a host computer or simulator, while integration tests exercise real peripherals.
examples:
def should_start(temp, interlock):
    return interlock and temp < 70

assert should_start(30, True)
assert not should_start(80, True)
print("logic tests passed")
commonMistakes: Testing only on physical hardware or only on the happy path.
lessons.explain: Embedded testing combines ordinary unit tests with hardware-aware techniques. Logic can often be tested on a host computer or simulator, while integration tests exercise real peripherals.

exercises.title: Resource-budget check
exercises.prompt: A device has 64 KB of RAM. Model a sensor buffer that stores 600 samples with 16 bytes per sample plus 8 KB for the rest of the program. Calculate the memory used, report whether it fits, and explain what you would change if the buffer exceeded the budget.

exercises.title: Debounced button press
exercises.prompt: Given a time-ordered sequence of noisy 0/1 button readings, write logic that reports one press only after the input has stayed stable for the required debounce interval. Demonstrate a bouncing press and a clean press.

exercises.title: Non-blocking periodic tasks
exercises.prompt: Simulate an embedded main loop where an LED toggles every 500 ms while a sensor is checked every 200 ms. Do not use a long blocking sleep; show from the timestamps that both periodic behaviors continue to run.

exercises.title: ADC reading to voltage
exercises.prompt: For a 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference, convert raw readings such as 0, 2048, and 4095 into voltage. Clamp or reject readings outside the valid range and explain the effect of ADC resolution.

exercises.title: PWM actuator controller
exercises.prompt: Model a PWM-controlled fan or LED that maps a 0–100% command to duty cycle. Validate invalid commands and show what output duty cycle is produced for low, medium, and maximum requests.

exercises.title: Choose the device bus
exercises.prompt: A controller must connect a debug console, several addressed sensors on two shared wires, and one high-speed local display. Decide which of UART, I2C, or SPI fits each connection and justify the wiring, addressing, and speed trade-off.

exercises.title: Calibrated sensor driver
exercises.prompt: Create a driver-style function that turns a raw sensor count into engineering units using calibration values. Detect an impossible reading or timeout and return an explicit error/fault instead of silently using bad data.

exercises.title: Controller state machine
exercises.prompt: Model IDLE, ARMED, and ALARM states. Define the events that allow each transition, reject an invalid transition, and print the state after a normal sequence and a fault sequence.

exercises.title: Watchdog-safe fault response
exercises.prompt: Simulate a control loop with a heartbeat/watchdog deadline. If the heartbeat is not updated in time, move the controller to a safe fault state and show that unsafe outputs are disabled.

exercises.title: Embedded fault-injection test
exercises.prompt: Write tests for a hardware-independent decision function by injecting a normal sensor value, an out-of-range value, and a timeout/failure. Show the expected safe behavior for each case.

exercises.title: Bounded telemetry buffer
exercises.prompt: Model a fixed-capacity telemetry/log buffer for a memory-constrained device. When the buffer fills, apply a defined policy such as dropping the oldest record, and prove the buffer never grows beyond its limit.

exercises.title: Integrated device loop
exercises.prompt: Build a small simulation combining a debounced input, periodic sensor sampling, a state-machine decision, and an actuator output. Demonstrate one normal operating sequence and one sensor/input fault without blocking the whole loop.

projects.title: Smart environmental monitor
projects.description: Build a Python simulation for temperature/light sensing, non-blocking updates, alarms, and structured logging.
requirements: Use at least two simulated sensor inputs
Add a state or fault model

projects.title: Event-driven reaction timer
projects.description: Model timers, input debouncing, and state transitions to build a precise reaction-timer simulation.

projects.title: Multi-sensor safety controller
projects.description: Create a fault-tolerant Python controller with driver boundaries, state machines, safe outputs, and tests.
requirements: Add fault handling and safe outputs

capstone.title: Production-style embedded controller simulation
capstone.description: Design a Python controller for a small device with multiple sensors and outputs, non-blocking timing, explicit fault handling, communication boundaries, and testable logic.
deliverables: Drivers + application logic + state management
At least two sensors and two outputs
Non-blocking timing model
Communication abstraction
Unit tests and a hardware/simulation test plan

careerApplications: Role-specific company use in firmware, IoT, robotics, automotive, devices, and hardware-software integration.

quiz.q: What best describes a microcontroller?
options: A CPU, memory, and peripherals integrated for dedicated control tasks
A desktop operating system running in the cloud
Only a RAM chip
A network switch

quiz.q: Why do RAM, flash, power, and timing limits matter in embedded design?
options: They determine whether the software can fit and meet the device requirements
They matter only after the product ships
Python removes all hardware limits
They affect only the display color

quiz.q: Which statement about flash and RAM is generally correct for a microcontroller?
options: Flash is typically non-volatile program/storage memory; RAM is volatile working memory
RAM is non-volatile and flash is always faster working memory
They are exactly the same resource
Neither stores program state

quiz.q: What is a pull-up or pull-down used for on a digital input?
options: To give the input a defined default level instead of leaving it floating
To increase CPU clock speed
To convert analog voltage into a digital number
To compress sensor data

quiz.q: Why is button debouncing needed?
options: One physical press can create several rapid electrical transitions
Buttons can only be read through SPI
It makes RAM non-volatile
It prevents all interrupts

quiz.q: What does edge detection look for?
options: A transition from one digital state to another
Only how long the signal stays high
The ADC voltage resolution
A network packet checksum

quiz.q: What is the main risk of a long blocking delay in a control loop?
options: Other time-sensitive work cannot run while the code is blocked
It automatically doubles CPU performance
It makes interrupts impossible on every platform
It converts PWM into ADC

quiz.q: In embedded software, interrupt latency is the time between:
options: An event occurring and the system beginning the required response
Two unrelated variable assignments
Power-on and flash programming only
Two UART characters regardless of software

quiz.q: Why use non-blocking timer/event logic?
options: To let multiple time-dependent tasks make progress without freezing the whole loop
To guarantee infinite RAM
To avoid defining any states
To replace all hardware drivers

quiz.q: What does an ADC do?
options: Converts an analog input level into a digital numeric reading
Converts Python into C++
Generates a network address
Stores code permanently

quiz.q: Increasing ADC resolution primarily gives you:
options: More discrete numeric levels across the input range
A faster CPU clock automatically
More GPIO pins
A larger UART cable

quiz.q: A 25% PWM duty cycle means the signal is active for approximately:
options: One quarter of each PWM period
All of every period
Exactly 25 volts
One quarter of the program lifetime

quiz.q: Which bus is commonly chosen for several addressed peripherals sharing two signal wires?
options: I2C
UART only
HDMI
PCIe only

quiz.q: What is a common characteristic of SPI?
options: High-speed synchronous transfers using separate clock/data lines and chip-select signals
Built-in device addressing over only two wires for every device
It requires no clock or framing agreement
It is only for internet routing

quiz.q: UART is commonly used as:
options: A simple asynchronous serial link such as a debug console or point-to-point device connection
A cache replacement policy
A CPU branch predictor
An ADC reference

quiz.q: Why put sensor/bus details behind a device driver boundary?
options: Application logic can use meaningful operations without depending on raw protocol details
It removes the need for any error handling
It guarantees every sensor is accurate
It prevents the device from using memory

quiz.q: What is calibration used for?

Changing Python indentation
Choosing a Git branch

quiz.q: What should application code do with an impossible sensor reading or timeout?
options: Handle it explicitly according to the device safety/error policy
Silently treat it as a valid normal reading

quiz.q: Why is an explicit state machine useful in firmware?
options: It makes allowed operating modes and transitions clear and testable
It eliminates all timing requirements

quiz.q: What is a watchdog intended to detect?
options: Software that has stopped making expected progress
A low-resolution ADC only

quiz.q: Deterministic control logic aims to make behavior:
options: Predictable for a given state/input and timing assumptions

quiz.q: What design choice makes embedded logic easier to unit test on a normal computer?
options: Separate pure decision/state logic from hardware I/O

Avoid functions and modules

Deleting all tests

quiz.q: A useful embedded debug log should help you reconstruct:

Only the programmer name

title: Systems Programming
blurb: Python systems programming: files, processes, threads, IPC, sockets, synchronization, and operating-system resource management.
description: Learn systems-level concepts through Python APIs and safe browser simulations.

lessons.title: Memory, lifetime & resource ownership
objectives: Distinguish object lifetime concepts
Explain deterministic cleanup
Identify resource leaks
lessons.explanation: Systems programming makes resource lifetime explicit. Stack storage typically follows scope and call lifetime, while heap objects can outlive the function that created them.
commonMistakes: Acquiring files, locks, sockets, or other resources without a guaranteed cleanup path.
lessons.explain: Systems programming makes resource lifetime explicit. Stack storage typically follows scope and call lifetime, while heap objects can outlive the function that created them.

lessons.title: References, mutability & ownership
objectives: Explain reference semantics
Avoid accidental shared mutation
Choose shallow or deep copying intentionally
lessons.explanation: A reference identifies an existing object rather than copying its full contents. With mutable objects, two names can refer to the same object, so a change through one reference can be observed through the other.
examples:
import copy
original = {"items": [1, 2]}
clone = copy.deepcopy(original)
clone["items"].append(3)
print(original, clone)
commonMistakes: Confusing assignment, shallow copy, and deep copy.
lessons.explain: A reference identifies an existing object rather than copying its full contents. With mutable objects, two names can refer to the same object, so a change through one reference can be observed through the other.

lessons.title: Files, descriptors & OS boundaries
objectives: Explain file descriptors
Handle file operations safely
Use context managers around resources
lessons.explanation: Operating systems expose files and many devices through descriptor-like handles. A program asks the kernel to read, write, open, close, or otherwise operate on those resources through system-call boundaries.
examples:
import os, tempfile
fd, path = tempfile.mkstemp()
os.write(fd, b"hello")
os.lseek(fd, 0, 0)
print(os.read(fd, 5).decode())
os.close(fd)
os.unlink(path)
commonMistakes: Assuming every read/write completes exactly as requested or ignoring OS errors.
lessons.explain: Operating systems expose files and many devices through descriptor-like handles. A program asks the kernel to read, write, open, close, or otherwise operate on those resources through system-call boundaries.

lessons.title: Processes & program execution
objectives: Explain process isolation
Launch child processes
Track exit status and output
lessons.explanation: A process is an executing program with its own address space, resources, environment, and operating-system identity. Starting a subprocess creates a separate execution context; the parent can pass arguments/environment, capture output, and inspect the exit status.
examples:
import subprocess
result = subprocess.run(["python", "-c", "print(6 * 7)"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(result.returncode, result.stdout.strip())
commonMistakes: Launching commands without checking the exit status or safely separating command arguments.
lessons.explain: A process is an executing program with its own address space, resources, environment, and operating-system identity. Starting a subprocess creates a separate execution context; the parent can pass arguments/environment, capture output, and inspect the exit status.

lessons.title: Threads, races & synchronization
objectives: Identify shared-state races
Protect shared state
Explain lock scope
lessons.explanation: Threads share process memory, which makes communication cheap but also allows data races when multiple threads access shared mutable state without safe coordination. Locks protect critical sections, condition variables let threads wait for state changes, and queues often provide a clearer ownership boundary for work.
examples:
from threading import Lock
lock = Lock()
total = 0
with lock:
    total += 1
print(total)
commonMistakes: Sharing mutable state between threads without a synchronization plan.
lessons.explain: Threads share process memory, which makes communication cheap but also allows data races when multiple threads access shared mutable state without safe coordination. Locks protect critical sections, condition variables let threads wait for state changes, and queues often provide a clearer ownership boundary for work.

lessons.title: IPC: pipes, sockets & shared memory
objectives: Compare IPC mechanisms
Design a simple message protocol
Handle ownership and failure
lessons.explanation: Inter-process communication moves information across process boundaries. Pipes provide a byte stream commonly used between related processes, sockets support local or networked communication, and shared memory can avoid copying but requires careful synchronization and a defined memory layout.
examples:
from multiprocessing import Pipe
left, right = Pipe()
left.send({"type": "job", "id": 7})
print(right.recv())
commonMistakes: Sending bytes through a pipe or socket without a framing/protocol rule.
lessons.explain: Inter-process communication moves information across process boundaries. Pipes provide a byte stream commonly used between related processes, sockets support local or networked communication, and shared memory can avoid copying but requires careful synchronization and a defined memory layout.

lessons.title: Concurrency design & worker pools
objectives: Bound concurrency
Use a task queue
Reason about backpressure
lessons.explanation: Worker pools bound concurrency by keeping a controlled number of workers that take tasks from a queue. This is different from starting an unlimited thread or process for every request.
examples:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def work(value):
    return value * value

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as pool:
    print(list(pool.map(work, [2, 3, 4, 5])))
commonMistakes: Creating unbounded workers or queues.
lessons.explain: Worker pools bound concurrency by keeping a controlled number of workers that take tasks from a queue. This is different from starting an unlimited thread or process for every request.

lessons.title: Profiling & systems debugging
objectives: Measure memory behavior
Read profiler evidence
Optimize after measuring
lessons.explanation: Profiling and debugging answer different questions. A debugger helps inspect control flow and state around a correctness failure, while a profiler measures where time or memory is actually spent.
examples:
import time
start = time.perf_counter()
result = sum(i * i for i in range(10000))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(result, round(elapsed, 6))
commonMistakes: Optimizing from intuition before measuring.
lessons.explain: Profiling and debugging answer different questions. A debugger helps inspect control flow and state around a correctness failure, while a profiler measures where time or memory is actually spent.

exercises.title: Guaranteed resource cleanup
exercises.prompt: Open a simulated resource through a context manager, deliberately raise an exception while using it, and prove that cleanup still happens. Explain why relying on a later garbage-collection cycle is not enough for OS resources.

exercises.title: Reference vs copy bug
exercises.prompt: Create nested mutable data, make both a shared reference and a copy, then change the nested value. Explain which objects changed and choose a copying strategy when independent state is required.

exercises.title: Safe low-level file I/O
exercises.prompt: Model reading and writing through a file descriptor or file object with explicit error handling and guaranteed close/cleanup. Demonstrate the normal path and a missing/unreadable file path.

exercises.title: Subprocess result handling
exercises.prompt: Run a harmless child process, capture stdout/stderr, inspect its exit status, and treat a non-zero status as a failure instead of assuming that process creation means success.

exercises.title: Process environment boundary
exercises.prompt: Launch a child process with a controlled environment value and show that changing the child environment does not mutate the parent process environment. Explain the isolation boundary.

exercises.title: Reproduce a race condition
exercises.prompt: Use multiple workers to update shared state in a deliberately unsafe way or simulated interleaving. Show the incorrect result and explain why the failure depends on timing.

exercises.title: Protect a critical section
exercises.prompt: Fix a shared-state update by protecting the smallest necessary critical section with synchronization. Compare the result with the unsafe version and explain the cost of excessive locking.

exercises.title: Producer-consumer queue
exercises.prompt: Build a producer/consumer example using a thread-safe queue. Use a clear completion signal and prove that every submitted item is processed exactly once.

exercises.title: Pipe message protocol
exercises.prompt: Design a tiny pipe/message protocol where each message has a clear delimiter or length. Parse several messages correctly and handle an incomplete message without treating it as complete.

exercises.title: Socket framing simulation
exercises.prompt: Given a byte stream where one application message can arrive in multiple chunks, reconstruct complete length-prefixed messages. Demonstrate that recv/read boundaries are not message boundaries.

exercises.title: Shared-memory coordination
exercises.prompt: Model two workers accessing shared data and identify what synchronization is required to prevent one worker from observing a partially updated state. Explain the trade-off versus isolated message passing.

exercises.title: Bounded worker pool
exercises.prompt: Process a list of tasks with a fixed maximum number of concurrent workers. Record completed results and show that worker count never exceeds the configured limit.

exercises.title: Backpressure under overload
exercises.prompt: Simulate producers generating work faster than consumers. Add a bounded queue or rejection/waiting policy and demonstrate what happens when capacity is reached instead of allowing unlimited memory growth.

exercises.title: Measure before optimizing
